5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is perhaps the most emotionally dramatic chapter in the entire Bible. It begins with a crisis — a sealed scroll that no one can open — passes through grief — John weeps uncontrollably — and arrives at an explosion of worship that fills all of heaven and earth. The transition from weeping to worship is accomplished by a single announcement: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and he can open the scroll. And when John looks for the conquering Lion, he sees — a Lamb, standing as though slaughtered.

The scroll sealed with seven seals is the interpretive key to the chapter. A scroll sealed with seven seals in the ancient world was typically a legal document of great importance: a will, a deed of purchase, or a covenant document. Most scholars understand it as the scroll of history — God’s redemptive plan for the world, the title deed to creation, the covenant document of the new age. Seven seals indicates absolute sealing: only the one who is truly worthy can break them and open what they guard. The entire drama of Revelation — the seals, the trumpets, the bowls — is the Lamb opening this scroll.

The Lion who is the Lamb — the great reversal at the heart of chapter 5 — is the christological center of Revelation and, in a sense, of the entire New Testament. John is told to look for a conquering Lion. He looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb. The conquest was accomplished through the cross. The power that governs history is the power of self-giving love. The one who has the authority to open the seals of history is the one who was willing to be the sacrifice that history required. This is the theological answer to every form of worldly power: the crucified one reigns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 put a scroll in the right hand of the one on the throne, written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Writing on both sides meant the contents were complete; seven seals was the number required for a Roman will, openable only by the rightful heir. A mighty angel heralds one question across creation — not who is strong enough but who is worthy?

Verses 3–4 answer it: nobody, in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Not the elders, not the living creatures, not Abraham or Moses or David. And John breaks down — I began to weep loudly — the only tears anyone sheds in the throne room of this book, and they are not rebuked. An unopened scroll means a world with no resolution: the martyrs never answered, Rome for ever, history running down like a clock nobody winds.

Verse 5 stops the weeping with an announcement rather than an argument: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Gen. 49:9–10; Isa. 11:1–10). The verb is the past tense of the word that ends every one of the seven letters. Whatever the churches are being asked to do, he has already done.

Verses 6–7 are the hinge of the book. John is told a Lion and sees a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain — arnion, the diminutive, a lambkin, which becomes John’s main name for Christ twenty-eight times over. The participle is perfect: a past slaughter whose marks are still present. Seven horns are complete power, seven eyes complete knowledge (Zech. 4:10). Then, without ceremony, he went and took the scroll.

Verses 8–10: the creatures and elders fall before the Lamb — worship no creature in this book may receive (19:10; 22:8–9) — holding harps and golden bowls of incense which are the prayers of the saints (cf. Ps. 141:2). The new song grounds his worthiness in his death: you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, made them a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.

Verses 11–12 widen the circle to myriads of myriads of angels (cf. Dan. 7:10) with a sevenfold ascription: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing. Verses 13–14 widen it to every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, addressing one doxology to the throne and the Lamb together; the living creatures say Amen, and the elders fall down and worship in silence.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion Is the Lamb

No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purpose until the Lion of Judah is announced — and John sees a Lamb standing, as though slain. He takes the scroll, and heaven and earth worship him who ransomed a people by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John wept at a world with no resolution; his tears were answered by a person, not an argument.

Now: No prayer offered in faith is lost; the prayers of the saints are held in golden bowls before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s right hand John sees a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and an angel asks the whole creation, “Who is worthy to open the scroll?” The scroll is God’s complete purpose for the world, and it waits not for someone strong enough but for someone worthy.

A full scroll. John is still in the throne room of chapter 4, and now notices something in God’s hand. Scrolls were normally written on one side; one written “within and on the back” is full — nothing to add, nothing left out. Ezekiel was handed such a scroll, with “words of lamentation and mourning and woe” (Ezekiel 2:10), and Daniel was told to “shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4). John’s vision is built from both.

Seven seals. Important documents, such as a Roman will, were sealed by witnesses and opened only by the one entitled to do so. Seven seals mean the document is completely shut.

What is in it? Not stated, and readers answer differently: the title deed to creation awaiting its heir; God’s decreed plan for history; the covenant inheritance of the saints. What the text shows is what happens when it is opened — the sweep of history from the cross to the end. The safest thing to say is the thing that matters most: this is God’s purpose for the world, complete and written, and at this moment shut. Feel that before explaining it. The plan exists, finished, in his hand — and it isn’t happening, because no one has opened it.

Worthy, not strong. “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?” The herald’s voice reaches heaven, earth and under the earth. Notice the question: not who is strong or clever, but who is worthy. Anyone can break wax. What is needed is someone with the right to break it. The future of the world waits not on power but on the moral standing of a person. A test: when you long for the world — or your own life — to be put right, do you look for power to fix it, or for the One who is worthy?

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one in heaven, on earth or under the earth could open the scroll, and John wept loudly. Without someone worthy, God’s purposes would stay sealed and the world would never be put right — and John’s grief over that is not rebuked.

A complete search. “In heaven or on earth or under the earth” — the ancient way of saying everywhere: the powers above, the living, the dead. It returns nothing. Not the elders or the living creatures who never take their eyes off God, nor the myriads of angels. On earth, every philosopher, reformer, general and king. Under the earth, every saint who died in faith. Abraham wasn’t worthy. Moses wasn’t. David, who wrote many of the songs sung in that room, wasn’t.

The only tears in the throne room. Nowhere else in this book does anyone in heaven weep, and near the end God “will wipe away every tear” (21:4). John didn’t become quietly emotional; he sobbed, and the tense suggests he kept on.

Why such grief? John grasps what a closed scroll means. If no one opens it, the martyrs under the altar are never answered, Rome goes on forever, the seven churches dwindle one by one, and nothing in God’s sealed purposes comes to anything — injustice with no verdict, suffering with no meaning, history running down like an unwound clock.

A grief believers know. It settles on someone reading the news for the fortieth year and noticing the same things keep happening, or on a woman standing in a cemetery in a country where nobody was ever tried for what was done. It is the despair of suspecting the world isn’t going anywhere.

Not rebuked. John doesn’t tell himself it will probably work out, or console himself with the throne in front of him. He weeps in heaven, before God, and Scripture records it without embarrassment. Nothing in this book calls grief over a world out of joint a failure of faith. And the weeping is answered — not by an argument, and nobody tells him he overreacted. A test: have you brought your grief over the world’s wrongs to God honestly, or hidden it as if it were unbelief?

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An elder tells John to stop weeping: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and so can open the scroll. The promised King has already won the victory that gives him the right to carry out God’s plan, and comfort comes through an announcement about him.

Two royal titles. Both carry Israel’s deepest hopes for a king. “The Lion of the tribe of Judah” recalls Jacob’s blessing: “Judah is a lion’s cub… The scepter shall not depart from Judah… until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Genesis 49:9–10). “The Root of David” recalls Isaiah’s shoot from the stump of Jesse, on whom the Spirit would rest, who would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:1–4, 10). The royal lion, and the living root of a dynasty cut down to a stump.

Already won. “Has conquered” — past tense, the same verb as the promise “to the one who conquers” that ends every letter. Whatever the churches are asked to do, he has done, and it is finished.

Earned, not inherited. He can open the scroll because he has conquered. The right to unroll God’s purposes wasn’t his merely by rank; it was won. Somewhere in history a battle was fought, and its outcome is why anything in this book is about to happen.

Hold the Lion for one more sentence. The elder has just announced, in the Old Testament’s most muscular language, that the conqueror has arrived. What John sees next is something else entirely — and that is the hinge of the whole book.

“Weep no more.” Not “you were wrong to weep” or “compose yourself.” The tears aren’t criticised; they are ended — by news about a person, not advice. That is the shape of real Christian comfort. Nobody is talked out of grief by being told things aren’t so bad. Grief stops when someone walks into the room. A test: when you comfort a grieving friend, do you offer arguments, or point them to Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John turns to see the Lion and sees instead a Lamb, standing, yet bearing the marks of slaughter, with seven horns and seven eyes; and the Lamb takes the scroll from God’s hand. Christ conquered by dying, and the crucified and risen Lamb alone has the right and the power to carry out God’s plan for history.

Told a Lion, he sees a Lamb. This substitution is the key to the whole book. Revelation keeps speaking of conquest, war, thrones and armies for seventeen more chapters, and this verse defines what every one of those words means. The Lion conquers as a Lamb. The victory was won by dying.

A lamb. John’s word is arnion, not the amnos of John 1:29; it was in origin a diminutive, and he uses it twenty-eight times of Christ until it becomes his main name for him. In the most thunderous book in the Bible, the conqueror is named with one of the gentlest words available.

Standing, as though slain. Two impossible things in one clause. “Slain” is the word for cutting a sacrificial animal’s throat — slaughtered, not merely killed — and the form means a past act whose result remains. The wounds aren’t a memory; they are present. He stands, risen and alive, and is visibly, permanently, the slaughtered Lamb.

The marks are the credential. The one thing never erased from the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. When Thomas needed proof, the risen Christ showed not a restored body but a wounded one (John 20:27). Heaven hasn’t tidied away the crucifixion. The marks are what the whole company falls down before.

Seven horns, seven eyes. A horn is strength; seven is complete power. Seven eyes, the sevenfold Spirit, is complete knowledge, from Zechariah: “the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:10). The little Lamb is all-powerful and all-knowing — a picture deliberately impossible to draw. It is meant not to be sketched but believed.

He takes the scroll. The sentence is flat, almost domestic, after six verses of held breath. No challenge, no ceremony. He walks up and takes it, and that reaching hand unlocks the future of the world. Heaven, earth and the grave were searched and every candidate failed on worth; then a Lamb with its throat cut walks out from among the elders and takes the scroll from God’s hand. A test: when you picture Christ’s power, do you picture the wounds? His strength and his cross are not two things.
verseByVerse.note: The Lion of v. 5 turns out to be a slain Lamb. Horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb takes the scroll, the living creatures and elders fall down before him with harps and with bowls of incense — the prayers of the saints — and sing a new song: he is worthy because he was slain and by his blood ransomed people from every nation, making them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth. The Lamb receives the worship due to God, our prayers are kept before him, and his death actually purchased a worldwide people.

Worship given to the Lamb. The posture given to the One on the throne in chapter 4 is given to the Lamb, without explanation or objection — in a book where an angel twice refuses worship outright (19:10; 22:8–9). No creature may receive it. The Lamb receives it in the Father’s presence, and heaven approves.

The prayers of the saints. Incense rose daily in the temple, and the Psalms supply the picture: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2). Here it is literal. Ordinary Christians’ prayers are in golden bowls in the throne room, held by the highest creatures, at the moment the scroll is opened. Take it concretely: the prayer of a believer in Smyrna the night before a hearing; a slave’s prayer in Laodicea nobody knew of; the distracted, badly worded prayer at your kitchen table that seemed to hit the ceiling and slide down the wall. None evaporated. They were collected, and the bowls are full.

Prayers that return. At 8:3–5 those prayers, with incense, are thrown back to earth and become thunder, lightning and earthquake. Prayers that seemed to achieve nothing come down again as the opening of God’s judgment. Nothing prayed in faith is wasted. A test: what have you stopped praying for because nothing seemed to happen? Start again; it is in the bowl.

A new song. Scripture calls for a new song when God does something unprecedented (Psalm 96:1; Isaiah 42:10). Chapter 4’s song was about creation; this one answers v. 2’s question, and the ground of worth isn’t power but death: “for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God.” “Ransomed” is the slave-market word: to buy someone out of ownership at a price, named here — his blood. The scope is fourfold, “from every tribe and language and people and nation,” a phrase John uses seven times, in varying order, as if to stop anyone making it a fixed list. And it is people who are bought, one by one, out of every group.

Does “by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe” teach that Christ died for a particular people? Reformed Christians read it so: Christ’s blood actually ransomed a people from every nation, not merely made salvation possible for all. Others hold that his death was for everyone and becomes effective through faith. The more likely reading is the first, since the song praises what his blood achieved; and it is a people from every nation, so the offer goes to every nation.

A kingdom and priests, on the earth. As in 1:6, from Sinai (Exodus 19:6), and already done: “you have made them.” Believers reign with Christ now in a real but hidden way. Premillennial Christians see “they shall reign on the earth” as the thousand-year reign; the more likely reading is that it is completed on the renewed earth (22:5) — the question is taken up at chapter 20. Either way, the destination of the redeemed isn’t escape from the material world but this earth made new, with the ransomed reigning on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Countless angels encircle the throne and cry, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain,” to receive every honour. The whole of heaven declares that the crucified Christ deserves everything there is — and the ground they give is his death.

Beyond counting. A myriad is ten thousand, the largest number Greek had a single word for, so “myriads of myriads” is the language running out. Daniel used the same expression of the Ancient of Days: “a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10). The ring of worshippers extends beyond counting, and they were singing out there all the while John wept.

Seven gifts. “Power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing” — seven, the complete set. Everything there is to give is given to a slaughtered Lamb. The list runs through every currency the Roman world traded in, sung for congregations shut out of guilds, fined and boycotted. They are told where all seven belong.

Two songs, the gospel between them. In chapter 4: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God,” grounded in creation. Here: “Worthy is the Lamb,” grounded in the cross. One throne, and the second song couldn’t have been sung before Calvary.

A line angels can’t sing. Verse 9’s song is sung by those ransomed by his blood; the angels sing of a redemption they have watched but not received — things “into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12). An unfallen angel’s honour doesn’t include being bought. The forgiven sinner in the back row of an ordinary church has a line in this song Gabriel can’t sing. A test: do you sing of redemption as someone who has been bought?

The argument is a wound. Not worthy to be pitied or remembered, but to receive everything — and heaven’s reason isn’t his seven horns or seven eyes but that he was slain. Ten thousand times ten thousand voices, and the argument they make is a wound.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every creature everywhere joins the praise of the One on the throne and the Lamb together, the living creatures say “Amen,” and the elders fall down in worship. All creation will acknowledge the Father and the Son as one, and the scroll the world waited for is in the hand that was pierced.

Full circle. The same three regions searched in v. 3, with the sea added. There the search found no one worthy; here the whole of it sings. A chapter that began with a silence that made a man weep ends with every created thing — the living, the dead, the powers above and whatever is in the deep — making one sound.

One doxology, two recipients. “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” Chapter 4 worshipped the One on the throne; chapter 5 the Lamb; now both are addressed together in one sentence, with no distinction, and no one finds it a problem. The Trinity isn’t argued anywhere in Revelation. It is simply what worship in heaven looks like.

Blessing first. To bless God is to speak well of him, to say back to him what he is — the one thing creation can give that God doesn’t already have.

Amen, and silence. The creatures nearest the throne add nothing; they agree. The elders fall down, crowns already on the floor, and John records no further word.

What changed. Fourteen verses ago: a sealed scroll, an unanswerable question, and a man weeping in heaven. Now every creature says the same thing at once. Nothing changed in between except that a Lamb walked forward and took a scroll.

Every seal by the pierced hand. The seals are about to break: conquest, war, famine, death, the souls under the altar, the sky rolled up. Every one is opened by the hand that was pierced. Whatever rides out of this scroll rides at the Lamb’s word, and goes no further than he permits. A test: what is riding out against you or your world right now? It came out of a scroll in his hand. Trust him with it, and join the song today.

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
The Lamb begins to open the seven seals, and with each seal a new dimension of history is revealed. The first four seals release the famous Four Horsemen — one of the most powerful images in Western literature. The fifth seal lifts the veil on the souls of the martyrs beneath the heavenly altar and their agonizing cry: “How long, O Lord?” The sixth seal unleashes cosmic convulsion on a terrified earth. The seventh seal — which will bring complete silence in heaven — is withheld until chapter 8.

Interpretive flag — Sequential or Recapitulatory? This is the second major structural decision point of Revelation. The sequential reading (predominant in dispensational premillennialism) understands the seals, trumpets, and bowls as three successive series of events: the seals run their course, then the trumpets begin, then the bowls pour out — covering the seven-year tribulation in ascending severity. The recapitulatory reading (predominant in amillennial/idealist interpretation) understands the three series as parallel sweeps, each covering the same period (the church age and/or the final tribulation) from different vantage points and with increasing intensity. Several features of the text favor recapitulation: (1) the sixth seal already appears to describe the final judgment (vv. 12–17), yet the narrative continues; (2) the sixth trumpet and sixth bowl also appear to describe the same climactic events; (3) the interludes (chapters 7, 10–11) break the sequential pattern; (4) the phrase “the great day of their wrath has come” (v. 17) sounds like a finale, yet much remains. The seals are read here as the first of three parallel sweeps, with the sequential reading noted respectfully.

The Four Horsemen are among the most theologically misread images in Revelation. They are not four distinct events in a future tribulation timeline. They are the recurring instruments of divine governance that have marked history since the fall: war, internecine conflict, famine, and death. They describe the ongoing reality of a fallen world under the Lord’s providential judgment — not unprecedented novelties but the intensified concentration of what the church has always known. The question the martyrs ask — “How long?” — is the question the church has been asking since Abel’s blood first cried from the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature calls Come! with a voice like thunder, and a white horse rides out whose rider has a bow and a crown that was given to him. Whether that rider is Christ, the gospel’s advance, or conquest itself is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse. Verses 3–4: a bright red horse, whose rider is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people should slay one another — mutual killing, the neighbour with the knife — and is given a great sword.

Verses 5–6: a black horse, its rider holding scales, and a voice from the midst of the living creatures quoting the price list. A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was one man’s daily ration. A labourer in full work can feed himself and nobody else. Do not harm the oil and wine sets a limit on the famine and also describes its injustice: bread is rationed while the luxury trade goes on undisturbed.

Verses 7–8: a pale horse — chlōros, the green of a corpse — and the only rider who is named. Death rides, and Hades follows to collect. They are given authority over a fourth of the earth, with the four instruments of Ezekiel 14:21. The fraction matters: the trumpets will touch a third, and only at the end does anything become total.

Verses 9–11 break the pattern: no horse, no rider. Under the altar, where the blood of every sacrifice was poured out (Lev. 4:7), are the souls of those slain — esphagmenōn, the word used of the Lamb at 5:6. They cry how long? like a third of the psalter. Verse 11 answers with a white robe each, permission to rest, and a reason for the delay that is very hard: until the number of their brothers who are to die in the same way is complete.

Verses 12–14: the sixth seal removes every fixed point in the universe — earthquake, sun black as sackcloth (goat hair, so the comparison is exact), moon like blood (Joel 2:31), stars falling like the winter figs a gale brings down, the sky rolled up (Isa. 34:4), every mountain and island moved. Verses 15–17: seven classes of people, from kings down to slaves, hide in caves and beg the mountains to fall on them — choosing burial over being looked at — and the chapter ends on an unanswered question: who can stand?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seals in the Lamb’s Hand

Conquest, war, famine and death ride out only when the Lamb opens the seals, and every one of them is given or permitted within a limit. The martyrs cry “How long?” and are robed and told to rest; the sixth seal removes every fixed point but the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches met the red horse and the pale one without being told why.

Now: Crying out for justice is not unbelief; handing vengeance to God is obedience. And who can stand? Those washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature thunders “Come!”, and a rider on a white horse goes out with a bow and a given crown, conquering. Every trouble that follows is released by Christ’s own hand and goes only as far as God permits.

Who opens it. “The Lamb opened one of the seven seals.” Not an angel, fate or an enemy. Every horror in this chapter is released by the hand that was pierced. Heaven speaks first — a living creature calls “Come!” — and earth responds.

Nothing takes itself. Watch the passive verbs: a crown “was given,” the rider “was permitted,” he “was given a great sword,” they “were given authority.” Four times. Nothing here seizes its own power.

Seals, trumpets and bowls — in sequence, or in parallel? The seals are the first of three sevens, and how a reader relates them shapes the whole book. On the recapitulation reading — Augustine, Hendriksen, Beale and the amillennial tradition — the three series are parallel passes over the same history, from the cross to the last day, each more intense. In favour: all three end at the same place — the sky rolled up and kings hiding (6:12–17); “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord” (11:15); “It is done!” (16:17). Three arrivals at the end are hard to fit on one line. On the sequential reading — the futurist and dispensational tradition, set out by Walvoord and MacArthur — the three follow in order and describe a defined future tribulation. In favour: the seventh seal opens onto the trumpets (8:1–2); the fractions escalate from a fourth (6:8) to a third (8:7–12) to everything (16:3); and the text never says it is starting over. Many hold that the series both overlap and advance, spiralling. The more likely reading is recapitulation with progression, and the visions are read that way here, with the alternative noted. Either way the point stands: whoever these riders are and whenever they ride, the Lamb sends them.

Who is the white rider? Many take him as Christ or the gospel’s victorious advance: white is holiness throughout Revelation; Christ rides a white horse at 19:11; “conquering” is the verb used of him at 5:5; and the gospel goes out first (Mark 13:10). Many others take him as conquest itself, or an antichrist who imitates Christ: his crown is a victor’s wreath, while the rider of 19:12 wears many royal diadems; his crown is given to him; he carries a bow, while Christ’s weapon in this book is the sword from his mouth; and the other three riders are plain disasters, so it would be odd for the first of a matched set to be the Saviour. The second reading is the stronger, though careful readers hold the first.

The furniture of a fallen world. The four ride together as one picture: conquest, then war, then famine, then death — the order in which they actually arrive. They have been riding since the first century. A test: when you hear of a new war, do you read it as proof God has lost control, or as one of the riders let out on a leash by the Lamb?
verseByVerse.note: The four horsemen draw on Zechariah’s visions. Some take the white rider to be Christ (compare 19:11); many see him as conquest, the first of four judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the second seal a fiery red horse rides out, permitted to take peace from the earth so that people kill one another. War and civil bloodshed are real evils, yet they happen only by God’s permission and within his control.

Peace taken away. The horse is fiery red. The first rider went out to conquer, and what follows conquest isn’t peace. Notice: the rider doesn’t bring war; he takes peace away, which assumes peace was there as a gift. A town where shops open, a night without sirens, children walking to school isn’t the natural state that occasionally breaks down. It is a mercy extended, and it can be withdrawn. A test: when did you last thank God for an ordinary peaceful day?

On a leash. “Was permitted” — the second of the chapter’s divine passives. Nothing here is out of control. That is a hard comfort, not an easy one: Scripture doesn’t say God is doing his best against forces he can’t restrain. Even the horse of war rides on a permission.

One another. “So that people should slay one another” — mutual killing: civil war, the neighbour with the knife, a country turning on itself. The twentieth century, the bloodiest yet, did much of its killing that way: citizens against their own, in Rwanda, Cambodia, the Soviet countryside, the Balkans.

A great sword. The word is the short blade of ordinary official violence, the same used of the state’s sword in Romans 13:4 — handed here to a horseman whose only business is killing.

If God permits this, is he responsible? Scripture holds two things and releases neither. God is never the author of evil, and no one who takes up a sword can plead that heaven made him do it. And nothing happens outside God’s rule, including this. Joseph said both in one sentence: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The brothers were guilty; God wasn’t idle.

The difference it makes. Watching news of war, a believer can hold one of two things. Either the world has slipped its moorings and God is off-stage hoping — so there is nothing to pray for and no end to expect. Or the red horse rides on a permission granted in the throne room, before a rainbow, by a Lamb with the marks on him. The second is harder to look at, and the only one with hope in it. Pray accordingly.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the third seal a black horse comes, its rider holding scales, while a voice announces famine prices — a day’s wage for a day’s wheat — but forbids harm to the oil and wine. Famine follows war, it falls hardest on the poor while luxuries carry on, and even its limits are set from God’s throne.

Famine follows the army. Fields trampled, men conscripted off the land, granaries emptied, roads unsafe. Famine is usually not a separate disaster; it is the second half of a war.

Scales. Grain weighed out is grain rationed, as the prophets warned: “ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven and shall dole out your bread again by weight” (Leviticus 26:26; cf. Ezekiel 4:16).

The price list. “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius.” A denarius was a labourer’s day’s wage (Matthew 20:2); a quart of wheat about one person’s daily ration. In normal times it bought several times as much. Do the sum as a first-century hearer would: a man works dawn to dusk and earns enough to feed himself, and nothing for his wife and children. Switching to coarse barley, he gets three days’ worth, and the family eats badly and is still hungry. Not bodies in the street, but something more familiar and grinding: a man in full work who can’t feed his household.

“Do not harm the oil and wine.” Often read as a limit on the famine, and limits are set throughout this chapter. But olives and vines are deep-rooted and survive what destroys grain, and both were the produce of estates. The line describes the injustice of every food crisis: bread trebles in price while the luxury trade goes on. The rich man’s cellar is untouched while a labourer counts grain by weight outside. Famines are rarely a simple lack of food; they are a failure of access, and those who die are those who can’t pay. A test: does your comfort make you blind to those for whom bread is the whole budget? Give to them this week.

From the throne. The voice comes “in the midst of the four living creatures,” from God’s immediate presence. The famine isn’t a gap in his attention. Its boundary was drawn in the throne room.
verseByVerse.note: A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was about one person’s daily ration — famine prices.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fourth seal a pale horse rides out, its rider named Death with Hades following, given authority over a fourth of the earth to kill by sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts. Death is real and terrible, but limited, and the One who opened the seal holds its keys.

Pale. The word is the yellow-green of vegetation; used of a body, the colour of a corpse. Elsewhere in the New Testament it is the green of grass. Here, the green of a face.

Named. The only rider with a name: “Death, and Hades followed him.” Hades is the realm of the dead, receiving what Death takes — one kills, the other collects. And the reader has heard both names before: the risen Christ said, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18). The two who ride out at the fourth seal are the two whose keys hang on the belt of the One who opened it. At 20:14 both are thrown into the lake of fire.

A fourth, not all. “Authority over a fourth of the earth” — the fourth divine passive, now with a fraction. It is easy to read past a number in a list of horrors. Death is given a portion, not the whole. Later the trumpets touch a third (8:7–12); only at the very end is anything total. The judgments escalate because they are measured out by Someone, in stages, with a purpose — stated later, when the rest of mankind “did not repent” (9:20–21). These aren’t the death-throes of an abandoned world but warnings loud enough to be heard. A test: when death comes close — a diagnosis, a funeral — do you hear it as a warning and an invitation to turn to God?

Covenant judgments. The four instruments come almost directly from Ezekiel’s “four disastrous acts of judgment, sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence” (Ezekiel 14:21) — the standing vocabulary of covenant judgment every reader of the prophets knew.

The whole age. The horsemen follow the order of Jesus’ warnings — wars, famines, and what he called “the beginning of the birth pains” (Matthew 24:6–8). That supports reading the seals as troubles that mark the whole age before the end, not only a final period. Not a coded map of the twenty-first century, but the ordinary, terrible furniture of history — conquest, civil war, hunger, death — each riding at the Lamb’s word, on a permission, within a fraction, before a throne.

Not an explanation, an identity. The churches of Asia were about to meet the red and pale horses personally. What they were given wasn’t an explanation of why. It was the identity of the hand on the seal.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fifth seal John sees under the altar the souls of those killed for God’s word, crying, “How long before you will judge and avenge our blood?” Martyrs’ deaths are offerings God honours, the faithful dead are alive and conscious with him, and it is right to ask God for justice.

A congregation. No horse, no rider, no “Come!” The camera leaves earth, and John sees a congregation. “Slain” is the same word used of the Lamb at 5:6; what was done to Christ has been done to them.

Under the altar. In the temple the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7), and “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). These people lie where the blood of the offerings went. Their deaths weren’t waste but an offering, placed where an offering belongs. Paul used the same image of his own death: “I am already being poured out as a drink offering” (2 Timothy 4:6).

Where are they now? A question asked at every Christian funeral, settled in passing. Between death and resurrection, believers are conscious, with God, able to speak — and not yet complete, because the body is still in the ground. Paul: “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23). Not unconscious; not yet finished; with him. A test: when you grieve a believer, do you picture them as gone, or as with Christ? Let this verse shape the picture.

How long? “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long…?” This is the cry of the psalms of complaint — “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1); “how long shall the wicked exult?” (Psalm 94:3) — which make up a large part of the Psalter. “Sovereign Lord” is the word for an absolute master; their complaint is precisely that he has the power to act and hasn’t yet.

Should believers pray for vengeance? Christ said to love enemies and pray for persecutors (Matthew 5:44), and Stephen died asking that the sin not be held against them (Acts 7:60). Four things settle it. First, they ask God to act, not to act themselves: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19) is a command to hand the matter over, not to pretend it doesn’t exist. Second, they name no one and ask no particular punishment; they ask the judge to judge. Third, they ask not for private satisfaction but for justice, which God has promised; a universe that shrugs at murder isn’t kind. Fourth, the two prayers aren’t rivals: Christ prayed for his executioners and also promised that every hidden thing will be revealed (Luke 12:2–3). The one who repents is forgiven; the one who doesn’t is judged. Praying for both is the whole gospel.

A burden lifted. Anyone seriously wronged — assaulted, defrauded, lied about, bereaved by someone never charged — often carries two burdens: the injury, and guilt for still minding. This verse removes the second. The holiest company in Scripture, in God’s presence, ask aloud how long justice will take, and no one tells them to stop. Bring your own “how long” to him in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each martyr receives a white robe and is told to rest a little longer, until the full number of fellow servants who will also be killed is complete. God vindicates his people now, gives them rest, and delays final judgment for a purpose — a number known to him, and time for enemies to be brought in.

A robe before an answer. They asked “how long?” and are given a garment and a word. The white robe was promised to Sardis (3:4–5), worn by the elders (4:4) and the multitude (7:9), and 7:14 says where the whiteness comes from — “washed… in the blood of the Lamb.” So it isn’t a reward for dying well but the court’s verdict delivered early. Whatever earthly courts said — and some of these people were executed as criminals under due process — heaven has dressed them in innocence. And “each”: a robe apiece, not a blanket amnesty.

Rest. Not “grit your teeth,” but permission to stop working. Their part is done. Whatever remains to be done about the wrong done to them is no longer their assignment.

A little longer. There is an end, and God calls the wait short — a measurement taken from where the arithmetic looks different than it does from a cell.

The hard part. “Until the number of their fellow servants… should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.” The delay isn’t administrative. God waits because more are to come and will die the same way. The answer to “how long until you avenge our blood?” is: until the rest of your brothers have shed theirs. That shouldn’t be softened.

Two things alongside it. First, God has a number, known to him — not a casualty estimate but a roll. No one in it is an accident; no one outside it is taken by mistake. Second, the delay is working on the other side of the ledger: every year judgment waits, an enemy of God can be brought in. The man who wrote much of the New Testament’s teaching on grace once watched over the coats at the first martyrdom (Acts 7:58; 8:1). The patience the martyrs are asked to accept is the patience that produced Paul. A test: who do you think is beyond God’s reach? Pray for them today; the delay may be for them.

Enough. The fifth seal doesn’t answer the timing question, and it is honest enough not to pretend. It gives a verdict delivered early, an end that is fixed, and a reason for the wait that isn’t indifference. For a congregation in Smyrna expecting arrests, that was the comfort available, and it has been enough for every generation since.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the sixth seal a great earthquake strikes, the sun goes black, the moon turns to blood, the stars fall, the sky rolls up like a scroll, and every mountain and island moves. Everything people treat as fixed and permanent will be shaken loose, leaving only God’s throne.

The stage struck. Six things go, from the ground upward: earth, sun, moon, stars, sky, mountains and islands.

Every image is quoted. “Black as sackcloth” — sackcloth was woven from dark goat hair, so the comparison is exact. Joel: “The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes” (Joel 2:31), quoted by Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:20). The sky rolled up like a scroll comes from Isaiah 34:4.

Literal, or the end of worlds? The prophets used this language of historical catastrophes. Isaiah’s darkened sun and stars describe the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:1, 10); Ezekiel’s darkened heavens, Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7–8); Isaiah 34’s rolled-up sky, Edom. In each case cosmos-collapsing language describes what it feels like when an empire that seemed permanent ends. So some take the sixth seal as the literal end of the physical universe at the close of a sequence; others, on the prophets’ precedent, as the recurring end of worlds — the day an empire falls — reaching its final instance at the last day. The recapitulation reading favours the second and is the more likely. Both agree what the language is for: when everything you treated as fixed is removed, it feels exactly like the sky being rolled up.

The fig tree. John’s own detail: the stars fall “as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale.” Late figs that never ripen hang on through winter, hard and green, and the first real storm brings them down. A homely image dropped into cosmic catastrophe, it reduces the stars — which sailors steered by, astrologers consulted and emperors were named after — to windfall.

Every fixed point. The ground that doesn’t move; the sun that always rises; the stars you find your way home by; mountains, the definition of permanence. In three verses, gone. That is aimed at people under pressure from something that looks immovable. A test: what in your life feels most immovable — an institution, your health, your savings, a threat? Hold it loosely; only one thing is permanent.

The throne isn’t in the list. Chapter 4 established the one fixed point; chapter 6 removes every rival. When the sky is rolled up there will be one thing left standing, and it is the thing described first.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone from kings to slaves hides in caves, begging the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of wrath has come — “and who can stand?” No status protects anyone on the day of judgment; the only refuge is the Lamb whose wrath it is.

From the top down. Kings, great ones, generals, the rich, the powerful — and then everyone, “slave and free,” the two words that divided the Roman world. Seven categories, the complete list. Every category that ordinarily protects a person is named first and named uselessly. A king has an army, a general is the army, the rich can buy their way out of most things. On this day the emperor and the man he owns end up behind the same rock.

Preferring burial. “Fall on us and hide us.” Given the choice between being crushed and being looked at, they choose the crushing. Hosea recorded the same cry (Hosea 10:8), and Jesus quoted it to the women weeping on the road to the cross (Luke 23:30).

The face. What they flee isn’t fire or an army but a face. No one may see it and live (Exodus 33:20). Israel’s great blessing was “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25). The hope of this book is that his servants “will see his face” (22:4). The same face, and here people beg geology to spare them from it.

The wrath of the Lamb. The two words shouldn’t fit. Lambs don’t have wrath — and that is the counterpart of 5:5–6: there John was told a Lion and shown a Lamb; here the Lamb is what people flee. Not a mild Christ who finally lost his temper, but the same Lamb with the same wounds, the wrath being the other face of the love that bore them. Nothing is more terrible than mercy refused long enough.

Who can stand? The chapter’s last words are a real question, and the next chapter answers it: the 144,000 sealed and a multitude no one can count, “standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (7:9).

Two places to stand. The chapter says plainly the world will be shaken, and has been since the first horse rode out. The question is where you will be when the last fixed point goes, and the text gives two options: behind a rock, or before the throne in a white robe. The difference isn’t courage or achievement. The multitude “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). The wrath they are spared is the Lamb’s, and so is the blood that spares them. A test: are you trusting your standing, your record or your goodness to hold up that day — or the Lamb’s blood alone?
