Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh trumpet sounds and heaven proclaims, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever,” and the elders worship God for taking his power and beginning to reign. The outcome of history is settled: Christ’s kingdom has already won, and it will be fully visible at his coming.

An announcement. Six trumpets brought hail, blood, wormwood, darkness, locusts and cavalry. The seventh brings an announcement — the sentence the whole book has climbed toward. Those who know Handel have heard it sung; the singing can carry a person past what it actually says.

One kingdom. “The kingdom of the world” — singular, not “kingdoms” as older translations had it. One worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands.

“Has become.” A completed act. Heaven doesn’t say the world will become God’s or is becoming his, but announces a transfer already made — a herald reading out a result, not a forecast.

The ending first. Eleven chapters remain. The dragon hasn’t appeared, neither beast has risen, Babylon hasn’t fallen, the white horse hasn’t ridden out. The outcome is declared before the conflict is described — the single most important structural fact about Revelation. It isn’t a thriller with the ending in doubt, but the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb.

Living inside a victory. The first hearers were told the empire would worsen, a beast would rule every tribe, and they would be conquered and killed. And in the middle: the kingdom of the world has already changed owners. They weren’t asked to hope for a victory but to live inside one not yet made visible. A test: do you face this week as one hoping Christ might win, or as one who knows he has?

A word left out. The divine title has been threefold from the start: “who is and who was and who is to come” (1:4, 8; 4:8). Here it is twofold: “who is and who was.” The third term is gone. Not an oversight: the One who is to come has come. The title held a future tense while there was a future to wait for, and at the seventh trumpet it drops out of God’s name.

Taken. “You have taken your great power and begun to reign.” He was always sovereign; what changes is that his reign becomes visible and unopposed. And the elders’ response isn’t analysis. Twenty-four figures with thrones of their own get off them and put their faces on the floor.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders sing that the nations raged but God’s wrath has come: the time to judge the dead, reward his servants great and small, and destroy the destroyers of the earth. Then God’s heavenly temple opens and the ark of his covenant is seen. God will judge justly, reward every faithful servant, and keep his covenant forever.

The raging answered. “The nations raged” quotes Psalm 2: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” — kings set against the LORD and his Anointed, God laughing and installing his King on Zion. Revelation has quoted that psalm since 2:27. Here it reports the raging in the past tense. It was answered.

Wrath and judgment. “Your wrath came” — one clause, not dwelt on, in a book that has spent six chapters on judgment. Then “the time for the dead to be judged”: everyone, including all who died thinking the matter closed. Nothing has been filed away.

Rewards for small and great. The longest clause, and its generosity is the point. Prophets, saints, and simply “those who fear your name” — and then a phrase that won’t let anyone be ranked out: “both small and great.” No tiers. The witnesses who shut the sky and the widow who kept praying and never told anyone are in the same sentence. And it is “rewarding”: God means to give people things for what they did, and the New Testament isn’t embarrassed about it (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 3:14; Hebrews 11:6). Grace doesn’t abolish reward; it is why reward is possible at all. A test: what hidden faithfulness are you tempted to think goes unnoticed? He has it in his book.

Destroying the destroyers. The same root twice, as the English keeps it. Those who ruined the world are ruined. The sentence is the crime, said back.

The ark. For a Jewish reader the most astonishing sentence in the chapter. The ark stood in the Most Holy Place, seen by one man once a year. It vanished when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC, and Jeremiah had said a day would come when no one would speak of it or miss it (Jeremiah 3:16). For nearly seven hundred years Israel’s holiest object had simply been gone. Here it is, in the temple in heaven, in plain view, doors open. The ark held the covenant tablets under a lid where blood was sprinkled yearly. To see it is to be told the covenant was never lost when the building fell, that God has kept his side, and that the place where blood was applied for sin is still in the room. The chapter that began by measuring a temple and leaving part to be trampled ends by opening the real one.

The storm grows. Lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake, hail: three elements at 4:5, four at 8:5, five here. The nations raged; his wrath came; the covenant stands open in the light.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there,<sup>2</sup>but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.<sup>3</sup>And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.”<sup>4</sup>These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.<sup>6</sup>They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.<sup>7</sup>And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them,<sup>8</sup>and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.<sup>9</sup>For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb,<sup>10</sup>and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.<sup>12</sup>Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.<sup>13</sup>And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.<sup>14</sup>The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.<sup>15</sup>Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”<sup>16</sup>And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God,<sup>17</sup>saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.<sup>18</sup>The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.”<sup>19</sup>Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a great sign — John says so before he describes anything — a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, pregnant and screaming in labour. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph’s dream, where Jacob himself supplies the key (Gen. 37:9–10): this is the covenant people, from whom the Messiah comes.

Verses 3–4: another sign, a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven diadems — royal crowns, not the victor’s wreath the woman wears, and the crowns that belong by right to the rider of 19:12. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars, and he stands in front of the woman waiting to devour the child.

Verse 5: she bears a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9) — and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years pass in a comma, because from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report but total failure.

Verse 6: the woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert — which is the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman — the covenant people, Israel and the church — bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, crowned with twelve stars, crying out in labour. She is the people of God — Israel from whom the Messiah came, continued in the church — glorious in heaven’s sight and suffering on earth, with pain that is going somewhere.

The war behind the war. Chapters 1–11 showed what happens on earth and in heaven as the scroll opens; chapter 12 pulls the curtain back further and shows why. From here to chapter 20 the reader watches the dragon, his two beasts and their city, and this chapter introduces them.

A sign. John says so before describing anything — his standing courtesy: this stands for something; read it as a sign.

Who is she? Joseph dreamed of the sun, moon and eleven stars bowing to him, and his father understood at once: Jacob, his mother, and the brothers (Genesis 37:9–10). Add Joseph and there are twelve. Sun, moon and twelve stars is Israel, the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes. Some take the woman as Mary, and she is in the picture: a real woman bore the child of v. 5. But this woman outlives the child’s ascension, flees to the wilderness, is pursued for 1,260 days, and has other offspring “who keep the commandments of God” (v. 17). That isn’t a biography. She is God’s covenant people — Israel, out of whom Christ came, and the church, the same people continued.

Glory and agony at once. Clothed with the sun, and crying out in birth pains. That is the whole doctrine of the people of God in one picture. From heaven the church is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars. From the street she is a woman in labour, making a great deal of noise, with something enormous waiting for her. Both are accurate. A believer shown only the first won’t recognise his own church; one who has seen only the second won’t believe there is anything else to see.

Pain with an outcome. Birth pain in Scripture is never mere suffering. Isaiah used it of Israel in exile (Isaiah 26:17–18; 66:7–9); Jesus of the troubles before the end — “All these are but the beginning of the birth pains” (Matthew 24:8); Paul of creation “groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). The pain is real, severe, and going somewhere. A test: when your church struggles, do you see only a woman in labour, or also the sun she is clothed with?
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven crowns sweeps a third of the stars down and stands ready to devour the woman’s child the moment he is born. Satan is a real, personal enemy who claims a sovereignty he doesn’t have, and all through history he has tried to destroy the promised Christ.

What Satan is. Another sign. This isn’t what Satan looks like but what he is. The dragon in the Old Testament is the chaos-monster of the deep — Leviathan, the twisting serpent God alone can master (Job 41; Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1) — and Ezekiel called Pharaoh “the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams” (Ezekiel 29:3).

A counterfeit crown. Seven heads: God’s number of completeness, worn by the dragon. Ten horns: power. Seven diadems — the sharpest detail. A diadem is a royal crown, unlike the victor’s wreath; the woman wears a wreath of stars, the dragon seven royal crowns. He claims a sovereignty he doesn’t hold, and at 19:12 the rider on the white horse appears wearing “many diadems,” settling whose crowns they really are.

A third of the stars. Read naturally alongside vv. 7–9, these are the angels who fell with him. A third again: even in his greatest success the dragon gets a limited portion, and two-thirds stayed.

The plot of the Old Testament. “The dragon stood before the woman… that… he might devour it.” Right after the fall God promised enmity between the serpent and the woman’s offspring: “he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Everything after is the serpent trying to reach the child first. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders Hebrew boys into the Nile. Athaliah destroys Judah’s royal family and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman obtains a decree against every Jew in the empire. And when the child is born, Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16). Matthew reports the massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it.

The second layer. The events are real — a real decree, a real sword, real children — and something behind them is also real, hostile, personal, and has been at this a long time. Paul says it without the picture: “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness” (Ephesians 6:12). A test: when you face opposition to the gospel, do you fight people, or pray against the powers behind them?

How little he does. He stands, waiting, with crowns he didn’t earn and a mouth open for a child not yet born. In the next verse the child is taken to God’s throne, and the dragon doesn’t lay a finger on him.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman bears a son who will rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God’s throne, and she flees into the wilderness to a place God has prepared, where she is fed for 1,260 days. Christ has escaped the dragon’s grasp and reigns, while the church lives through this age in a hard place where God provides for her.

The child is Jesus. The quotation settles it: “You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel” (Psalm 2:9), the Messiah’s coronation psalm, applied in this book to Christ (19:15) and to those who conquer (2:27).

A life in a comma. Between “she gave birth” and “caught up to God and to his throne” there is nothing — no childhood, Galilee, sermons, miracles, cross or empty tomb. The whole Gospel passes in a comma. Because this chapter isn’t telling the story of Jesus but the story of the dragon’s attempt on him, and from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report between the birth and the throne except total defeat. He stood with his mouth open, and the child went straight past him to God’s seat.

Caught up. Snatched, seized with force — the word for the man “caught up to the third heaven” (2 Corinthians 12:2) and the church “caught up” to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). A rescue at speed.

Not avoiding the cross. The compression could mislead. The cross is everywhere in this book — the Lamb standing as though slain is its central image, and v. 11 says the saints conquered “by the blood of the Lamb.” The point is that the cross wasn’t a victory for the dragon. He devoured nothing. The child went to the throne, by a route through a grave that couldn’t hold him.

The mother in the desert. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the wilderness. That is the church’s position between the ascension and the end. The wilderness is where Israel went after the exodus — dangerous, without resources, and the place of daily provision, where a nation was fed forty years by bread arriving each morning; where Elijah was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:6; 19:5–8). A hard address, and not abandonment.

A place prepared. “Prepared by God” — the verb Jesus used of the place he goes to prepare (John 14:2). The desert wasn’t an accident of flight; the accommodation was booked. “She is to be nourished” — by an unnamed hand, for the 1,260 days the book keeps repeating. A test: in your own wilderness stretch, have you noticed how you are being fed? Name one provision and thank him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: war in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon and his; the dragon fights back, is defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Michael appears in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here — the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1), and the archangel who would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9).

Verse 9 gives him four names in one sentence, and each is a job description: the great dragon, raw destructive power; that ancient serpent, the same one, from the garden; the devil, diabolos, slanderer; and Satan, Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four mean the same thing. He is also the deceiver of the whole world, and the verb thrown down is repeated three times in the verse.

Verse 10 explains it, and the explanation is a court case: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Verse 11 defines the book’s central verb in three clauses — they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Verse 12 gives the two reactions: heaven rejoices, earth and sea are warned, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The voice reciting your record has lost its standing, because the charges were paid. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, and Satan — the ancient serpent, the devil, the deceiver of the whole world — is thrown down to the earth with his angels. Through Christ’s victory, Satan has lost his place in heaven, though he still rages on earth.

Michael. Named only in Daniel, Jude and here. In Daniel, “the great prince who has charge of your people” (Daniel 12:1; cf. 10:13, 21). Jude calls him an archangel who, disputing with the devil, “did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you’” (Jude 9). A creature, and a careful one.

What was Satan doing in heaven? The Old Testament answers plainly, and it is the key to the chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (Job 1:9). In Zechariah he stands to accuse the high priest, who is in filthy garments — and the accusation is true (Zechariah 3:1–4). Satan’s place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench.

When was Satan thrown down? Some place it before creation, linking Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28; futurists place it in the middle of a coming tribulation. But the song that follows says it happened when “the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come,” and the saints conquered “by the blood of the Lamb” (vv. 10–11). Jesus spoke the same way: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18); and on his last night, “Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). The more likely reading is that Satan was cast down at the cross. He lost his place as accuser; he didn’t lose his rage. That is why “your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5:8), and why he knows his time is short (v. 12).

Four names, four jobs. “The great dragon”: raw destructive power. “That ancient serpent”: the same one from the garden, connected to Genesis 3 without help. “The devil”: slanderer. “Satan”: adversary, accuser. Two of the four mean much the same, and the next verse makes that the point.

The deceiver. His method hasn’t changed since the garden, where the first move wasn’t a threat but a question: “Did God actually say…?” (Genesis 3:1). He isn’t chiefly described here as torturer or tempter but as a liar with a legal practice. A test: what lie about God are you most tempted to believe this week — that he is holding out on you, or that he won’t forgive? Answer it with what God has actually said.

Thrown down, three times. “Thrown down… thrown down… thrown down with him.” He didn’t withdraw or resign. He was removed, by force, and the sentence won’t stop saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven rejoices that the accuser of believers has been thrown down; they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, not loving their lives even to death. Satan can no longer condemn those whose sins Christ has paid for, and his fury on earth is that of a defeated enemy whose time is short.

A court case. Heaven explains what happened, entirely in legal terms. The dragon is called “the accuser of our brothers… who accuses them day and night before our God.” Take it literally, because it explains what many Christians feel and can’t name. A voice in God’s presence was reciting a list — and not inventing charges. That is the terrible part: the file in Zechariah 3 was accurate. The accusations against you are, on the whole, true.

Thrown out. Not because the charges failed or God stopped listening. The next sentence gives the reason, and defines the book’s central verb, promised to all seven churches. Here is what conquering consists of.

By the blood of the Lamb. First, and the ground of the rest. The accuser wasn’t defeated by argument, or by the saints’ record. He was defeated because the charges were paid. A prosecutor whose every allegation has been settled by someone else has nothing to do in the room. There is no case left (Romans 8:33–34). A test: when your conscience replays your sins, do you argue your record, or point to the blood?

By the word of their testimony. Second, following from the first. Not what they achieved but what they said — the true thing about Christ, before people who didn’t want it. That saying is a weapon.

Not loving their lives. Third, the cost. Not hatred of living, but that when it came to a choice between their lives and their testimony, the testimony won (cf. John 12:25). Some died. A person not clinging to his own life has nothing left that can be threatened.

The shape of courage. It doesn’t begin with bravery. It begins with a verdict already delivered in blood, produces speech, and only then costs something. No one here is asked to be fearless first.

Rejoice — and woe. Heaven celebrates; earth is warned. And the devil’s great wrath isn’t because he is winning but “because he knows that his time is short!” That reframes much Christian experience. The pressure a believer feels isn’t an advancing enemy but the fury of one thrown out of court, who has read the timetable. A cornered animal is dangerous because it is cornered. And “short” as heaven measures it isn’t always short as a suffering church measures it — but it is short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down, he pursued the woman. The logic matters — he goes after the mother because he cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and cannot go back to the courtroom.

Verse 14: the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness, to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. The wings are the exodus — I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4; cf. Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31) — and the time is Daniel 7:25, the third form of the same number John has now used three ways in two chapters.

Verses 15–16: the serpent pours a river out of his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth came to the help of the woman and swallowed it — as the ground opened on Korah (Num. 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots.

Verse 17: the dragon, furious, goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring — reaching back to Genesis 3:15 — defined by exactly two marks: those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the chapter ends on a quiet, ominous line: And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thrown down to earth, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given the two wings of the great eagle to fly to her place in the wilderness, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. Persecution of the church is the rage of a defeated enemy, and God carries and feeds his people through it, as in the exodus.

Displaced rage. He goes after the woman because he has been thrown down. He can’t reach the child on the throne or return to the courtroom, so he turns on the mother. The church’s persecution in this age is the displaced rage of a defeated prosecutor. That doesn’t make it less real, and this book never pretends it does. But it settles what it means: not evidence the dragon is gaining ground, but that he lost the only ground that mattered.

Eagles’ wings. The exodus: “You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4; cf. Deuteronomy 32:11). The chapter now holds a complete exodus: a tyrant killing children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unnamed hand, eagles’ wings, and next a water-crossing where the enemy is undone by his own flood. John tells seven congregations under Roman pressure that they are living in Exodus — and they know how it ends.

Given. She doesn’t grow the wings or buy them. Isaiah promised the same to exhausted people: “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31).

A time, and times, and half a time. The third form of the same number, taken directly from Daniel 7:25. Forty-two months, 1,260 days, a time and times and half a time — used interchangeably within two chapters, itself a strong sign John means one period by them.

Where God feeds without competition. For the second time the wilderness is a place of nourishment, not exposure (cf. v. 6). The desert is where the dragon can’t follow and the food arrives anyway. Any Christian who has been through a stretch with nothing in it — no prospects, company or visible progress — is told what that place is for. It isn’t where God loses track of his people. It is where he feeds them without competition. A test: in a barren season, are you looking for the food he sends — his word, his people, his presence?

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent pours a river from his mouth to sweep the woman away, but the earth swallows it; furious, the dragon makes war on her other offspring — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus — and stands on the seashore. Satan attacks with floods of lies, God rescues by unexpected means, and the marks of his people are simple: obedience and confession.

Two mouths. The dragon’s mouth pours a river; the earth’s mouth swallows it. What comes from the dragon’s mouth is what always has — he is “the deceiver of the whole world” (v. 9), and his one method is speech. The flood is a torrent of lies.

A flood of words. In the Psalms, overwhelming waters picture slander and hostile testimony: “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck… and the flood sweeps over me” (Psalm 69:1–2). That is how a reputation is destroyed: not one accusation, which can be answered, but a volume arriving faster than anyone can respond, until the truth is under water.

Help from the ground. The rescue comes from the least likely place. The earth in this book is usually where the trouble is. Here it opens its mouth and swallows a river, as the ground swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots. God isn’t limited to the instruments a believer would expect. He has used a pagan king’s decree, a famine, a shipwreck and an earthquake in a prison to protect his people, and here the ground. A test: are you dictating to God how he must rescue you? Watch for his unexpected help.

The rest of her offspring. Frustrated with the mother, he turns on the children, and John defines them precisely, reaching back to Genesis 3:15. Two marks only. “Keep the commandments of God”: obedience — ordinary, unglamorous, in what God has actually commanded, not what we would prefer to be judged on. “Hold to the testimony of Jesus”: confession — they haven’t let go of what they say about him.

A short list. Not those who understand this book, or identified the beast correctly, or never suffered. Obedience and confession, held on to. That is what the dragon makes war on, and all it takes to be on his list. A test: are you marked by those two things this week?

On the beach. “And he stood on the sand of the sea.” (Some manuscripts read “I stood”; the ESV notes it, and “he” is the better reading.) The dragon walks to the shoreline and looks out at the water — and the next sentence is “And I saw a beast rising out of the sea.” He is calling something up. But the reader now has everything needed to watch without panic: the child is on the throne; the accuser is thrown out with no case to bring; the woman is fed in a place prepared; the saints conquer by blood already shed and words already spoken. The dragon on that beach is a defeated prosecutor with a short time, doing the only thing left to him.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.<sup>2</sup>She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.<sup>3</sup>And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.<sup>4</sup>His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.<sup>5</sup>She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne,<sup>6</sup>and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.<sup>7</sup>Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back,<sup>8</sup>but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven.<sup>9</sup>And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.<sup>10</sup>And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God.<sup>11</sup>And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”<sup>13</sup>And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.<sup>14</sup>But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.<sup>15</sup>The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood.<sup>16</sup>But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth.<sup>17</sup>Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the political theology chapter of Revelation. The dragon, standing on the seashore, summons two beasts — one from the sea, one from the land — and delegates to them his authority, his throne, and great power. Together the dragon and the two beasts form a Satanic trinity that parodies the Holy Trinity: the dragon parodies the Father, the beast from the sea parodies the Son (including a parody death and resurrection), and the beast from the land parodies the Spirit (pointing away from itself to the first beast, as the Spirit points away from himself to the Son). The unholy trinity is the political and religious power structure of every totalitarian system that demands ultimate allegiance.

Interpretive flag — The Beast from the Sea: This is the third major structural decision point. The preterist reading identifies the beast as Nero Caesar — and the gematria (numerical value of letters) of “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew adds up to 666. The mortal wound that was healed (v. 3) refers to the Nero redivivus myth: rumors after Nero’s death in AD 68 that he had survived and would return from the east with the Parthian army. The historicist reading has identified the beast with various historical powers including the papacy. The futurist/dispensational reading sees a still-future individual world ruler, a literal Antichrist who will arise in the last days, be given global political power, and demand global worship. The idealist/amillennial reading understands the beast as the pattern of totalitarian political power that demands ultimate allegiance in every age — with Rome as the first-century embodiment and every subsequent empire that makes similar demands as its successor. The idealist position is followed here, while the specific Nero/Rome referent is fully acknowledged as the primary first-century layer.

Interpretive flag — 666: Three readings predominate. (1) Gematria: “Neron Kaisar” in Hebrew letters (nun-resh-vav-nun / qoph-samek-resh) adds to 666; the spelling without the final n adds to 616, which is the reading of some early manuscripts. The specific first-century referent. (2) The number of incompleteness: six is one less than seven (the number of divine completeness); 666 is the triple intensification of falling short of the divine — the beast is humanity at its most grandiose, still falling short of the glory of God. (3) The number of humanity: six was associated with humanity in some traditions (created on the sixth day). The beast is the ultimate expression of humanity’s totalitarian self-divinization. All three readings illuminate the symbol; none is exhaustive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a beast rises out of the sea with the dragon’s own features — seven heads, ten horns, royal diadems — and blasphemous names on its heads, which is what Roman coins and inscriptions actually gave the emperors. It is like a leopard, with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth: Daniel’s four beasts (Dan. 7:2–7) compressed into one. And the dragon gave it his power, his throne and great authority — the offer Christ refused in the desert (Luke 4:6).

Verses 3–4: one head has a mortal wound that was healed, and the whole earth marvels. The Greek uses the same participle used of the Lamb at 5:6, so the parody is deliberate. The world worships dragon and beast together, chanting Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? — the song of the exodus (Ex. 15:11) with a different object, and the meaning of the name Michael turned to the wrong address.

Verses 5–6: the beast was given a mouth of haughty and blasphemous words and was allowed authority for forty-two months (cf. Dan. 7:8, 25). It blasphemes God’s name and his dwelling — and John glosses the dwelling himself: that is, those who dwell in heaven.

Verses 7–8: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them, with authority over every tribe and people and language and nation; and all the earth-dwellers worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Verses 9–10 turn to the reader: If anyone has an ear, let him hear — captivity to captivity, sword to sword (cf. Jer. 15:2) — Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A beast rises from the sea, with ten horns, seven heads, ten crowns and blasphemous names, combining leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power, throne and authority. Satan works through political power that claims divine honours — the same beast in every age, wearing different costumes.

The dragon’s likeness. The dragon stood on the beach at the end of chapter 12; this is what he calls up. Seven heads, ten horns, royal crowns — exactly the dragon of 12:3. What comes out of the water is what the dragon looks like when he takes a form that can hold public office.

Two pointed differences. The dragon wore seven crowns on his heads; the beast wears ten on its horns — more crowns, worn on the instruments of force. And blasphemous names on its heads. To a first-century reader that wasn’t a metaphor: coins and inscriptions across Asia gave emperors titles like divine, son of god, saviour of the world, and lord and god. The beast is wearing them.

Daniel’s four beasts in one. Daniel saw four beasts from the sea — a lion with eagles’ wings, a bear, a leopard, and a terrifying fourth with ten horns (Daniel 7:2–7): four kingdoms. John names three in reverse order and gives their features to one animal. What Daniel saw as a succession of empires, John compresses into a single creature. The point isn’t chronology but that there has only ever been one beast in different national costumes. Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome aren’t four problems but four appearances of one thing, which reappears in every century. Anyone who has decided the beast is one particular regime should notice John has just merged four.

Who or what is the beast from the sea? In John’s day it was the Roman empire demanding worship. The Reformers saw it in the papacy; futurists see a final world ruler. The more likely reading is that it is the persecuting power of the state set against God, which took its first shape in Rome, has reappeared again and again in history, and will come to a final form before Christ returns.

A throne from the dragon. “To it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.” The devil offered Christ the same in the desert: “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me” (Luke 4:6). Christ refused; the beast accepts. That is the whole difference between the two kingdoms in this book: one takes a throne from the dragon, the other a cross from his Father. And “gave” — everything the dragon has, he was permitted to have. Throughout the chapter the beasts are given or allowed things (vv. 5, 7, 14, 15); the chain of permission runs past the dragon to the throne.

From the sea. The sea is chaos, frozen flat before God’s throne (4:6) and gone in the new creation (21:1). Empires come up out of the churn. A test: when a government demands the loyalty that belongs to God, do you recognise the beast’s face, whatever flag it flies?
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the beast’s heads seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole world marvels, follows it, and worships both the dragon and the beast: “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” Satan imitates Christ’s death and resurrection to win worship, and people worship power because it seems unbeatable.

A counterfeit resurrection. “Mortal wound” is literally “slain to death,” using the same word as the Lamb “standing, as though it had been slain” (5:6). The beast is a deliberate parody: a figure with a death-wound, alive anyway, demanding the worship that belongs to the One who really died and rose.

Satan copies. The key to this chapter and the next two. A beast with a resurrection; a second beast with horns like a lamb; a mark on the forehead; an image that speaks; a city called great. Satan invents nothing. He copies, and the copies are close enough to fool people who haven’t looked carefully.

What is the healed wound? Some link it with the legend that Nero, who killed himself in AD 68, would return from beyond the Euphrates — a rumour that produced several impostors. Others with the empire’s near-collapse in the civil wars of AD 68–69, when four emperors ruled in a year, and its full recovery under Vespasian. Others with a future event. The more likely reading is that it is a parody of the Lamb who was slain and lives: the persecuting power seems destroyed, rises again, and the world marvels. The wound is what makes the beast credible.

The world’s hymn. “Who is like the beast?” parodies the song at the sea: “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness…?” (Exodus 15:11). Same sentence, different object. And Michael, who threw the dragon out of heaven, means “Who is like God?” The beast’s worshippers chant the archangel’s name at the wrong address.

Worship of power. “Who can fight against it?” No one claims the beast is kind, just or true. They worship it because it can’t be beaten — the reasoning of someone who has decided that whatever is strongest must be obeyed.

Not an exotic sin. Very few people consciously decide to worship a tyrant. They conclude that resistance is pointless, that the thing is too big to oppose, and that a sensible person accommodates himself to it. That conclusion, reached quietly and without ceremony, is what the verse describes. The first act of worship is usually a calculation. A test: where have you quietly decided that something — a culture, an employer, a movement — is too big to stand against, and so gone along?

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is given a mouth for proud blasphemies and allowed authority for forty-two months; it slanders God’s name and his dwelling — the people who dwell in heaven. The beast’s power is on a limited licence from God, its main weapon is its mouth, and attacking God’s people is attacking God.

Given; allowed. Two divine passives in one verse, the reason a Christian can read this chapter without despair. The beast didn’t acquire its mouth; it was given one. It didn’t seize its term; it was allowed one. Its authority is on licence, and the licence has an expiry date.

The same clock. Forty-two months — the number of chapter 11, of the woman in the wilderness, and of Daniel’s little horn (Daniel 7:25). The beast’s authority runs exactly as long as the church’s testimony (11:3) and the woman’s protection (12:6, 14). One clock governs the persecuting and the preserving.

Daniel’s mouth. Of the little horn: “in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things” (Daniel 7:8); “He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:25).

God’s dwelling is his people. It blasphemes God’s name, and “his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven” — John’s own gloss, in case anyone imagines a building. Slandering the church is slandering God, the logic of the Damascus road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). What is done to the body is done to the head.

The beast talks. Ten horns, the dragon’s authority, a healed death-wound — and both verses describing its activity are about its mouth. That should recalibrate how a believer expects pressure to come. The great opposition in this book isn’t chiefly a police force but a narrative: a version of reality, repeated with enormous confidence and reach, in which God is small, his people contemptible, and the beast the only realistic option. Christians braced for a knock at the door are sometimes overwhelmed instead by forty years of being told, pleasantly, that what they believe is ridiculous. A test: whose story about the world are you absorbing most hours of the week?

A mouth against a mouth. Against a mouth, the church is issued a mouth: “the word of their testimony” (12:11), and behind it the sword from Christ’s mouth (1:16; 19:15). Keep speaking his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is allowed to make war on the saints and conquer them, and is given authority over every nation; all earth-dwellers worship it — everyone whose name is not written in the Lamb’s book of life. Faithfulness doesn’t guarantee survival, but those whose names the slain Lamb has written will not worship the beast.

The hardest sentence. Permitted to make war on Christians, and permitted to win. The verb is “conquer” — the promise that ends every letter, used of Christ at 5:5 and of the saints at 12:11 — here used of the beast against them, as at 11:7. Revelation won’t tell the church faithfulness guarantees survival. It says the opposite, twice. Congregations are overrun; believers imprisoned and executed. The beast wins, visibly, for forty-two months.

Two kinds of victory. Hold it beside 12:11: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” Same verb, same people, opposite outcome, resolved in the last clause. The beast conquers their bodies; they conquer him by dying without letting go. Two victories run at once, and only one is visible from the street.

The bought territory. “Every tribe and people and language and nation” — the fourfold phrase of 5:9. The beast’s reach is universal, given, and covers exactly the territory already bought by Someone else.

Earth-dwellers. John’s term (8:13) for those whose whole account is settled here — not geography; the saints live on earth too and are never called that.

The register. The most reassuring clause in the chapter. There is a book, belonging to “the Lamb who was slain.” Names were written in it “from the foundation of the world” — before anyone had done anything to deserve entry or exclusion. And those whose names are in it don’t worship the beast.

Could I be deceived into worshipping the beast? The verse says the opposite. The worshippers are those whose names are not written; those whose names are written are kept. That isn’t a promise that a believer will never be frightened, waver or fail — Peter denied Christ three times in a courtyard. It is a promise about who does the holding: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The register isn’t a list of people who held out. It belongs to the One with the wounds, and the entries were made before the world existed. A test: is your confidence resting on your grip on Christ, or his grip on you?

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls each listener to hear: whoever is appointed to captivity or the sword will go to it — this calls for the saints’ endurance and faith. Christians shouldn’t expect escape from every suffering; God calls us to stay faithful and keep trusting him through it.

For you personally. The formula closed all seven letters, always with “what the Spirit says to the churches.” Here those words are gone. Having described a beast conquering the saints, John turns to whoever is listening: this part is for you.

A sentence already passed. The saying comes from Jeremiah: “Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity” (Jeremiah 15:2).

Not fatalism. The verse’s last sentence rules that out. It means a Christian facing the beast shouldn’t expect an escape route, spend his strength hunting one, or conclude when arrest comes that something has gone wrong with God’s arrangements. If captivity is appointed, that is where you are going. No fourth option is being withheld.

Bleak? Only until it is set against the alternative: a Christianity that promises deliverance from every hard thing, and so leaves a believer, when the door actually opens, concluding God has failed. This verse removes that conclusion in advance. Nothing done to a Christian by the beast is outside what was appointed, and none of it surprises the One who holds the keys.

Endurance and faith. The Christian response to the beast in two words. Endurance: holding a position under weight. Faith — or faithfulness; the word covers both, and both fit.

What isn’t on the list. Not resistance, organisation, clever manoeuvring, political leverage, or withdrawal into a compound. The beast has the dragon’s authority and the worship of the whole earth, and the instruction to the church is: stay where you are and keep trusting him.

The refusal to move. Any Christian under long pressure will recognise the realism. Most of what the New Testament asks of believers in trouble isn’t spectacular; it is the refusal to move. A similar call returns at 14:12. Twice, at the darkest points, the reader is told what is asked of him is endurance and faith, and nothing else. A test: what would faithful endurance look like in your hardest situation this week? Not escape — staying, and trusting.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–12: a second beast rises out of the earth — the opposite element, so that between them the dragon has the whole world covered. It has two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. Named three times later as the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), its entire function is to make the world worship the first beast.

Verses 13–15: it performs great signs, including fire from heaven — Elijah’s credential on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) — and by the signs it is allowed to work it deceives the earth-dwellers, telling them to make an image for the beast. It is allowed to give the image breath so that it speaks and orders the death of anyone who will not worship it. Behind this stands Daniel 3: an image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, and a furnace — and three men who said But if not (Dan. 3:17–18).

Verses 16–17: it marks all — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. Verse 18 sets the puzzle: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark — the beast’s name — without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second beast rises from the earth, with two horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon, and it makes the world worship the first beast. False religion looks gentle and familiar, but its message is the dragon’s — and its job is to win worship for the beast.

Land and sea covered. The first beast came from the sea, this one from the land. Between them the dragon has the world covered — exactly what the angel of 10:2 contested, one foot on each.

The unholy trinity. The dragon, the sea beast, and this one, later named “the false prophet” (16:13; 19:20; 20:10). Set against Father, Son and Spirit, the parody is exact. The dragon gives authority to the beast, as the Father gives all things to the Son. The beast bears a death-wound, lives, and is worshipped. And the false prophet draws no attention to himself; his whole function is to make the world worship the beast — just what the Spirit does for Christ (John 16:14).

Lamb’s horns, dragon’s voice. The most useful sentence in the chapter for recognising deception. It looks like a lamb — horns like the Lamb at the centre of this book. From a distance it is harmless, even familiar. Then it opens its mouth, and out comes the dragon. Jesus: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15). Paul: Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, and his servants as servants of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14–15). The New Testament warning about deception isn’t that it will look frightening, but familiar — and the test isn’t appearance but speech.

A usable test. Don’t ask whether a teacher, movement or message feels Christian, looks Christian, or uses Christian words — the horns are convincing. Ask what it actually says when it speaks at length, and whether that is what the dragon says: that God isn’t to be taken at his word, that his commands are a cage, that safety lies in accommodation. Apply it to the voices you listen to this week.

A department, not a rival. It works “in its presence” with the first beast’s authority, and its business is organising worship. In Asia this had a concrete shape: the imperial cult was run by a provincial council of local notables, and its priests weren’t Romans from abroad but leading men of the cities — neighbours, patrons, people the church knew. The pressure to worship didn’t arrive from the sea. It came up out of the local ground.
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second beast performs great signs, even calling fire from heaven, deceives the earth-dwellers, has them make an image of the first beast, and gives it breath to speak and to kill those who won’t worship it. Miracles alone prove nothing; deception uses religion and wonders to make false worship plausible, and faithful people must refuse even at the cost of their lives.

Real signs. The word is the one John’s Gospel uses for Jesus’ miracles. This isn’t mere conjuring. Scripture is consistent that supernatural power proves nothing by itself: Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues (Exodus 7:11, 22); Moses warned that a prophet’s sign might come true while he led Israel to other gods, and that God was testing them by it (Deuteronomy 13:1–3); Jesus said false christs and false prophets would “perform great signs and wonders” (Matthew 24:24). A test: are you drawn to a ministry chiefly by its wonders? Test it by its words about Christ.

Elijah’s fire. Fire from heaven was Elijah’s sign on Carmel, when it settled who the true God was before a nation (1 Kings 18:38). The false prophet reproduces the credential of Israel’s greatest prophet, and the two witnesses of chapter 11 had Elijah’s powers too. Both sides have fire. Only one has the truth.

Allowed. Even the deceiving miracles run on a licence.

An idol that talks. The Old Testament mocks idols because they can’t: “They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear” (Psalm 115:5–6), the psalm John used at 9:20. Here this idol talks back, and what it says is a death sentence. How it speaks — ancient temples did use hidden speaking-tubes and moving statues — doesn’t matter. The demand is the same either way: bow, or die.

Daniel 3. An image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, a furnace for refusers. Three men said no, in words that could be carved over this chapter: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us… But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:17–18). “But if not” is the endurance of the saints in three words.

Force needs plausibility. The first beast supplies the force; the second the plausibility — signs, wonders, reasons, respectable local men explaining it is only a formality. Raw power alone has never commanded worship. It needs someone with lamb’s horns to make the case. A test: what “only a formality” are you being asked to perform that would deny Christ? Say “but if not” — and refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second beast makes everyone — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, the beast’s name or number. The mark is not a device but an allegiance, a counterfeit of God’s seal, enforced by economic pressure — and no believer takes it by accident.

Everyone. Three pairs covering every social division: status, wealth, legal condition. No one is exempt by being important or overlooked for being insignificant. The demand reaches the senator and the slave in one sentence.

A counterfeit seal. The original was shown first: God’s servants sealed on their foreheads (7:3), the 144,000 with the Lamb’s and the Father’s name written there (14:1). Everyone in this book is marked; there is no unmarked category. The only question is whose name is on you.

Hand and forehead. Israel was told to bind God’s words “as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes” (Deuteronomy 6:8). Hand and forehead: what you do and what you think. The beast demands what God demanded, in the same two places — a parody, not merely an atrocity.

Buy or sell. Here the chapter stops being theoretical for most readers. The pressure isn’t chiefly death but trade. Keep your convictions and lose your livelihood, or make one small formal gesture and go on feeding your family. In Asia that was real: a tradesman who wouldn’t join the guild ritual lost the guild’s work, probably the pressure behind the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira. Later, under Decius, a certificate that one had sacrificed — copies survive on papyrus — was the difference between a working life and ruin. A test: what would you give up to stay faithful at work? Decide before the pressure comes.

Not a barcode. The mark isn’t a barcode, microchip, credit card, vaccine or implant. Every generation since printing has identified it with its newest technology, and every one has been wrong, with no loss of confidence. The text rules out the technological reading: the mark is “the name of the beast or the number of its name.” Not a device but an identity — a declaration of who owns you and whose name you will say. Whatever administrative form loyalty takes in a given century, what is demanded is worship, and what is at stake is allegiance.

What if I take it by accident? No one in this chapter takes it by accident. It is the visible sign of worship already given, by people who have already marvelled, worshipped, and decided no one can fight the beast. No one stumbles into it. And those whose names are in the Lamb’s book are not the ones at that counter.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls for wisdom to calculate the beast’s number — the number of a man — 666. The number most likely pointed John’s first readers to Nero and marks the beast as humanity making itself god, always falling short of God’s perfection — not a code for guessing a future name.

A puzzle with a key. No verse has been used more irresponsibly, so start with what it says. It invites calculation: “let the one who has understanding calculate.” John sets a puzzle to people who had the key. And “the number of a man” may mean a particular man or a number characteristic of humanity; both are grammatically possible.

Letters as numbers. In Hebrew and Greek the letters double as numerals, so every name has a numerical value. It was a common game; graffiti from Pompeii reads, in effect, “I love her whose number is 545.” First-century readers knew at once what John was asking.

What does 666 mean? The most widely held identification is Nero: his Greek name and title, “Neron Kesar,” written in Hebrew letters, add up to 666. And some ancient manuscripts read 616 — exactly the total of the Latin form, “Nero Caesar,” without the final n. A variant that shifts the number by precisely one dropped letter is hard to explain as coincidence; early readers apparently knew the name and adjusted to their spelling. The historicist tradition of the Reformation applied it to the papacy. The futurist tradition takes it as the name of an Antichrist still to come, calculable only when he appears. And a reading that needs no name: six is one short of seven, the number of completeness; six three times is falling short raised to the highest pitch. The more likely reading combines these: the number marks the beast as the height of human self-deification, which in John’s day had Nero’s face. It is a portrait, not a code for calculating a future name.

A magnificent almost. Whatever the beast is and whenever it appears, it is a world-conquering almost. Seven heads it didn’t earn, ten crowns it was given, a resurrection it counterfeited — and it can’t reach seven.

A history of confident error. Every century has found its man — emperors, popes, sultans, Napoleon, Hitler, and a line of modern politicians made to fit by ingenious arithmetic. What all these identifications shared was certainty. John asks for wisdom and understanding, not cleverness, and they aren’t the same. A test: does your interest in this verse make you wiser and more faithful, or just more speculative?

What to take away. Not a name but a recognition. The beast is whatever demands the allegiance that belongs to God, backed by force, made plausible by religion, enforced through the power to buy and sell. It has worn many costumes and will wear more. Every one is a six — gigantic, unopposable to look at, worshipped by the whole earth, and one short of the number that belongs to the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads.<sup>2</sup>And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.<sup>3</sup>One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast.<sup>4</sup>And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”<sup>5</sup>And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months.<sup>6</sup>It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.<sup>7</sup>Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation,<sup>8</sup>and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.<sup>9</sup>If anyone has an ear, let him hear:<sup>10</sup>If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon.<sup>12</sup>It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.<sup>13</sup>It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people,<sup>14</sup>and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived.<sup>15</sup>And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.<sup>16</sup>Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead,<sup>17</sup>so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.<sup>18</sup>This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

14.title: The Lamb, the Harvest, and the Three Angels
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is a triptych of three visions, each answering the terror of chapter 13 with a counter-vision of divine certainty. First: the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000 — the redeemed in their completeness, standing where the beast could not reach them. Second: three angels flying in midheaven, each with a message that together constitute the gospel, the judgment, and the warning. Third: the great harvest of the earth — the grain harvest of the redeemed and the grape harvest of the wicked, two harvests that together depict the final judgment in all its terrible binary clarity.

The chapter is the hinge of Revelation. Behind it lies the cosmic backstory (chapters 12–13) and the long unfolding of the seals and trumpets (chapters 6–11). Before it lies the bowl judgments, Babylon's fall, the Rider on the white horse, and the new creation. Chapter 14 stands at the center and declares: the outcome is certain. The Lamb is on Mount Zion. The harvest is coming. The one who endures to the end will be saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 13 ended with a mark on the hand or forehead and a number; chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name. Verse 1: on Mount Zion stands the Lamb, and with him the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7, complete, wearing his name and his Father’s. Everyone in this book is marked; the alternative to the beast’s mark is not an unmarked crowd.

Verses 2–3: a voice like the roar of many waters and loud thunder — and, in the same breath, like harpists playing on harps. They sing a new song before the throne, and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. Not because the words are difficult, but because a song about being ransomed cannot be sung truly by someone who has not been.

Verses 4–5 describe them: they have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; they are firstfruits (aparchē, the first sheaf that both belongs to God and guarantees more is coming); and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless — language taken from the servant of Isaiah 53:9 and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13, and amōmos, the word for a sacrificial animal without defect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb on Mount Zion

Against the beast’s mark stand the 144,000 with the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, singing a new song only the redeemed can learn. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are blameless because they were bought.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not one of those sealed in chapter 7 is missing.

Now: Ask whether the song of the cross is a statement you admire or your own account.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder.
