The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who bear his and his Father’s name on their foreheads and sing a new song that only the redeemed can learn. In contrast to the beast’s marked followers, Christ’s people are complete, secure with him, and worship from the experience of being ransomed.

A different forehead. Chapter 13 ended with a mark and a number; chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name. Everyone in this book is marked. The alternative to the beast isn’t an unmarked crowd but a marked one, wearing a different name in the same place.

Mount Zion. The hill where, in the Psalms, God installs his King in the teeth of the raging nations: “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (Psalm 2:6). Hebrews says Christians have already come there: “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). Earthly hill or heavenly city, the sense is the same: where the King stands and the enemy doesn’t.

None missing. In 13:1 a beast rose from the sea; here the Lamb simply stands, and his company is counted and complete. Not one of the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7 is missing. The sealing worked. They are the same as in chapter 7: the complete people of God, sealed with the name of the Lamb and his Father — not a literal number from ethnic Israel, nor the special class of “anointed” taught by Jehovah’s Witnesses.

Waters, thunder and harps. “The roar of many waters” is the voice of the risen Christ (1:15) and of God’s glory returning (Ezekiel 43:2); thunder is God’s voice at Sinai; and in the same breath, harps, the most delicate sound of the ancient world. Overwhelming and beautiful at the same volume. Nothing in human music does both; a waterfall isn’t tender and a harp can’t be heard over one. Any picture of heaven’s worship that is merely soothing has lost half of it.

A new song. Sung when God has done something unprecedented (Psalm 96:1), and sung once before in this book (5:9): “by your blood you ransomed people for God.” That is this song’s subject too.

No one else can learn it. Not because the words are hard; a song about being ransomed by blood can be printed and read by anyone. It can’t be sung truly by someone who hasn’t been ransomed. In chapter 5, myriads of angels praised the Lamb, but the new song was the song of the redeemed — things “into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

A quiet test. In any ordinary service, when a hymn about the cross is sung, are you singing a true statement or your own account? The difference isn’t musical or emotional; someone can be moved by a tune he has no part in. The 144,000 sing what could only be learned by having it happen to them. Can you sing it that way this Sunday?

verseByVerse.quote: It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The 144,000 have not defiled themselves with women, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, are firstfruits redeemed for God, and have no lie in their mouths. Christ’s people keep themselves for him alone, follow him without conditions, belong to God as a pledge of the full harvest, and are truthful in a world of deceit.

What does “virgins” mean here? Three readings are held. First, literally, of celibate men. Whatever else is said, it can’t mean marriage defiles: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4), and Paul calls forbidding marriage a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3). Peter was married, and this book is addressed to ordinary households. Second, spiritual fidelity. In the prophets idolatry is adultery and God’s people a bride chasing lovers (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16). This book is about to describe a prostitute, Babylon, who intoxicated the nations (v. 8), and ends with a Bride. Paul used the image of a church: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). Third, holy-war imagery. The 144,000 came from a tribal muster, the way Israel counted an army, and soldiers on campaign abstained from sex: David’s men had kept themselves from women (1 Samuel 21:4–5); Uriah wouldn’t go home while the ark and army were in tents (2 Samuel 11:11; cf. Deuteronomy 23:9–10). The more likely reading is that the second and third are both in play, saying one thing: this company kept itself for one Lord in a world offering many. A test: what rival love is courting your heart this week?

Following wherever. “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes” — the simplest definition of a Christian in the book, startlingly plain after two chapters of beasts. “Follow me” was the first thing Jesus asked of fishermen and the last thing he said to Peter, twice (John 21:19, 22). The weight is on “wherever.” Following is easy while the road goes somewhere you would choose. The Lamb goes to a cross, through death, and meanwhile among lampstands in difficult towns. To follow wherever is to have surrendered the veto in advance — what distinguishes a disciple from an admirer. Where are you still holding a veto?

Firstfruits. The first sheaf, brought to God before the rest was gathered (Leviticus 23:10). A firstfruit belongs to God and guarantees more is coming. Paul calls Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

No lie. Echoing the Servant, in whose mouth was no deceit (Isaiah 53:9), and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13. In a book whose villain is “the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9), truthfulness isn’t a minor virtue. It is the mark of the other side. A test: where are you shading the truth to make life easier?

Blameless. The word for a sacrificial animal without defect — what is said of the Lamb. No one here achieved it. They were “redeemed,” bought (v. 3); the blamelessness was purchased and given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: an angel flies directly overhead — at the zenith, where everyone can see — with an eternal gospel for every nation and tribe and language and people, and calls out three imperatives: fear God, give him glory, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water, because the hour of his judgment has come. The list is deliberate: those are the four things the first four trumpets struck (8:7–12).

Verse 8: a second angel announces Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great — Isaiah’s watchman’s cry (Isa. 21:9; cf. Jer. 51:8) — she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. Babylon is announced as finished three chapters before she is even described.

Verses 9–11: a third angel warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torment goes up for ever, and they have no rest, day or night.

Verse 12 turns to the reader with the sentence already used at 13:10: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. Verse 13 gives the second of the book’s seven beatitudes, and one of the few sentences John is specifically commanded to write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on — with the Spirit adding a comment of his own: that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel, Fall, and Warning

An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel: fear God and worship the Creator. A second announces Babylon fallen. A third warns that worshippers of the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed. Then: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The empire was at its height when its fall was announced in the past tense.

Now: Fear God rather than the beast; the warning is given so that the saints endure, and their deeds follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel for every nation, calling all people to fear God, give him glory and worship the Creator, because his hour of judgment has come. Even in judgment God sends the good news to everyone, and calls them to turn from false fears to the true God who made them.

Three angels, the gospel’s order. Three announcements follow, in the order the gospel always arrives: an appeal, a warning about the world, a warning about the alternative.

Overhead, to everyone. At the zenith, like the eagle of 8:13, where everyone below can see. No one will say the message was hard to come by. And it goes “to those who dwell on earth” — the very people who have settled for this world and worshipped the beast. The gospel is proclaimed to the group that has rejected it for eight chapters.

An eternal gospel. The only time the noun “gospel” appears in Revelation, and some question whether this is the gospel, since the cross isn’t mentioned. But its content — that the Judge of all the earth has come to do right, and his creatures may still turn to him — is good news of the most concrete kind to people under a beast. And the cross has already been proclaimed at length: chapter 5 is the gospel, and the slain Lamb has been at the centre of every scene since.

The ground is creation. “Fear God and give him glory… and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water” — exactly the four things the first four trumpets struck (8:7–12). This is Paul’s argument to pagans without a Bible: “turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them” (Acts 14:15); “The God who made the world and everything in it” (Acts 17:24). Where there is no shared Scripture there is a shared sky, and everyone owes his existence to Someone. A test: when you speak to unbelieving friends, do you start where Paul started — with the God who made them?

Fear God. The command modern readers find hardest. Not terror, nor comfortable respect, but taking God seriously as what he is — the settled, awed recognition that there is Someone there of a different order. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). And it is aimed at people who have spent the book terrified of a beast. The remedy for fearing the wrong thing isn’t fearlessness but fearing the right thing, which frees a person from everything else. What are you afraid of this week? Set the fear of God against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Another angel, a second, followed, saying, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second angel announces, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,” who made all nations drunk on the wine of her immorality. The proud, godless world-city — Rome in John’s day and every such system since — is as good as fallen, because God has decided it, though it still seduces people with its pleasures.

The headline first. Babylon appears for the first time, in one verse, announced as finished. Chapters 17–18 describe her at length; this headline runs ahead of the story.

Isaiah’s watchman. “Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground” (Isaiah 21:9; cf. Jeremiah 51:8). The doubling is a herald’s shout, the way news of a great collapse actually gets called out.

The grammar of certainty. Babylon hasn’t fallen yet in the story; she isn’t even described for three chapters. The angel announces the collapse of an empire at the height of its power. Prophets do this constantly: what God has decided is reported as done, because from his side it is. That is what a Christian in Ephesus needed. The empire in front of him wasn’t wobbling; it was collecting his taxes, running his courts and threatening his trade. And the message read in his congregation used the past tense. A test: what power over your life do you need to hear announced as already fallen?

Who is Babylon? The historical Babylon had been ruins for centuries, so the name is a type, as Sodom and Egypt were at 11:8. For John’s readers it unmistakably meant Rome, which had destroyed the temple as Babylon did; Peter sends greetings from “She who is at Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13), almost certainly Rome. But the name is older than Rome and outlives it. Babylon begins at a tower built so that people could make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4), and that project has never closed. Babylon is the city humanity builds without God — wherever it is, whatever it is called, however good its roads.

A glass, not a sword. “She who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.” Seduction, not conquest: the nations weren’t forced; they were poured a drink. And intoxication — lost judgment, the certainty at two in the morning that everything is fine. That is how the world’s system recruits, and why the church so often fails to notice. The beast comes with a sword and is obvious. Babylon comes with a glass, is charming, pays well, and doesn’t seem to ask for anything at all. A test: where is the world pouring for you — comfort, status, money, pleasure — and how much have you drunk?

verseByVerse.quote: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, "If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third angel warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink God’s undiluted wrath and be tormented with fire and sulfur in the Lamb’s presence, with no rest forever. Those who finally reject God for the beast face real, eternal judgment — a warning given only after the gospel has been proclaimed to all.

Without softening, without relish. The most terrible warning in the New Testament, to be read exactly as it stands.

Two cups. Babylon poured a drink; so does God. Those who drank hers will drink his. And “poured full strength”: ancient wine was nearly always mixed with water; unmixed wine was for getting drunk. The cup of God’s wrath is an Old Testament image — “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed… all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8; cf. Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15) — and here, for the first time, nothing softens it.

The water left out. Every judgment so far was diluted: a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a limit on the locusts, a fence around the winds. That was the mixing — God’s patience. This is the cup with the water left out.

Two eternities. Fire and sulfur is Sodom (Genesis 19:24). Smoke rising forever is Isaiah’s picture of Edom (Isaiah 34:10). And “they have no rest, day or night” is the exact reverse of the living creatures who never cease worshipping (4:8) and the martyrs told to rest (6:11). Two eternities side by side; the difference is what a person is doing in them.

Is the punishment of the lost conscious and unending? Some evangelicals hold that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, pointing to the Bible’s language of destruction and perishing and arguing that the smoke rising forever describes a permanent result rather than a continuing experience. That view is held by people who love the Bible and want to be faithful to it. But the historic and majority position of the church, and the plain reading of these words, is that the punishment of the finally impenitent is conscious and unending, because “they have no rest, day or night” describes an experience, not a residue. That is the more likely reading.

In the presence of the Lamb. Not a distant dungeon God has forgotten. And the One present is the Lamb — who was slaughtered, wept at a tomb, and prayed for the men driving the nails. No one finally lost will be able to say the Judge didn’t offer himself first.

On whom it falls. Said twice: “these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.” Not the unlucky or confused or never-asked. This warning is the third of three, and the first was an eternal gospel flown overhead to every nation. Nobody reaches v. 11 without being flown over by v. 6.

A particular face. For the reader thinking of someone he loves: Scripture doesn’t tell us the destination of anyone still alive and never invites us to work it out. It tells us the Judge is the Lamb, the gospel is still being flown overhead, and intercession is a priestly act — what you were made a priest to do (1:6). Pray, and keep praying. Remember that Paul once watched over the coats at Stephen’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a call for the saints to endure, keeping God’s commands and faith in Jesus; and a voice declares, “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord,” for they rest from their labours and their deeds follow them. Knowing God’s judgment helps believers stand firm, and Christians who die are blessed — at rest, and nothing they did for Christ is lost.

What it is for. A similar call came at 13:10, both times right after the darkest material — the beast conquering the saints, and now the undiluted cup. Twice John writes something almost unbearable, then turns to the reader: this is what it is for.

The same two marks. Keeping God’s commandments and holding faith in Jesus, as at 12:17. Obedience and trust. The list hasn’t grown, and won’t.

Not fear but endurance. After three verses about hell, the response asked for isn’t fear or a campaign. It is endurance — staying under the weight. Knowledge of judgment in this book is never given to frighten Christians, but to let them keep standing when the beast has every advantage, because they know how the accounts are finally settled.

A sentence heaven wanted written. “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” The second of Revelation’s seven blessings, and one of few sentences John is specifically commanded to write (cf. 19:9; 21:5). Not blessed are the strong, victorious or escaped. Blessed are the dead. To congregations that had buried people and expected to bury more, at the point where the beast is killing all who refuse the mark, God stops the vision to dictate a sentence about those who didn’t survive.

In the Lord. That carries everything. Death isn’t blessed in itself; it is “the last enemy” (1 Corinthians 15:26), thrown at last into the lake of fire (20:14). What is blessed is dying in him — Paul’s “dead in Christ” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

The Spirit adds his word. “Blessed indeed… that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!” They rest — the word for exhausting toil, and the rest given the martyrs (6:11). Whatever heaven is, it is first described here as the end of being tired. And their deeds follow them — not going ahead as a credential, nor left behind as a legacy, but following, like servants walking behind their master into a house. Nothing done for Christ is left at the graveside: the visits no one recorded, giving that cost something, years of raising children in the faith, prayers in an empty kitchen. All of it walks in behind the one who did it (1 Corinthians 15:58).

For the funeral. This verse is for the graveside, for the person who knows he is dying, and for the one just home from the hospital who can’t think what to do next. The dead who die in the Lord are blessed; they are resting; and everything they did is on its way in after them. A test: what labour for Christ are you tempted to think is wasted? It will follow you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Harvest of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14–16: one like a son of man (Dan. 7:13; cf. Rev. 1:13) is seated on a white cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle. An angel comes out of the temple with word that the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe, and he swings his sickle and the earth is reaped — in a single sentence, with no resistance recorded.

Verses 17–19: a second angel with a sharp sickle comes out of the temple, and a third comes from the altar, having authority over the fire, and orders the vintage: gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe. The grapes are thrown into the great winepress of the wrath of God (cf. Isa. 63:3; Joel 3:13).

Verse 20: the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia — about a hundred and eighty miles, roughly the length of Palestine, and four times four times a hundred, four being the number of the earth in this book. The figure means the whole world, completely.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest of the Earth

One like a son of man reaps the ripe harvest, and the vintage of the earth is trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The timing is set by the one who has watched the field.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order for the vintage came from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers were received.

Now: The delay was never indifference but patience; the judge who reaps is the one who was trodden outside the city for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, "Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe." So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees one like a son of man on a white cloud, crowned and holding a sharp sickle; an angel from the temple says the harvest is ripe, and he reaps the earth with one swing. Christ will gather the earth’s harvest at the hour the Father has set — the long delay was patience, waiting for the harvest to ripen.

The Son of Man. “One like a son of man” on a cloud is Daniel 7:13, the phrase used of the risen Christ in 1:13. A victor’s crown on his head — and in his hand, not a sword or sceptre, but a farm tool.

Is this Christ or an angel? Some take the figure as an angel, since in the next verse an angel tells him to start reaping — an odd thing for a creature to say to the Son of God. The objection is fair. But an angel coming “out of the temple” brings word from the Father’s presence, and Jesus said, “concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Mark 13:32). A message from the sanctuary that the hour has come is exactly what the Son said he awaited. The more likely reading is that this is Christ.

Two harvests. Whether they are two pictures of one judgment or two gatherings is debated. The grain harvest here has not one hostile word: a sickle, a ripe field, a reaping. The grape harvest (vv. 17–20) is plainly wrath. So many take the first as the ingathering of the redeemed and the second as the judgment of the wicked, matching the parable of the wheat and weeds, where the reapers gather the wheat into the barn (Matthew 13:30, 39). Others take both as judgment, since Joel puts sickle and winepress together (Joel 3:13). The first is the more likely.

The right day. “The hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe” — literally dried out, over-ready. Anyone who has waited on a crop knows there is a right day. Cut too early and the grain is green and worthless; wait too long and it shatters on the ground. The point isn’t the violence of reaping but that a decision about timing is made by Someone who has been watching the field.

How long? The question running since 6:10. The delay was never indifference or failure of nerve, but a harvest not yet ready. Peter says what was ripening: the Lord “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). A test: if the harvest came today, would you be gathered into the barn? Make sure of it now, while the patience lasts.

One swing. After thirteen chapters of seals, trumpets, beasts and dragons, the end arrives in a single sentence with no resistance recorded. No battle, no dialogue. The instrument that finishes the age is a sickle swung once by a man on a cloud.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, "Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse's bridle, for 1,600 stadia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another angel with a sickle gathers the vine of the earth at the command of the angel from the altar and throws it into the great winepress of God’s wrath, trodden outside the city, and blood flows for 1,600 stadia. God’s judgment on the wicked answers his people’s prayers and is terrible in scale — yet outside the city Christ has already been trodden for all who will trust him.

From the altar. The order comes from the angel “who has authority over the fire,” from the altar the reader has visited three times: where the saints’ prayers were burned with incense (8:3–4), where fire was thrown to earth (8:5), where the voice released the sixth trumpet (9:13). Beneath it the martyrs cried “how long?” (6:9–10). The vintage of God’s wrath is ordered from the place where the church’s prayers were received. The martyrs asked; this is the answer arriving.

The winepress. A stone trough where men trod grapes barefoot while the juice ran into a vat — hard, ordinary work, and one of the oldest pictures of judgment in Scripture. “I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me… their lifeblood spattered on my garments” (Isaiah 63:3); “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Go in, tread, for the winepress is full” (Joel 3:13). John quotes both.

Outside the city. The detail that should stop a Christian reader. That is where the sin offering was burned under the law, and where Jesus died: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). There are two treadings of that press outside that city. At the first, one man went in alone, and the blood was his own. Everyone at the second will have refused the first. That is the mercy hidden in the most violent verse in the book. A test: have you taken refuge in the first treading — his blood shed for you?

The scale. 1,600 stadia is about 184 miles, roughly the length of the land of Israel — a distance any reader could picture. And 1,600 is four times four times a hundred: four is the number of the earth in this book, and a hundred squares it — the whole world, completely. Blood as high as a horse’s bridle across a country isn’t a casualty forecast. It is a statement of scale and horror in the only register that can carry it.

Are the two harvests two different events? The more likely reading is that they are two sides of the one final coming: the grain harvest, the gathering of God’s people (Matthew 13:30), and the grape harvest, the judgment of the wicked. Jesus said, “the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels” (Matthew 13:39).

No comment. The chapter ends there, deliberately. Revelation doesn’t make judgment palatable or apologise for it. It sets it right after v. 13 — “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” — so the reader holds both. The Lamb stands on Zion with his people, counted and complete; an eternal gospel flies overhead; Babylon is announced fallen while standing; the dead in the Lord rest, their deeds following them in; and the field has been watched by Someone who knows the day. The hand on the sickle has a wound in it.
verseByVerse.note: The 1,600 stadia (v. 20) are about 184 miles; a stadion was about 607 feet — roughly the length of the land of Israel.

21.title: All Things New: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the destination toward which every page of Revelation has been moving. Every sealed scroll, every trumpet, every suffering saint, every martyr’s cry of ‘How long?’ — all of it was moving toward this: “Behold, I am making all things new.” The new creation is not the consolation prize for a plan that nearly failed. It is the goal, the telos, the end for which the whole story was told.

The chapter falls into two great movements. The first (vv. 1–8) describes the new heaven and new earth from a distance — the cosmic renewal, the descent of the holy city, the voice from the throne declaring the end of tears and death, and the character of those who will inherit and those who will not. The second (vv. 9–27) zooms in: the angel takes John in the Spirit to a high mountain and shows him the new Jerusalem in breathtaking architectural detail — dimensions, gates, foundations, materials, light, temple, nations.

The key to the chapter is understanding what the new Jerusalem is. It is not primarily a city in the architectural sense; it is a person — “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.” The new Jerusalem is the church, the bride of Christ, dwelling with God in the fullness of the covenant relationship that all of redemptive history has been building toward. The city and the bride are the same reality: the people of God in their final, perfected, glorified state, living in the presence of God as his dwelling place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The New Heaven and the New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea was no more; and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The word for new is kainos, which usually means new in kind, renewed. And the direction is downward.

Verses 3–4: the dwelling place of God is with man — skēnē, a tent — with the covenant formula complete: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. Then four abolitions: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore (cf. Isa. 25:8).

Verses 5–6: God the Father speaks in the first person for the second and last time in the book — Behold, I am making all things new; Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true; It is done!; I am the Alpha and the Omega; and the offer, to the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14).

Verses 7–8: the last promise to the conqueror — I will be his God and he will be my son, the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:14 handed to anyone who holds on — and then the eight excluded categories, beginning startlingly with the cowardly and ending with all liars, whose portion is the second death.
verseByVerse.theology:
All Things New

A new heaven and earth — renewed, not replaced — and the holy city coming down as a bride. God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John, cut off by the sea from his churches, hears that the sea will be no more.

Now: God answers grief not by explanation but by removal, with his own hand on the face.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.

The whole Bible has been travelling toward this sentence. It opened with In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth, and it now says it again with one word changed.

And which word matters. The word John uses, kainos, usually stresses newness of quality rather than mere recency — new in kind, fresh, renewed. John uses kainos, here and in verse 5 and of the new Jerusalem and the new name and the new song.

That is not a technicality. It is the difference between God scrapping his creation and God renewing it. Paul says the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 8:21) — set free, not replaced. Peter looks for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Pet. 3:13). The resurrection body is the pattern: the same body, transformed and glorified, with the wounds still in the hands.

So a Christian’s hope is not that he will escape the material world into something vaporous. It is that this world — soil, water, weather, bodies, work, cities — will be put right. God does not abandon what he made. He never has.

And the sea was no more. This one troubles people who love the sea, and it should be answered rather than passed over. John is not making a statement about oceanography. In this book the sea has a settled meaning: it is the ancient image of chaos, which is why the throne room has it frozen flat as glass under God’s feet (4:6); it is where the beast comes up from (13:1); it is what swallowed the dead who had no graves (20:13). And there is a personal edge to it that John’s first readers would have felt at once — he is writing from an island, and the sea is the thing keeping him from his churches. The promise is not that there will be no water. It is that there will be nothing left that separates, threatens or devours.

And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

Watch the direction, because almost every popular picture of the Christian hope gets it backwards. The city comes down. Nobody is going up. The last movement in the Bible is not humanity being evacuated to heaven; it is heaven arriving on a renewed earth, which is what Christians have always prayed for without noticing: your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.

And the city is a bride. Not a bride’s residence — the city and the bride are the same thing, which verse 9 will make explicit when an angel offers to show John the Bride and then shows him a city. The dwelling place turns out to be the people. That is why the description that follows can be architectural and personal at once, and why nobody should try to draw it.

The reader has seen an angel offer this tour before. In 17:1 one of the seven bowl angels said Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute, and carried John into a wilderness. The same rank of angel, in almost the same words, now carries him up a mountain to see a Bride. Two women, two cities, and the book has been asking since chapter 17 which one a reader has been dressing for.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.”

The word for dwelling place is skēnē — a tent, a tabernacle — and the verb is its cognate. God will pitch his tent with them.

Follow that one word through the Bible and the whole story is on a single thread. God walked with the man and the woman in a garden in the cool of the day, and they were sent out. He told Moses, let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst, and a tent was pitched in the middle of the camp (Ex. 25:8). Solomon built a house and the glory filled it, and Ezekiel watched that glory leave. Then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us — pitched his tent among us — and John, who is writing this, is the man who wrote that sentence (John 1:14). Then the Spirit came and made a temple out of ordinary people (1 Cor. 3:16). And here is the end of it: no tent in a camp, no house on a hill, no veil, no exclusions. God with man, permanently, in the open.

And the covenant formula that runs through the whole Old Testament arrives complete: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. It was said to Abraham, to Israel at Sinai, through Jeremiah and Ezekiel, always as a promise. Here it is reported as a fact.

Note the three words God himself. Not an angel, not a representative, not glory at a safe distance. The thing the whole Bible has been arranging is not improved circumstances for human beings. It is his presence.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.

This is the second time the promise has been made in this book (7:17), and both times it says the same extraordinary thing: God does it himself, with his hand, on a face. Not an angel with a cloth. Not time healing it. Isaiah promised it first — he will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isa. 25:8).

Then four abolitions, and they should be taken one at a time rather than blurred into a general improvement.

Death shall be no more. The thing that has taken everyone a reader has ever loved, and will take him. Gone, and 20:14 has already shown how — thrown into the lake of fire.

Neither shall there be mourning — the loud public grief of a funeral, the thing you do at the graveside. Nor crying — the private version, the sound a person makes alone in a car. Nor pain — and the word covers both the body’s pain and the labour that wears a person out, which takes the reader back to the curse in Genesis 3 and undoes it.

And every one of them is answered by removal, not by explanation. Nobody in this verse is told why it happened. The promise is not that the tears will finally make sense. It is that they will be wiped off a face by God, that the thing that caused them will be dead, and that the former things have passed away.

Will we remember those we loved who are lost? Scripture does not explain how, and we should not claim to know more than it says. But it does say that we will be ourselves, known and knowing (1 Cor 13:12), and that God himself will wipe away every tear. We will see as God sees, and share his perfect justice and his perfect love. Whatever we remember, nothing will spoil the joy he gives. And that is a reason now to pray and to speak to those we love while there is time.

Which is the verse to hold when the reason for a grief has never arrived and probably never will. God does not, in the end, argue with a bereaved person. He comes over and attends to the face.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.”

This is the second and last time in the whole book that God the Father speaks in his own voice in the first person. The first was at 1:8, where he said who he is. This is what he does. Two sentences, twenty chapters apart, bracketing the dragon and the beast and the bowls and the burning city.

And every word of it repays attention. I am making is present tense — it is happening, not merely scheduled. All things, with nothing excepted. And the object is not what most people assume: he does not say I am making all new things. He says I am making all things new. Nothing is being discarded and started over. The same things — this world, these people, the bodies in the ground — are being made new.

Also he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.”

The third and last time John is told to write a particular sentence, and the pattern of the three repays a look. At 14:13: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. At 19:9: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. And here: I am making all things new. Every one of the three is a promise a suffering church would find nearly impossible to believe, and every one of them is given its own explicit command to record it and its own guarantee of truthfulness.

And he said to me, “It is done!”

One word in Greek, gegonan — the same word as at the seventh bowl (16:17) — and it echoes the cry from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30). The first made the second bearable and the third certain, and the same voice now says it over a finished world.

I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. The title from 1:8, and it has waited twenty chapters to be used again. He was the first letter when there was nothing to write about, and he is the last one now that everything has been written.

To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.

And here, at the very summit of the book, after the great white throne and the lake of fire, comes an offer. Not a reward, not a settlement, not a wage. A drink, given away.

The words are Isaiah’s: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isa. 55:1). And they are Christ’s, said to a woman at a well at noon (John 4:14), and shouted on the last day of the feast: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

Without payment is one word, dōrean — as a gift, gratis, for nothing. It is the same word Paul uses of being justified by his grace as a gift (Rom. 3:24).

And note the only qualification named: the thirsty. Not the deserving, not the improved, not the people who worked it out. The single requirement for the water of life is wanting it, and the book will make the same offer one last time in its final chapter with the doors held open (22:17).

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son.

The last of the promises to the conqueror, and the reader should hear the whole series close. Seven times in chapters 2 and 3 something was promised to the one who conquers — the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority over the nations and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed before the Father, a pillar in the temple, a seat on the throne. Here is the eighth and final one, and it is not a thing at all.

I will be his God and he will be my son. That sentence was said to exactly one man in the Old Testament. God said it to David about his heir: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Sam. 7:14). It is the promise that made the royal line, and the New Testament applies it to Christ (Heb. 1:5). And here it is handed, without qualification, to anyone who conquers — which chapter 12 defined as anyone who holds on to Christ at cost.

Which means the final reward of this book is not real estate. It is adoption. Everything else on the list — the tree, the crown, the stone, the throne — turns out to have been describing what belongs to a son in his father’s house.

But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.

Eight categories, and the first one will stop any honest reader: the cowardly. Not the murderers, not the idolaters. The cowardly, listed first, in a book written to people who had every reason to be frightened.

That has to be handled carefully, because it will land on the wrong person if it is not. The word does not mean a Christian who is afraid. If fear disqualified, the list would include Elijah under a broom tree, Peter in a courtyard, and every one of the apostles on the night of the arrest. Christ said fear not to John in the first chapter of this book precisely because John was on his face and terrified.

What the word names, in this setting, is the person whose fear made the decision — who denied the name, took the mark, said the words about Caesar and went home safe. It is the opposite of the endurance the book has been calling for. Cowardice here is not an emotion; it is an act of apostasy carried out for the sake of safety.

So a believer who reads verse 8 and is frightened by it is, by that very reaction, showing that it is not describing him. The people in this list are not troubled by it. And the paragraph has an escape written into it two verses earlier, in the widest terms the Bible ever uses: to the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment. Peter denied Christ three times with oaths and was given breakfast on a beach and a commission.

Does all liars mean that any lie damns, so that a Christian who has lied is lost? No. The list describes the settled character of those who belong to the lie and reject the truth (22:15), not believers who have sinned and repented. Every believer has lied; the blood of Christ cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). The warning is for those who make falsehood their way of life, and a call to everyone to come to Christ.

And the last item on the list closes a loop of its own: all liars. It shuts a loop that has run through the whole book. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world; the second beast deceives by signs; Babylon deceived the nations by her sorcery. And of the redeemed on Mount Zion John wrote, in their mouth no lie was found (14:5). Two companies, and one of the things that finally separates them is whether they told the truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–11: one of the seven bowl angels — the same rank, and almost the same words, as 17:1 — says Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb, and carries John to a great high mountain (17:3 was a wilderness). He promised a Bride and shows a city: the people are the place. It has the glory of God, radiant like jasper, clear as crystal — the description of the one on the throne at 4:3.

Verses 12–14: twelve gates, three on each side, bearing the names of the twelve tribes (cf. Num. 2; Ezek. 48:30–35); twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles (cf. Eph. 2:19–20). Verses 15–17: the city is measured with a golden rod — 12,000 stadia, about fourteen hundred miles, its length and width and height are equal — and its wall 144 cubits, twelve times twelve.

Verses 18–21: a wall of jasper and a city of gold like clear glass; twelve foundation stones named one by one, most of them from the high priest’s breastpiece (Ex. 28:17–21); twelve gates each made of a single pearl; and a street of gold like transparent glass.

Verse 22: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. Verses 23–25: no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light and its lamp is the Lamb (cf. Isa. 60:19); the nations walk by that light and the kings bring their glory in; the gates never shut, and there is no night. Verses 26–27: they will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations — and nothing unclean, detestable or false enters, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bride, the City

The Bride is shown as a city coming down from God, bearing the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. It is a cube — the Most Holy Place enlarged — with no temple, for its temple is God and the Lamb; no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; gates that never shut; and only those written in the Lamb’s book inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the high priest carried over his heart once a year is now the city’s foundation, and every gate is a pearl.

Now: Nobody will be nearer to God than anybody else, and there will be no night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, "Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.”

John records the angel’s job description at length — one of the seven who had the seven bowls of the seven last plagues — and the reason is that he wants the reader to make a connection. At 17:1 it was one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls who said Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute. The same rank, the same opening word, and a different woman.

And the locations answer each other. To see the prostitute, John was carried into a wilderness (17:3). To see the Bride, he is carried to a great, high mountain — which is where Ezekiel was taken to be shown a city (Ezek. 40:2). One woman is seen in a desert; the other from a height.

And showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God.

He promised a Bride and produced a city, and John does not treat that as a change of subject. The people are the place. That is the same identification the New Testament makes everywhere — the church is a building, a temple, a body, a household, a bride — and it is why the measurements that follow can be enormous without being absurd.

And the direction is stated for the second time in nine verses: coming down out of heaven from God. It is not built up from the earth. Babylon began at a tower whose builders said let us build ourselves a city… and let us make a name for ourselves (Gen. 11:4). Every human city since has been that project. This one is lowered into place, finished, by somebody else.

Having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.

The first thing said about the city is not its size or its gates. It is that it has the glory of God — the weight of God’s presence that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter and the temple so that the priests could not stand. The thing that had to be curtained off is now the city’s ordinary lighting.

And jasper, clear as crystal is exactly how John described the one seated on the throne in 4:3. The city looks like him. A bride wearing her husband’s appearance is not a bad definition of what the church is finally for, and it is what Paul meant by being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed— on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed — on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.

Start with the wall, because it is named first and it is the strangest thing here. A wall in the ancient world had one purpose: to keep an army out. This city has no army to fear. The last enemy was dealt with a chapter ago and thrown into the lake of fire (20:10, 14), and in a few verses John will say the gates are never shut anyway (v. 25). So what is a wall doing in the new creation?

It is not there out of fear. It is there because a wall says that this place has an inside, and v. 27 will state the boundary plainly: nothing unclean will ever enter it. Measure that against everything you have ever loved. Every good thing you have known could be got at — the marriage, the friendship, the church, the health, the work of a lifetime; something always found a way in and spoiled it, and usually from the inside. Here at last is a good thing with a boundary that holds. The wall is not the anxiety of a city under siege. It is the settled fact of a city that will never be spoiled again.

And at the gates, twelve angels. The first time angels are posted anywhere in the Bible, they are outside a garden with drawn fire, and their work is to keep people out (Gen. 3:24). Here twelve of them stand at twelve gates that never close. Nothing about the posting has changed except what it is for: the sentries are still at their stations, and there is nothing left for them to do but watch the nations walk in.

Twelve gates, three on each side, is the layout of the camp of Israel in the wilderness, where three tribes camped on each side of the tabernacle (Num. 2), and it is the plan of Ezekiel’s city, which ends with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (Ezek. 48:30–35).

And the gates face all four directions, which is the point of listing them. A city with gates on one side has a preferred approach and a back. This one can be entered from anywhere — from the east where the exile went, from the north where the invasions came, from the south where Egypt was, from the west where Rome was. Nobody arrives at the wrong side.

And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

Twelve tribes on the gates and twelve apostles in the foundations. Israel and the church, built into one structure, and neither of them is an extension bolted on to the other. Paul said the same thing without the architecture: the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Eph. 2:19–20).

And there is something quietly astonishing about names in foundations. Twelve men are named in the stonework of the eternal city, and every reader knows what those twelve were like: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, a man who denied Christ with oaths and a man who would not believe the resurrection without putting his hand in the wound. Their names are cut into the foundations of the new creation.

Set that beside the city they are being contrasted with. Babylon’s great ones were her merchants (18:23). This city’s great ones are twelve provincial nobodies, most of whom suffered and many of whom died for saying that a crucified man had come back.

verseByVerse.quote: And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel's measurement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls.

Measuring, in this book, means claiming and protecting. John was given a rod at 11:1 and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers, and expressly not the outer court, which was given over to be trampled. The measuring there was partial, and it was a mercy. This one is total: the city, its gates and its walls, all of it, with a rod of gold.

The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.

Two things, and both are enormous.

The size first. Twelve thousand stadia is roughly fourteen hundred miles — about the distance from Jerusalem to Rome. And it is that in every direction, including up. Nobody is meant to picture this successfully. What the figure does is answer a fear that no Christian likes to admit: whether there will be room. Twelve, the number of God’s people, times a thousand.

Then the shape, and this is the detail everything in the chapter has been building toward. Its length and width and height are equal. The city is a perfect cube.

There is exactly one cube in the Bible. In Solomon’s temple, the inner sanctuary — the Most Holy Place — was twenty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty high (1 Kings 6:20). A cube, and the only one, and it was the place where the ark stood behind the veil, which one man entered once a year with blood, having washed, and did not linger in.

The new Jerusalem is that room, expanded to the size of a continent, with everybody living inside it. That is the single most important fact about the city, and it explains verse 22 in advance: there is no temple in the city because the city is the temple, and there is no veil because there is nothing left to keep anyone out.

He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement.

A hundred and forty-four is twelve times twelve, the number that has run through the book since the 144,000 were sealed. And the odd clause at the end — by human measurement, which is also an angel’s — is John telling the reader that the figures are not being given in some other currency. Whatever the numbers are doing symbolically, they are not a code that would come out differently in heaven.

And the proportions are deliberately impossible. A wall of a hundred and forty-four cubits — about two hundred feet — around a city fourteen hundred miles high. It would not keep anything out and could not be seen from most of the city. Which is the point: this wall is not for defence. There is nothing left to defend against. It is a boundary, marking what is inside as holy, and its gates never close.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes give 12,000 stadia as about 1,380 miles; 144 cubits is about 216 feet. The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass.

Gold that light goes through. It is not a description of a material anybody has ever handled, and John says something similar three verses later about the street. Whatever this city is made of, its most precious substance has stopped being opaque. Nothing in it casts a shadow or hides what is behind it.

The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.

Twelve stones, listed one by one, with their positions numbered. John takes a whole verse and a half to do it, and the slowness is the effect. This is a man walking along a wall naming colours.

The list has an address. The high priest of Israel wore a breastpiece set with twelve stones in four rows, one for each tribe, and he carried them on his heart… to regular remembrance before the LORD whenever he went into the holy place (Ex. 28:17–21, 29). Most of John’s stones are on that list, and several of the names differ only because the Greek translation of the Old Testament rendered them differently.

So the foundations of the city are the high priest’s breastpiece, laid out flat and built into the ground. What one man carried over his heart into the holy place is now the foundation everybody walks on. And the carnelian and the jasper — the first and last of the twelve tribal stones — are the two colours John used of the one seated on the throne in 4:3.

And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl.

A pearl is the one precious thing in the ancient world that is not mined or cut. It is made by an oyster, slowly, in response to an injury — a grain of grit that could not be expelled, covered over layer by layer for years until the wound is the treasure.

Jesus told a parable about a merchant in search of fine pearls who found one of great value and sold everything he had to buy it (Matt. 13:45–46). The gate into the eternal city is that pearl, and there are twelve of them, and every one is a single stone, which means every one of them took a very long time and began with a wound.

And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.

The most valuable substance the ancient world knew, used for the surface people walk on. Babylon’s manifest began with gold and silver and jewels and pearls (18:12), and merchants wept when they could no longer sell it. Here the same materials are paving.

That is not a statement that wealth is unimportant. It is a statement about proportion. Everything the world killed for turns out, in the only city that lasts, to be surfacing — and a reader who has spent a lifetime arranging his affairs around such things is being shown what they are for.
verseByVerse.note: The twelve jewels recall the stones on the high priest’s breastpiece, engraved with the names of the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.

One sentence that overturns the entire religious history of the world.

Consider what a temple is. Every civilisation has built them, and every one of them answers the same problem: God is holy and people are not, so there must be a designated place, a mediating class, a set of rules for approach, and a barrier between the God and the worshipper. Israel’s was the most carefully regulated of them all. There was a court the nations could enter, a court beyond that for Israel, a court beyond that for men, a court beyond that for priests, and behind a curtain a room one man entered once a year with blood in his hands.

Ezekiel spent nine chapters on a temple. The Jews of John’s day had watched theirs burn twenty-five years before he wrote and expected another. And John looks at the city of God and reports that there is no temple in it.

Not because worship has ended. Because the arrangement a temple exists to manage has ended. The problem a temple solves — how sinful people can be near a holy God without being destroyed — has been solved somewhere else, by somebody, and the verse names him: its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.

And the last two words are the answer. There is no temple because there is a Lamb. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51) — from the top, by somebody reaching down — and this verse is that tearing carried to its conclusion. He is not merely the priest and not merely the sacrifice. He is the building.

Which is also why the city is a cube. The Most Holy Place was the one room in the world where God’s presence was unveiled, and the whole city is now that room. Everybody lives inside the holy of holies. There is no outer court, no restricted section, no closer and further; nobody is nearer to God than anybody else, and nobody is waiting outside for a priest to come back and tell him it went well.

Every Christian who has ever felt that God is available in certain places and at certain times, that some people have better access, that the holy is somewhere he visits rather than somewhere he lives — this verse is the end of all of it. The final condition of the redeemed is not going to a holy place. It is living inside one, with the one who made it standing in the middle.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.

The second thing missing, after the temple: the sun. Genesis 1 gives two great lights on the fourth day, and Isaiah promised a day when the sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but the LORD will be your everlasting light (Isa. 60:19).

They are not destroyed. There is no need of them, which is different. A lamp is not a criticism of the sun; it is simply irrelevant at noon. The sun and moon have been doing a job on loan for the whole of history, and the owner has arrived.

And its lamp is the Lamb. The word is a household lamp, the small clay dish with a wick that lit a single room after dark. The glory of God is the light of the city, and the Lamb is the fitting that carries it — which is precisely what he has been since the first chapter, where his face was like the sun shining in full strength (1:16), and precisely what he said of himself: I am the light of the world (John 8:12).

By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it.

This is Isaiah 60 again, almost word for word: nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising… the wealth of the nations shall come to you (Isa. 60:3, 5). And it is startling in a book that has spent nineteen chapters on the kings of the earth committing immorality with a prostitute and making war on the Lamb.

Those kings are dead; these are not the same men. What John is describing is not an amnesty for Babylon but the redemption of the nations as nations — and it raises a question worth asking honestly. What is their glory? The text does not say, and guessing is a poor substitute for reading. But the phrase does imply that what the peoples of the earth have made and been is not simply erased. Something is carried in.

That is a real word to anyone who has wondered whether ordinary human work has any future — whether the making of music, the building of things, the raising of crops and children and languages and cities is all going into a fire. This verse says that the gates are open and something is being brought in through them.

And its gates will never be shut by day — and there will be no night there.

A gate is shut for one reason. Every walled city in the ancient world closed its gates at sundown, and that was the moment the day’s safety ended: after dark, whatever was outside stayed outside, and anybody who had not got home was not getting home.

This city has gates that never shut, and John adds the reason with a dash: there will be no night there. The two clauses are one thought. The gates stay open because the hour at which a gate is shut never comes.

Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning knows what is being taken away. Night in Scripture is not simply darkness; it is when the thief comes, when the enemy moves, when a person is alone with what he has done, when the sick get worse and the frightened get more frightened. There is none of it, ever again, and the gates of the city are open at what would have been midnight.

verseByVerse.quote: They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

The two verses have to be held together, because each guards the other.

Verse 26 is the widest sentence in the chapter. The glory and the honour of the nations — not of one nation, and not of the church only. Whatever is genuinely glorious in what human beings have made and become, from every people on earth, is carried through those open gates. The multitude of chapter 7 came from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, and they do not arrive empty-handed.

And verse 27 immediately shuts the door on any sentimentality about it. Nothing unclean will ever enter. The gates are always open and they are not unguarded. This is not a city where everything is welcome; it is a city where everything that is welcome has been made clean.

Three exclusions, and they are not a list of the worst crimes anyone could think of. Unclean is the ceremonial word — what could not come into the sanctuary. Detestable is the word used all through the Old Testament of idolatry, and it was written on the prostitute’s forehead in 17:5. False closes the loop one final time: the dragon deceived, the false prophet deceived, Babylon deceived, and the redeemed are the ones in whose mouth no lie was found (14:5).

But look at how the sentence actually ends, because the criterion is not a moral audit. But only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

That is the last mention of the book in Revelation, and it lands exactly where it did at the great white throne: not on what a person achieved but on whether his name is in a register belonging to a Lamb who was slain, written from the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15).

Which means the two halves of these verses are not in tension at all. Nothing unclean enters — and the whole book has been showing how the unclean become clean, in the most impossible image it could find: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Nobody walks in on his own record. Everybody who walks in has had something done to him first.

So the chapter closes with the door open and the qualification stated. A city fourteen hundred miles high, made of the Most Holy Place, with the glory of God for daylight and the Lamb for a lamp, its foundations set with the stones a high priest wore over his heart and its gates each cut from a single pearl that began as a wound — and the gates never close, and the only people inside are the ones whose names were written in a book before the world was made.

God himself is with them. There is no temple, because he is there. There is no sun, because he is there. There is no night, because he is there. And there are no tears, because he has been over and attended to their faces with his own hand.
