22.title: Come, Lord Jesus: The River, the Tree, and the Final Invitation
22.overview:
The final chapter of Revelation — and of the entire Bible — has the quality of a great symphony resolving into its final chord. Everything that has been promised, everything that has been anticipated, every thread of the biblical story, gathers here and arrives. The river of the water of life. The tree of life with twelve kinds of fruit. The servants of God seeing his face. His name on their foreheads. No more night. And then, three times: ‘I am coming soon.’ And the great response of the church across all the ages: ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’

The chapter is framed by the river and tree (vv. 1–5) and the final testimony and invitation (vv. 6–21). The garden returns — but infinitely elevated. Eden had a river flowing from it (Genesis 2:10); the new Jerusalem has a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. Eden had the tree of life (Genesis 2:9); the new Jerusalem has the tree of life bearing twelve kinds of fruit, one each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in the garden is restored in the city, but the city is greater than the garden: the tree is no longer guarded by cherubim with flaming swords (Genesis 3:24) — it stands in the middle of the street, its fruit available to all.

The closing testimony of the book weaves together three voices: the angel confirming the truth of what has been shown, Jesus speaking in the first person (‘I, Jesus, have sent my angel...’; ‘I am coming soon’), and the Spirit and Bride together issuing the great invitation: ‘Come.’ The book ends not with explanation but with longing — the longing of the church for her Lord, the longing of the Lord for his people, the longing of the Spirit for the consummation of all things. This is the last word of the Bible, and it is the word the whole church has been praying for two thousand years: Come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The River and the Tree of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the street; and on either side of it the tree of life, bearing twelve crops a year, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (cf. Ezek. 47:1–12). The Bible has been away from a river and a tree since Genesis 3, where cherubim with a flaming sword were set to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 2:9–10; 3:24). The promise made to Ephesus in the first letter (2:7) is being kept.

Verse 3: No longer will there be anything accursed — the sentence of Genesis 3:17–19 lifted — but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. Verse 4: They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. Verse 5: no night, no need of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The River and the Tree

The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands open with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, and his servants will see his face.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The way to the tree, guarded since Eden, stands open in the middle of the street.

Now: Heaven is not first a place but a face — seen at last, and lived through.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month.

A river and a tree. The Bible has been away from these two things for one thousand one hundred and eighty-six chapters, and here they are again.

Genesis 2 has a river flowing out of Eden to water the garden, and the tree of life… in the midst of the garden (Gen. 2:9–10). Genesis 3 ends with the man and the woman put out, and cherubim with a flaming sword set to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 3:24). From that verse to this one, nobody eats from it. The whole of Scripture happens in the interval between a tree being fenced off and a tree being handed back.

And the promise made to the first of the seven churches is being kept: To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God (2:7). Ephesus was told that in a letter. Here is the tree.

But this is not simply Eden reopened, and the differences are the point. Eden was a garden; this is a garden inside a city, with the river running through the middle of the street. Eden had one tree of life; here the tree stands on either side of the river, which is impossible to draw and easy to understand — wherever a person walks, it is on both sides of him. Eden could be lost. This cannot.

God does not restore his people to the place they started. He takes them somewhere better than the place they started, and the road ran through a cross.

Note where the river comes from: flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. One throne, two names, and John does not pause to explain how. And what flows out of it is not judgment but water. Ezekiel saw the same thing — water trickling from under the threshold of the temple, deepening as it went until it was a river nobody could cross, with trees on both banks whose leaves would not wither (Ezek. 47:1–12).

Yielding its fruit each month. Twelve crops a year, from a tree that never has an off season. Anyone who has grown anything knows that fruit trees rest — there are months with nothing on them. This one does not stop.

The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.

The phrase puzzles readers, and rightly: there is no sickness in this city, and the previous chapter has just abolished pain. Ezekiel is the source again — their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing (Ezek. 47:12). The Greek word behind healing is therapeia, from which we get therapy, and it can mean care and tending as much as cure.

The most natural sense is not that anybody is ill but that the nations are being kept well — that the life of the city is continually supplied rather than merely started. And there is something else in it. The word nations has been a hostile word for most of this book: the nations raged, the nations drank Babylon’s wine, the beast had authority over every nation. Here the nations are the ones being tended. The long wound in human history — peoples divided at a tower, scattered, at each other’s throats ever since — has leaves growing for it.
verseByVerse.note: Eden’s river and tree of life return, now in a city.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer will there be anything accursed.

One clause, and it reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible. When the man and the woman were sent out, God said cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you… till you return to the ground (Gen. 3:17–19). Everything hard about human existence — the labour that exhausts, the ground that resists, the body that fails — has stood under that sentence.

And it is lifted. Not managed, not compensated for, not explained — removed, and the removal was accomplished by somebody becoming a curse for us, because it is written cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13). There are two trees at the end of this book. On one of them the curse was absorbed; from the other one the fruit is handed out twelve times a year.

But the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. The throne has been the fixed point of the vision since chapter 4, and it has always been in heaven. Now it is in it — in the city, on the renewed earth, at the end of the street with the river running out of it.

And then the sentence that the whole Bible has been walking toward, and it is five words long.

They will see his face.

Stop there, because nothing in Scripture is bigger than this. Moses — who spoke with God as a man speaks to his friend — asked for exactly this one thing, and was told you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live. He was put in a cleft of the rock and covered with a hand and shown God’s back (Ex. 33:18–23). The high priest went behind a veil once a year and saw nothing. Isaiah saw the hem of a robe and cried out that he was undone. In chapter 6 of this book, kings and generals begged mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne (6:16).

And here, without ceremony, in a subordinate clause: they will see his face. The thing Moses was refused. The thing the whole sacrificial system existed to make impossible without blood. Ordinary people — a slave from Laodicea, a widow from Thyatira, a man who denied Christ once in a courtyard and never got over it — looking directly at God, and living.

John wrote the same promise in a letter, and admitted he could not fill it in: Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). And Jesus put it in a beatitude: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 5:8).

That is what heaven is. Not a location with good weather; not a reunion, though there will be one; not the end of trouble, though trouble ends. It is a face. Everything else in these two chapters — the gold, the jewels, the river, the open gates — is furniture in a room where that is happening.

And his name will be on their foreheads. The last of the marked foreheads in this book, and the counterfeit has been eliminated. The seal of 7:3, the Lamb’s name at 14:1, and the beast’s mark at 13:16 have all been leading here: everyone is labelled, and these are labelled with him.

And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever. Said for the second time in eight verses (21:23–25), which is John’s way of underlining. And the last word of the description is reign — the promise made to Laodicea, the weakest church on the road, arriving in full.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: the vision is over and the book begins closing itself by matching its own opening — the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place (cf. 1:1). Then the speaker changes without warning: And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book — the sixth beatitude, almost word for word the first one at 1:3.

Verses 8–9: John falls down to worship the angel a second time and is stopped a second time, in almost the words of 19:10 — I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.

Verses 10–11: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near — the exact reverse of what Daniel was told (Dan. 12:4, 9) — followed by the hardest verse in the chapter: Let the evildoer still do evil… and the holy still be holy.

Verses 12–13: the second I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done (cf. Isa. 40:10), and three pairs of titles: Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end. Verses 14–15: the seventh and last beatitude — Blessed are those who wash their robes — and the list of those outside, ending with everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Verse 16: I, Jesus, have sent my angel… I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Testimony of Jesus

The book closes as it opened: blessed is the one who keeps its words. The angel refuses John’s worship again — Worship God. The book is left unsealed, for the time is near. Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, root and descendant of David, the bright morning star, is coming soon; blessed are those who wash their robes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole vision was given for the churches, to be read aloud in small rooms.

Now: While the door is open, ask which way your life is already heading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, “These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place.”

The vision is over. From here to the end, the book is closing itself, and it does so by going back to its first sentence. Compare 1:1: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John. The same chain of custody, the same phrase, the same servants. John is signing off by matching the letterhead.

The God of the spirits of the prophets is an unusual title and it is doing specific work. It says that the same God who spoke through Isaiah and Ezekiel and Daniel — whose words have been quoted on nearly every page of this book — is the one who has spoken here. Revelation is not a new departure. It is the last chapter of a document that has been in progress for fifteen centuries.

“And behold, I am coming soon.”

The speaker changes without warning — the angel has been talking, and suddenly it is Christ. He will say this three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 12, 20), and it is the drumbeat the book ends on.

And the word is the one from 1:1, so the difficulty is the same difficulty and deserves the same honest answer rather than an embarrassed one. The three answers given there still stand: the word is about speed and not the calendar, the New Testament dates nearness from the cross, and a great deal of what this book describes did arrive within the lifetimes of the people who first read it. What the last page adds is Peter, who was answering this very objection while it was still fresh: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you (2 Pet. 3:8–9). The delay is not indifference. It is mercy, and somebody is being brought in during it.

Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.

The sixth of the seven beatitudes, and it is almost word for word the first one, at 1:3. The book opens and closes with a blessing on the same person — not the one who understands it, or charts it, or identifies the beast, but the one who keeps it. Whatever else a reader takes from Revelation, that is the bracket he is being asked to live inside.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me.

He does it again. He did it at 19:10, was stopped in almost these words, and here at the very end of the book, with the correction still in his own manuscript three chapters earlier, he goes down a second time.

That is not flattering to John and he wrote it down anyway, which is itself a kind of testimony. He is not presenting himself as a man who learned his lesson. And it should be a comfort to anyone who has repeated a fault he had already repented of: the last recorded action of the apostle who wrote this book is a mistake he had made before.

Notice also when it happens. Not in the middle of the terror — not at the dragon or the beast or the lake of fire — but immediately after the river and the tree and the face. It is the beauty that undoes him. The instinct is right; only the direction is wrong, and a man overwhelmed by glory reaches for the nearest thing that is holding it.

But he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.”

Two words at the end, and they are among the shortest complete instructions in Scripture. Worship God. Twenty-two chapters of visions and this is the summary.

And look at how the angel describes himself, because the list is longer than it was at 19:10. He is a fellow servant with John, with your brothers the prophets, and — this is new — with those who keep the words of this book. That last group is the reader. An angel of God has just put himself in the same category as an ordinary Christian who reads Revelation and does what it says.

Which is the answer, given twice for emphasis, to a permanent danger in the church. The people through whom God speaks — preachers, writers, movements, teachers — are always in danger of receiving what belongs to God, and the danger is greatest when what they have brought is genuinely glorious. The remedy is not to think less of the messenger. It is two words.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.”

The exact reverse of what Daniel was told. Daniel finished his visions and was instructed: shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end (Dan. 12:4, 9). John is told to leave it open, and the reason given is the difference between the two men: for Daniel the time was far off; for John the time is near.

And it is the reverse of what John himself was told at 10:4, when the seven thunders spoke and he was reaching for his pen and heard seal up what the seven thunders have said. There is exactly one sealed sentence in Revelation and we do not have it. Everything else in the book is open, on purpose, by instruction.

Which should settle the way this book is approached. It is not a locked document awaiting a key, and it never was. Its author’s explicit command is that it be left unsealed, and its blessing falls on the person who keeps it rather than the person who cracks it.

Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.

This is the hardest verse in the chapter and it must not be softened into something comfortable. Read carelessly it sounds like God shrugging — a permission slip for wickedness and a fatalistic verdict that nobody changes.

Three things settle what it is doing.

First, its position. It comes immediately after the time is near and immediately before behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me. It is bracketed by urgency on both sides, which is the opposite of fatalism. Ezekiel was given a similar word when Israel had stopped listening (Ezek. 3:27), and Daniel too (Dan. 12:10).

Second, its form. It is a prophetic announcement rather than a divine permission. What it says is that a moment arrives after which character is fixed — that there is a point beyond which a person’s direction of travel becomes his destination. Everyone knows this is true of habits within a lifetime; the verse says it is finally true of lives.

Third, and most importantly, what it does to the reader. This is not addressed to the evildoer as an instruction. It is placed in front of somebody holding a book, at the point where the book is nearly finished, and its effect is to ask: which of those four words describes the direction you are already going? Because the door is open now and the invitation is six verses away — let the one who desires take the water of life without price — and it will not be open indefinitely.

Read like that, verse 11 is not God abandoning anybody. It is the most serious way of saying today. And a reader who finds the verse frightening is being frightened in exactly the direction it intends, while there is still time to move.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; John is told not to, because the time is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.”

The second of the chapter’s three announcements, and this one has the reward already in his hand. Bringing my recompense with me — not sent for afterwards, not calculated on arrival. Isaiah said it first of the coming of God: behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him (Isa. 40:10; 62:11).

To repay each one for what he has done. The book has raised this twice already — to Thyatira at 2:23, and at the great white throne at 20:12 — and the answer has not moved. A record has never yet admitted anybody, and it has never yet failed to identify anybody. It is the evidence of whose a man is, and the measure of what he is handed afterwards. Nobody will be standing in that scene holding an invoice.

And hold on to each one. In a scene involving every human being who has ever lived, nothing is averaged. The visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the cup of cold water — each one, by name.

There is a fear on the other side of that verse, and it keeps quiet Christians awake. A man converted at sixty, or a woman who has spent twenty years ill in a back bedroom, reads repay each one for what he has done and thinks: there is nothing of mine to bring.

Two things answer him. The first is that what gets repaid is not what he achieved but what Christ produced in him, and Christ does not fail to produce — the vine bears the fruit and the branch only carries it (John 15:5). The second is the parable Christ told about precisely this complaint: the men hired at the eleventh hour were paid the same as the men who had borne the burden of the day, and the owner’s answer was that he had wronged nobody (Matt. 20:1–16). Nobody will stand in that scene feeling short-changed, and nobody will stand in it thinking he earned what he is holding.

“I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”

Three pairs, and they gather up everything the book has said about who is speaking. Alpha and Omega was said by God the Father at 1:8 and 21:6. The first and the last was said by the risen Christ to John on Patmos at 1:17, and it is Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-identification — I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isa. 44:6). The beginning and the end completes it.

The titles move between the Father and the Son through this book without a seam and without an explanation, and that is not carelessness. Revelation never argues for the deity of Christ; it simply speaks as though the question could not arise. The one who is coming soon with his recompense is the one who was there before the first letter of history was written and will be there after the last.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates.

The seventh and last beatitude of Revelation, and it lands on the one act the whole book has been describing. Not blessed are those who understood it. Not blessed are those who suffered, though many did. Blessed are those who wash their robes — and 7:14 has already said in what: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

There is a textual detail here that a reader should have, because it is one of the most interesting in the New Testament and the ESV footnotes the verse. Some manuscripts read blessed are those who do his commandments instead of wash their robes. In Greek the two phrases are startlingly close — hoi poiountes tas entolas autou against hoi plunontes tas stolas autōn — and a tired copyist could slip from one to the other without noticing. The earliest and best manuscripts read wash their robes, which is what the ESV follows and what the imagery of this book requires.

And it matters more than a footnote usually does, because the two readings say different things about how a person gets in. One makes the entrance depend on obedience; the other makes it depend on being washed. The manuscripts favour the second, and so does every page of Revelation from chapter 5 onward.

Note also the two things the washing gives, and both are things that were lost. The right to the tree of life — the tree guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword since Genesis 3:24, now available by right rather than by trespass. And that they may enter the city by the gates, which is a strangely ordinary phrase after everything that has come before: not carried in, not admitted by a side door, but walking through the front gates like a citizen coming home.

Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

Dogs was not a term of affection in the ancient world; these were scavengers in the street, and the law used the word of what was excluded from the sanctuary (Deut. 23:18). Paul used it of men who insisted on adding requirements to the gospel (Phil. 3:2).

Where is outside, if the new earth is renewed? It is not a place beside the city where the lost live on in sight of it. It is the lake of fire, the second death (21:8, 27; 20:15), described in the language of a city wall: those who will not enter are shut out.

And the list ends where every such list in this book ends: everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Two verbs, and the first is the sharper. Not merely tells lies — loves them. The dragon has been the deceiver of the whole world since 12:9, and the redeemed on Mount Zion were described in one clause: in their mouth no lie was found (14:5). At the very end, the line between the two companies runs through whether a person loved the truth.
verseByVerse.note: The last of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Some manuscripts read “do his commandments” for “wash their robes” (ESV note) — the reading of the King James Version.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches.”

The name at last. It is the only place in the book where he says I, Jesus, and it comes after twenty-one chapters of titles — the Lamb, the faithful witness, the first and the last, the Word of God, King of kings. At the end he uses the name his mother used, the human name given to a carpenter’s son in a village.

And the audience is named too: for the churches. Not for scholars, not for a final generation, not for the curious. This enormous vision — thrones and dragons and bowls and a city fourteen hundred miles high — was produced for congregations, to be read aloud in rooms. The book ends where it began, at 1:11, with seven small assemblies on a postal road in Asia.

“I am the root and the descendant of David.”

Both at once, and the pairing is deliberate and impossible. To be David’s descendant is to come after him — the promised son of the royal line, born in David’s town, of David’s house. To be David’s root is to be what David grew out of; a root is not produced by the tree, it produces the tree.

Jesus once set that riddle himself, in the temple, and nobody would answer it. If the Christ is David’s son, he asked, why does David call him Lord? David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son? (Mark 12:35–37). This verse is the answer, given by the man who asked the question. He is David’s son by birth and David’s Lord by nature, and the two facts belong to one person.

“The bright morning star.”

And here a promise made twenty chapters ago is finally identified. Thyatira — the church in the least important town on the road, told simply to hold on until he came — was promised the morning star (2:28), and the promise was never explained. It is himself.

Behind it stands the prophecy of Balaam, of all people: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel (Num. 24:17). And the morning star is the one that rises last, when the sky is at its darkest and the night has gone on longest. It does not announce more night. It means the sun is on its way.

Which is what this book has been saying to frightened congregations from its first page. It never promises that the dark will be short. It promises who is standing in it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 17: The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14; 7:37). Verses 18–19: the covenant scribe’s closing warning against adding to or taking from the words of the prophecy (cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:5–6), with penalties that fit the offences exactly.

Verse 20: He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” — the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible — and the church’s answer, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! Verse 21: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come”; whoever hears is to say it too; whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. The book is not to be added to or taken from. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon,” and the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The earliest church prayed Marana tha — Our Lord, come.

Now: The most terrifying book in Scripture ends with grace, offered to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.

This is the last invitation in the Bible, and it is the widest sentence in the most frightening book in Scripture. After the dragon and the beast and the lake of fire and the great white throne, the second-to-last thing God says to the human race is come and have a drink.

Four movements, and they should be taken in order because the sentence is built like a chain.

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” The Holy Spirit and the church, speaking together, with one verb between them. That is the entire mission of the church in five words, and it settles the relationship: the church does not invite people on its own authority and the Spirit does not work around the church. They say it together.

And let the one who hears say, “Come.” The invitation is handed on. Anyone who has heard it becomes one of the people saying it, and there is no interval and no qualification — not the one who has matured, not the one who has been trained. The person who has just heard is immediately in the chorus.

And let the one who is thirsty come. Now the direction reverses. The first two clauses were the church calling out; this one is somebody walking in. And the only qualification named in the whole verse is thirst — not worthiness, not understanding, not improvement. Wanting it is the entrance requirement.

Let the one who desires take the water of life without price. And the last clause takes away even the word thirsty, which might sound like a condition, and replaces it with the one who desires — whoever wishes, whoever will. Then the price is stated, and it is the same word used at 21:6: dōrean, as a gift, for nothing.

Isaiah shouted it seven hundred years earlier: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! (Isa. 55:1). Jesus shouted it on the last and greatest day of the feast: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). And he said it quietly to one woman at a well at noon (John 4:14).

Consider where this verse is placed. Two verses earlier the dogs and sorcerers and murderers were outside the gate. One verse later comes a solemn warning about tampering with the book. And in between, unfenced, is the freest offer in Scripture. That is not carelessness. It is the last word on the character of the God who has been running this entire book: the one whose judgments filled sixteen chapters ends by holding out a cup and asking nothing for it.

Does let the one who desires mean that salvation depends on our will? The offer is free and open to all, and anyone who comes will receive. But a fallen heart does not thirst for God unaided; the thirst itself is the Spirit’s work, drawing people to Christ (John 6:44). The invitation is real, and so is the grace that makes people want to come.

So the answer to the question raised at 20:15 — whether a name is written in the book of life — is not have I done enough? Nobody has. It is whether a person is thirsty, and whether he will come and take what is being handed to him for nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.

The warning is severe and it is not unprecedented. It is the standard closing formula of an ancient covenant document, and Moses used it twice: You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it (Deut. 4:2; cf. 12:32). Proverbs says the same of the words of God (Prov. 30:5–6). John is doing what a covenant scribe did when the text was finished: sealing it against tampering.

Two things about what it means, because it has been misapplied in both directions.

It is not a prohibition on the work of textual scholarship. Comparing manuscripts to establish what John actually wrote is the opposite of tampering with what John wrote — it is the effort to make sure nothing has been added or lost. The ESV’s own footnote at verse 14 is that work being done honestly and in the open.

And it is not, strictly, a statement about the whole Bible. John says this book, four times in two verses, and he means the one he has just finished. The principle plainly extends to Scripture as a whole, and the church has always applied it that way; but the verse is not a note about canon.

What it is aimed at is a live danger in the first century and every century since: people who take a prophecy and improve it. Adding means supplying what God did not say — the date, the identity, the extra requirement, the private revelation that completes what Scripture left open. Taking away means removing what God did say — quietly setting aside the judgment, or the exclusivity, or the return, because it is unpopular or uncomfortable.

And the penalties fit the offences exactly, as everything in this book does. Add to the words, and what is added to you is the plagues; take away from the words, and what is taken from you is the tree and the city. In each case a person receives the operation he performed.

Can a true believer lose his salvation by taking away from this book? The warning describes those who falsify God’s word, and shows that such people never truly belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19). For believers it is a solemn reason to handle Scripture with reverence, and one of the means God uses to keep them faithful.

There is a quieter application in it than the obvious one. Very few readers will ever publish an edition of Revelation. A great many will be tempted to do to it privately what the verse forbids publicly — to add a chart the text does not authorise, or to subtract the parts that are hard to hear. The instruction of this book from beginning to end has been to keep its words, which means neither more nor less than what is written.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.”

The third and last of the announcements, and the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible. Not a command, not a warning, not a doctrine. A promise about arriving.

Everything he is has been unfolded across twenty-two chapters — the one who walks among the lampstands, the Lamb who was slaughtered and is standing, the rider with a sword out of his mouth, the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star. And the last thing he says is that he is on his way and will not be long.

Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

And the church answers. It is the only appropriate reply and it is barely a sentence — an agreement and a request. In Aramaic, the language these congregations prayed in before the Greek took over, it was one word: Marana tha, Our Lord, come. Paul dropped it untranslated into a letter to Corinth (1 Cor. 16:22), which means it was already a prayer people said without needing it explained.

That is the state of the church between the two comings, and it is the answer to everything the book has shown. Not a strategy. Not a timetable. A prayer that somebody would come, said by people who cannot make him come and are certain he will.

And it is a fair test of a Christian’s actual condition, gently applied. A person who says Come, Lord Jesus and means it is a person who has nothing here he would be unwilling to have interrupted. That is not a rebuke to anybody who finds the prayer harder than he expected; it is simply what the prayer measures, and Revelation was written to people who could say it because they had already lost most of what a person might have wanted to keep.

The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.

And the last verse of the Bible is a benediction.

Consider what this book has contained. Four horsemen. A third of mankind dead. A dragon waiting to devour a child. A beast given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation. Bowls of undiluted wrath. A city drunk on the blood of the saints, burned in a single hour. A great white throne with the books opened and no place found for earth or sky. It is, by a distance, the most terrifying document ever written.

And the last word is grace.

Not a warning, though there have been many. Not a summary of the judgments. Not instructions for a final generation. The same word Paul ended every one of his letters with — unearned favour, given to people who have nothing to bring — extended here to all, and then one more Amen, which means it is firm, it is so.

So the Bible closes. It opened with a garden, a river and a tree, and a man and a woman walking with God in the cool of the day; and it closes with a city, a river and a tree, and a countless multitude out of every nation looking directly at his face. Between the two lies the whole of human history, and at the centre of it a Lamb standing as though slaughtered, who took a scroll nobody else was worthy to open, and opened it.

Did Jesus mean Surely I am coming soon, after two thousand years? Soon means that his coming is the next great event, near and sudden, not that it would come within a set time. Peter explains the delay: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and his patience gives time for repentance (2 Pet 3:8–9). The right response is the church’s prayer: Come, Lord Jesus!

He is the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. He was dead, and behold he is alive for evermore, and he has the keys of Death and Hades. He is coming soon. And the last thing he leaves with his church, after everything, is grace.
verseByVerse.note: “Come, Lord Jesus” matches the Aramaic prayer Maranatha that Paul quotes.

15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the shortest chapter in Revelation — eight verses — but it is one of the most carefully constructed. It serves as the vestibule to the seven bowl visions of chapter 16, doing what chapters 4–5 did before the seals and what chapters 8:1–5 did before the trumpets: grounding the coming sequence in the worship and sovereignty of God before a single bowl is poured. Before heaven acts in judgment, heaven first breaks into song.

The chapter presents two contrasting scenes held in deliberate tension. The first (vv. 1–4): the victorious on the sea of glass, harps in hand, singing the Song of Moses and the Lamb. The second (vv. 5–8): seven angels emerge from the heavenly temple dressed for a solemn task, given seven golden bowls by one of the four living creatures, while the temple fills with the glory of God so completely that no one can enter until the seven bowls are finished. Praise and solemn purpose belong together. The song is not premature celebration; it is the theological foundation without which the coming acts of God would be misread.

The Song of Moses and the Lamb is one of the richest theological moments in the book. It binds together the two great saving acts of God — the Exodus and the cross — into a single song of praise. The God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. The Lamb who was slain is the LORD who drowned Pharaoh’s army. The song the victorious sing is drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy — the whole Hebrew Scripture gathered into the church’s final praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: another sign in heaven, great and amazing — the third and last of the book’s three signs, after the woman (12:1) and the dragon (12:3). Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished. The verb is from teleō, the same root as the word from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30).

Verse 2: the sea of glass of 4:6 is now mingled with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, holding harps — a direct contradiction of 13:7, where the beast was allowed to conquer them. The position is the far shore of the Red Sea with Egypt behind it.

Verses 3–4: they sing the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb — one song under two names. Its words are not from Exodus 15 but are a mosaic of Scripture: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2), Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4), Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7), All nations will come and worship you (Ps. 86:9). Four clauses, and every one is about God — not one word about the beast, the persecution, or their own endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished — it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a great and amazing sign: seven angels with the seven last plagues, which complete God’s wrath. God’s wrath against sin is not endless or out of control; it has a fixed end — and for believers it was finished at the cross.

Getting the reader ready. The shortest chapter in Revelation does one job: preparation. Chapter 16 pours out seven bowls in twenty-one verses, faster and heavier than anything in the book; chapter 15 is the eight verses before it.

The third sign in heaven. The only other signs in heaven were in chapter 12: the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the red dragon (12:3). A woman, a dragon, and seven angels with the last plagues: the mother, the enemy, and the end.

Great and amazing. An odd pair for a plague, and John will use them of God’s deeds in v. 3. Not merely dreadful but astonishing, as something enormous and long-expected is when it finally begins.

Finished. “For with them the wrath of God is finished.” The verb is from the same root as Jesus’ cry from the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30). Something is brought to its appointed completion, and the sentence says so before a single bowl is lifted.

Wrath has an end; mercy doesn’t. A reader after six chapters of dragons and beasts might fear God’s wrath is a bottomless reservoir that, once started, never stops. This verse says the opposite: it has an end, in view from the moment it begins, and a last plague after which there are no more. That isn’t true of his mercy, and the contrast is the point. Scripture says his steadfast love endures forever and never says that of his anger: “his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime” (Psalm 30:5); “He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love” (Micah 7:18). Judgment always has a stopping point written in; grace doesn’t.

Where it was finished for you. If God’s wrath against sin can be completed, the question worth asking is where it was completed for a Christian — and the answer is the cross, where the same verb was used by the same author. There are two places in this book where God’s wrath reaches its end. One is a hill outside Jerusalem, and it happened before any of this began. A test: are you living as if God’s anger still hangs over you? If you are in Christ, it was finished there.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a sea of glass mixed with fire, and beside it those who conquered the beast, its image and its number, holding harps of God. Believers whom the beast killed have actually conquered it, simply by refusing to worship it, and now stand safe like Israel beyond the Red Sea.

Fire in the glass. The sea of glass lay before the throne in chapter 4, flat, still, transparent — chaos frozen under God’s feet (4:6). Now there is fire in it: judgment, the fire taken from the altar and thrown to earth (8:5). Heaven’s floor has begun to glow.

Conquered by the conquered. At 13:7 the beast was allowed “to make war on the saints and to conquer them.” Here the same people “had conquered the beast.” Same verb, opposite direction, same encounter. Both are true, and holding them together is the most important thing this book asks of a suffering Christian. From the street, the beast won: believers were arrested, tried and killed, and nothing undoes that. From the sea of glass, they won: they are standing with instruments in their hands, and the beast isn’t in the room.

How defeat becomes victory. 12:11 explained it: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The winning wasn’t survival but refusing to let go, and losing their lives was part of the means, not a failure of it.

A victory of refusals. What they conquered: “the beast and its image and the number of its name.” Not an army but a demand. They weren’t asked to defeat anything, only not to bow, not to worship an image, not to take a number that would let them keep trading. Their whole victory consists of things they didn’t do.

For the Christian who thinks his faithfulness too passive to count. The company on the sea of glass stormed nothing. They declined. They said no to a formality, again and again, at rising cost, and heaven files that under “conquered.” A test: what quiet “no” is faithfulness asking of you this week?

On the far shore. “Standing beside the sea” pictures Israel on the far bank of the Red Sea, with Egypt at the bottom of it — as the next verse makes plain. Those who came through stand on the shore, and the first thing they do is sing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conquerors sing the song of Moses and the Lamb, praising God’s great deeds, his just and true ways, his unique holiness, and the coming worship of all nations. Those who suffered most praise God’s justice without complaint, sing his own words back to him, and look to the day when the nations worship him.

One song, two names. The grammar allows a single song called by two names, and the content proves it: there is one deliverance in two chapters. The song of Moses is Exodus 15, sung beyond the sea with Pharaoh’s army drowned behind them. Israel came out of Egypt through water; these came out of the beast’s empire through fire and death; and it is the same song, because the God who did the first did the second.

Sung in quotations. The words aren’t from Exodus 15 but a mosaic of Psalms and prophets: “Great are the works of the LORD” (Psalm 111:2); “all his ways are justice” (Deuteronomy 32:4); “Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?” (Jeremiah 10:7); “All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Psalm 86:9). Heaven’s redeemed sing in quotations; their worship is built from the Scriptures they were given — a quiet argument for filling the mind with them now. A test: how much Scripture could you sing or pray from memory?

All about God. Not a word about the beast, the persecution, what they suffered, or their endurance. Four clauses, every one about God: his deeds, ways, name, righteous acts.

“Just and true are your ways.” These singers are qualified to say it. Anyone can affirm God’s justice from a comfortable chair. These were killed for refusing a number, came out the other side, and the first thing they say about how God ran history is that it was just. No complaint — not because the question was never asked (it was, loudly, in 6:10), but because it has been answered. A test: can you say “just and true are your ways” about the hardest thing in your life, trusting that it will be answered?

You alone are holy. “Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name?” The expected answer: no one. And the ground is holiness, sung three times in chapter 4. “You alone”: there is one of him, and the beast that demanded worship for forty-two months isn’t in the category.

All nations will come. The widest sentence in the chapter, startling in a book so full of judgment. The nations who raged (11:18), drank Babylon’s wine (14:8), and served the beast (13:7) will come and worship — Psalm 86:9 quoted straight, and the promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). This isn’t universalism; the same book says some are finally outside (21:8; 22:15). It is the assurance that the multitude from every nation (7:9) isn’t a consolation prize. God will have the nations, and what brings them in is “your righteous acts have been revealed” — not that God overwhelmed the world, but that he was seen clearly.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 5: the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The phrase is the Old Testament’s name for the tabernacle, the tent that housed the ark, which housed the tablets called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50). The bowls come out of the place where the covenant is kept.

Verse 6: out come the seven angels, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests — priestly dress (Lev. 16:4; Dan. 10:5), and precisely how the risen Christ was described at 1:13.

Verse 7: one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, who never cease to say holy, holy, holy — hands over seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The word is phialē, a shallow libation dish that empties in a moment, not a jug.

Verse 8: the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by a worshipper. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgement rests on the covenant kept since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it — pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavenly sanctuary, the tent of witness, is opened, and the seven angels with the seven plagues come out dressed like priests in pure, bright linen with golden sashes. God’s final judgments rest on his covenant, come from his holy presence, and are carried out by pure servants as an act of holy service.

The tent of witness. An old, precise name for the tabernacle, which housed the ark, which held the two tablets — called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them and didn’t (Exodus 38:21; Numbers 1:50).

From where the covenant is kept. The bowls come not from an armoury or a prison but from the tent holding the terms both sides signed. That is the difference between these judgments and mere destruction: what is coming has a legal basis, and the document has been in the same box since Sinai.

Opened again. At 11:19 the temple opened and the ark was seen; here the sanctuary opens again, this time not to show something but to release seven angels.

Priests, not soldiers. Linen is what the priest wore into the holy place (Leviticus 16:4); Daniel’s heavenly man was “clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold” (Daniel 10:5); and a golden sash across the chest is exactly how the risen Christ was dressed (1:13). That refuses two easy pictures at once. These aren’t demons let loose, nor soldiers. They are ministers in priestly dress, coming from a sanctuary, carrying out a service. God’s judgment isn’t a loss of control or an outsourcing; it is worship carried out.

Clean hands. “Pure, bright linen” — “bright” is the word for the Bride’s dress (19:8). Nothing that comes through that door is dirty. Whatever one says about the severity of chapter 16, one can’t say the hands carrying it were unclean. A test: do you trust that God’s judgments, when they come, will be entirely just — or do you secretly suspect him? Look at the linen.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the living creatures gives the seven angels seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and the sanctuary fills with smoke from God’s glory, so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished. The time for warning ends and judgment is poured out — so while the door of mercy is open now, we must pray and come to God through Christ.

Handed over by worshippers. One of the living creatures — nearest the throne, crying “holy, holy, holy” without ceasing (4:8) — passes the bowls. Nothing in this chapter lets judgment be handled by anyone outside the worship of God.

A libation bowl. The word is a shallow, wide dish for pouring an offering — not a jug or jar. It empties at once. A trumpet is a warning, blown to be heard, giving time to respond. A libation bowl is tipped once and gone. The instrument itself says the era of warnings is over.

The same bowls. At 5:8 the elders held “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” Same vessels, same throne room. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of wrath. The martyrs asked “how long?”, and this is the vessel in which the answer is delivered.

Glory-smoke. When the tabernacle was finished, “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter” (Exodus 40:34–35). At Solomon’s dedication “the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried, “Woe is me!” (Isaiah 6:4–5). Each time, the smoke meant God had come to dwell, and the exclusion was temporary and joyful. Here it is colder: no one could enter “until the seven plagues… were finished.”

No intercession. The sanctuary is where a priest goes in to plead, bringing blood and asking mercy for someone else. For the duration of the bowls, no one goes in. There is no intercession while the plagues are poured, because its time has run out. That is the most sobering sentence in the chapter: there comes a point when the door is shut — not because God won’t hear, but because the case is closed, the warnings given, the answering begun.

“Until.” Also the mercy in the verse: even the shutting has an end date, the one in v. 1.

It is open now. For anyone reading while the door is still open, the application is simple. The sanctuary stands wide, and there is a great High Priest inside who “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). While that is true, pray — for yourself, and for the people whose names you wouldn’t want read out on the day the smoke fills the room. Name them to him today.
