16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the third and final series of seven judgments in Revelation, and it is the most intense. Where the seals affected a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third, the bowls are poured on the whole earth without fraction. The escalation is deliberate: the time for partial warning has passed. These are the last plagues, and with them the response of God to the accumulated rebellion of history reaches its completion.

The bowl series follows the Exodus plague pattern more closely than either the seals or the trumpets. Bowls one through five draw on the Egyptian plagues, though not in their order: sores (bowl 1, cf. Exodus 9:8–11), water turned to blood (bowls 2–3, cf. Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (bowl 5, cf. Exodus 10:21–23). The Exodus pattern is not decorative. It carries a theological message: the God who liberated Israel from Egypt is the same God who now acts in the final Exodus. The pattern of redemptive history repeats at the cosmic scale.

The chapter reaches its climax at the seventh bowl: a loud voice from the throne declares ‘It is done!’ and the greatest earthquake in human history splits the great city into three parts. Babylon is remembered before God and given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, every mountain disappears. The chapter ends not with despair but with the certainty that the one who declared ‘It is done’ from the cross has declared it again from the throne — all things are now moving irresistibly toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: a loud voice from the temple — almost certainly God’s own, since 15:8 has just closed the sanctuary to everyone else — orders the seven angels to pour. Verse 2: the first bowl brings harmful and painful sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image (cf. Ex. 9:8–11).

Verse 3: the sea becomes like the blood of a corpse and everything in it dies — against the second trumpet, which killed a third (8:8–9). Verse 4: the rivers and springs become blood, as the Nile did (Ex. 7:20–21).

Verses 5–7 stop the sequence and defend it. The angel in charge of the waters — whose department has just been ruined — declares Just are you, O Holy One… they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve! And then the altar itself answers: Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!

Verses 8–9: the fourth bowl turns the sun up, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory. Verses 10–11: the fifth falls on the throne of the beast and its kingdom goes dark (cf. Ex. 10:21–23); people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne — the trumpets’ targets, now without limit. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgements true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and the mark becomes the wound.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands the seven angels to pour out the bowls of his wrath, and the first brings painful sores on those who bear the beast’s mark and worship its image. The final judgments come from God himself, fall on those who chose the beast, and often hand people over to the consequences of what they insisted on.

The voice from the closed temple. No one could enter the sanctuary (15:8), yet a voice comes out of it — almost certainly God’s own. Whoever else is involved, the order to begin comes from the throne.

The trumpets again, without limits. The targets match the trumpets in order: earth, sea, rivers and springs, sun, darkness on a kingdom, the Euphrates, and a final convulsion with hail (compare 8:7–12; 9:13–14). What has changed is the extent: the trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike everything. That parallel is one of the strongest arguments for reading the three sevens as recapitulation — the same ground covered again with greater intensity (see on 6:1–2).

Egypt, densest of all. Sores (Exodus 9:10), water to blood (7:20), darkness (10:22), frogs (8:6), hail (9:24): five of the ten plagues in one chapter. The empire is Egypt, and the God who broke Egypt hasn’t changed his methods.

The drumbeat. Three times John records that those struck cursed God and did not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21).

Sores. The sixth Egyptian plague brought boils, and the magicians “could not stand before Moses because of the boils” (Exodus 9:11). Whatever Egypt’s wisdom could imitate, it couldn’t imitate health.

The mark festers. The sores fall precisely on “the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” The bowls aren’t indiscriminate. In chapter 13 the mark was the ticket to a working life; here the mark itself festers. What was taken as a passport turns out to be the wound.

Handed over. That removes the sense of arbitrariness. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence. He hands people over to what they insisted on — “God gave them up,” three times in one paragraph (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). A test: what have you insisted on having that may become your wound? Let it go while you can.
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second bowl turns the sea to blood like a corpse’s, killing every sea creature, and the third turns the rivers and springs to blood. What God partly struck before in warning, he now strikes completely, showing that everything the world lives on is upheld by him.

A corpse’s blood. Deliberately revolting: not bright blood but a corpse’s — dark, thickened, going bad. Anyone who has been in a room with a body knows what is meant.

No fraction. The second trumpet turned a third of the sea to blood (8:8–9). Here “every living thing died that was in the sea.” The restraint that governed every judgment since chapter 6 — a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a fence around the winds — is gone. This is the undiluted wrath of 15:1.

The Nile returned. The first plague turned the Nile to blood; the fish died and the river stank (Exodus 7:20–21). It was the river into which Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown (Exodus 1:22). Egypt got the Nile back in the condition Egypt had put it in.

What the world lives on and by. The sea is where the beast came from (13:1) and where trade ran; rivers and springs are a settlement’s drinking water. Together they are commerce and survival, and both are now blood.

Warning, then verdict. At the third trumpet Wormwood made a third of the springs bitter (8:10–11). Bitter water can still be drunk by a desperate man; blood can’t. The trumpet made the water unbearable; the bowl makes it impossible. That is the distance between a warning and a verdict.

Nothing is neutral machinery. Everything the world depends on belongs to Someone. The sea a merchant sails, the spring a village was built around, the sun a farmer plants by — none of it is neutral machinery that happens to work. It is upheld moment by moment by the One who is cursed for withdrawing it. A civilisation can assume for centuries that the water will be there, be right every day, and still be wrong about why. A test: when did you last thank God for clean water, a working body, ordinary daylight?

A pause. Then John does something he does nowhere else in the bowls: he stops. Three verses of worship follow, because heaven has something to say about whether this is fair.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel over the waters declares God just, because those who shed the blood of saints and prophets are now given blood to drink, and the altar answers, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!” God’s judgments are perfectly fair; the punishment fits the crime, and even the martyrs who waited for justice agree.

The book’s answer to “Is this fair?” The question a reader has carried since chapter 6 is answered not by John, an apostle or an argument, but sung in the middle of the plague — by the angel whose waters have just been ruined. If anyone had grounds to object, it was him. He declares the judgment just.

The crime served back. “For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink.” The oldest principle of justice. Egypt drowned Hebrew children in a river and had to drink the river. These people made the earth run with the saints’ blood, and now there is nothing else to drink. What God does to the wicked is what the wicked did, returned.

“It is what they deserve.” Not comfortable words. But notice who doesn’t say them: no human being in this book pronounces that sentence over another. The martyrs asked “how long?” and left the verdict to God (6:10). Vengeance is God’s (Romans 12:19), because only he can be trusted to get it exactly right. A test: is there someone you want to see “get what they deserve”? Hand that verdict to God, and pray for them.

Holy, not merely strong. “O Holy One, who is and who was” — the third term gone again, as at 11:17: the One who is to come has come. And the attribute picked out is holiness, not power. The angel isn’t saying God may do this because he is strong enough, but that it is consistent with what he is.

The altar answers. Under the altar are the souls of those slain for God’s word, who cried, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood?” (6:10). This is the altar answering its own question. The words come back — “holy and true” there, “true and just” here — and the verdict of those who actually paid for the injustice is yes. Not “at last,” not “it took long enough.” Yes.

For the reader who finds this hard. The one group whose opinion might carry most weight — the murdered, who wanted this and waited for it — declare it just when it comes. No one in heaven, seeing the whole file, thinks God has overdone it.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth bowl lets the sun scorch people with fire, and they curse God, who has power over the plagues, and refuse to repent and give him glory. Suffering does not automatically lead to repentance; it reveals and hardens the direction a heart is already facing.

“It was allowed.” Even at full strength, with the limits off, the divine passive holds. Nothing in this book acts on its own authority, not even the sun.

One sun, two companies. The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12); the fourth bowl turns it up. And the reversal is pointed, because the multitude was promised, “the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat” (7:16). For the sealed, the sun is shaded by God’s tent spread over them; for these, it is a furnace. The same created thing behaves differently depending on whose you are.

They cursed. The verb used of the beast’s mouth in 13:6. Under the plague they have begun to sound like what they worshipped.

They know. They cursed “the name of God who had power over these plagues.” No ignorance, no confusion about the source, no atheism. They have correctly identified who is doing this and curse him for it. Suffering hasn’t hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him with the evidence in front of them.

Pain doesn’t produce repentance. “They did not repent and give him glory.” The answer, again, to a hope many quietly carry — that if things got bad enough, people would turn. Chapter 9 said it after a third of mankind died; chapter 16 says it three times more. Pain reveals what was already there, and hardens as reliably as it softens.

A warning for believers. Not chiefly about other people. Every Christian meets small versions: the illness, loss or disappointment that could go either way, and the direction isn’t decided by the size of the trouble. Two men lose the same thing in the same week; one is driven to his knees and the other never prays again. The difference isn’t the weight but which way a person was already facing when it landed. A test: which way are you facing now, before the next trouble comes?

What repentance is. “Repent and give him glory” — not merely feel sorry, but hand God back the glory given to something else. Exactly what these people won’t do: they gave it to a beast and aren’t taking it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth bowl falls on the beast’s throne and plunges its kingdom into darkness; people gnaw their tongues in pain and curse God for their sufferings, still refusing to repent of their deeds. God exposes the emptiness of every godless regime, and those who measure God only by their comfort end in bitter cursing.

Aimed at the throne. The first four bowls fell on creation. The fifth falls on a government, precisely: not on subjects or armies but on “the throne of the beast.” The reader last heard of such a throne in Pergamum, “where Satan’s throne is” (2:13). Christians had lived under its shadow the whole book. It goes dark.

Egypt’s darkness. The ninth plague was darkness so thick no one rose from his place for three days, “but all the people of Israel had light where they lived” (Exodus 10:23). Egypt’s chief god was the sun, whose son Pharaoh claimed to be. To darken the empire is to show its god can’t keep a lamp lit.

The regime exposed. The earlier bowls damaged the world; this one exposes the regime. Every empire that demands worship rests on an appearance of permanence — the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted, and it is inconceivable that any of it should stop. One bowl, and the kingdom is in the dark. It couldn’t even manage light.

Gnawing tongues. A small, credible detail: what a person does with pain he can’t escape or usefully cry out about. And the sores from the first bowl are still there; the plagues accumulate; nothing has healed.

Worship and behaviour. In v. 9, “did not repent and give him glory”; here, “did not repent of their deeds.” The first is worship, the second conduct. They won’t change what they adore or what they do.

For their pain. What they curse God for: “their pain and sores.” Not anything they have thought about him, nor any account of who he is. Their whole complaint is their own discomfort. It is possible to spend a life measuring God only by how one feels, and this is where that ends.

A test before the bowl. When you last had a grievance against God, what was it actually about? If the honest answer is that he hadn’t arranged your comfort as you would have, that is the same complaint at a survivable scale — and there is still time to bring it to him and repent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east — and when Cyrus took Babylon his engineers diverted that river and his troops walked in up the empty bed, exactly as Isaiah had said (Isa. 44:27–28). Verses 13–14: three unclean spirits like frogs (Ex. 8:6) come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — the unholy trinity together for the first time — and go to the kings of the world to assemble them for battle.

Verse 15 interrupts, in brackets, in Christ’s own voice: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Verse 16 names the muster point: Armageddon, its only occurrence in the Bible.

Verse 17: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the temple and the throne says It is done! — gegonen, a perfect tense, the completion promised at 15:1. Verse 18: the storm signs at full strength, with an earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth.

Verse 19: the great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Verse 20: every island flees and no mountains are found (cf. 6:14). Verse 21: hailstones of about a hundred pounds fall (Ex. 9:24) — and they cursed God, for the third time in the chapter, which is the last thing humanity does in it.
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates for the kings of the east, and three froglike demonic spirits come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet to gather the world’s kings for battle on God’s great day. God opens the way to the final conflict, and evil gathers the world against him chiefly through lies.

The river goes. The Euphrates, the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel came from. At the sixth trumpet four angels bound there were released (9:14); now the river itself goes.

A road cleared. A dried river is Scripture’s picture of God clearing a road: the Red Sea for Israel (Exodus 14:21), the Jordan into the land (Joshua 3:16). And when Cyrus took Babylon, ancient historians say his engineers diverted the Euphrates and his troops walked in up the empty riverbed — as Isaiah foretold when God said to the deep, “Be dry; I will dry up your rivers,” and named Cyrus (Isaiah 44:27–28). A first-century reader knew exactly how the last great Babylon fell.

The gate opened. The water is removed to make invasion easier. God isn’t defending the beast’s kingdom; he opens the gate for what will destroy it. Even the enemies of God’s people serve his purposes without knowing it.

Who are the kings from the east? John’s readers feared the Parthian armies beyond the Euphrates. Futurist readers expect a literal eastern army. The more likely reading is that John uses that fear as a picture of the nations gathered by the dragon for the final battle (v. 14), not a prediction of a particular invasion.

Three mouths. The unholy trinity appears together for the first time, and all three do the same thing: they speak. The dragon is “the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9); the beast was given “a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words” (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs. Evil’s whole arsenal in this book is rhetorical.

Frogs. The second plague of Egypt (Exodus 8:6), and unclean to a Jewish reader. Also deliberately ridiculous. Everything about the villains so far has been magnificent: seven heads, ten diadems, a healed wound, the worship of the earth. When their propaganda is finally shown, it hops.

A persuasion campaign. The frogs are a diplomatic service: they go to the kings, perform signs, and assemble a coalition. The last war begins not with mobilisation but persuasion, by demons who look absurd and are believed anyway. The decisive struggle isn’t chiefly about weapons or power but about what the world is told and whether it believes it. The dragon’s one method, from a garden conversation to the last coalition, is to say something untrue convincingly. A test: what are you being persuaded of this week that contradicts what God says? Check it against his word.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ breaks in: “Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on” — and the kings are gathered at the place called Armageddon. At the world’s darkest hour Christ’s concern is that his people stay alert and faithful, and the famous last battle will be no contest at all.

Christ interrupts. In the middle of a sentence about demonic frogs assembling the world’s kings, another voice cuts in; the ESV rightly brackets it. Christ has scarcely spoken in his own voice since chapter 3 and won’t again until chapter 22. Here, at the darkest point, he breaks in. The armies gather — and the Lord’s concern at that moment is a Christian in Thyatira staying awake and keeping his clothes on. The cosmic scale never displaces the person reading.

Like a thief. He said it to Sardis (3:3) and on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:43); Paul and Peter repeat it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The point isn’t stealth but unpredictability — arriving on a night no one expected. So there is no point planning to get ready later.

Awake and dressed. The third of the book’s seven blessings. The image would have made a Christian smile before it made him think: according to the later Mishnah, a temple guard found asleep at his post had his clothes burned — caught asleep meant public shame. And garments in this book are settled: white robes for those who conquer (3:5), robes washed in the Lamb’s blood (7:14), the Bride’s fine linen, “the righteous deeds of the saints” (19:8). Laodicea was told to buy white garments so that “the shame of your nakedness may not be seen” (3:18) — the same phrase. So the instruction isn’t heroic: stay awake; keep your clothes on. Not that a Christian do something about the coalition, but that he be found alert and dressed. A test: if Christ came tonight, what would he find you doing — and wearing?

Is Armageddon a literal battle at Megiddo in Israel? The word occurs only here in the Bible, and much popular literature rests on it. The likeliest derivation is “mountain of Megiddo.” Megiddo guarded the pass into the plain of Jezreel and was the most fought-over place in the land: Deborah and Barak fought “at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo” (Judges 5:19); Ahaziah died there (2 Kings 9:27); good King Josiah was killed there by Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29). To say Megiddo was to say the battlefield. Premillennial and dispensational Christians expect a future gathering of armies there. But Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain; some therefore read “mountain of assembly,” the phrase of the fallen day star who says, “I will sit on the mount of assembly” (Isaiah 14:13); and the battle is “on the great day of God the Almighty” (v. 14), the same final conflict as 19:19 and 20:8. In a book that calls one city Sodom, Egypt and Babylon, the more likely reading is that Armageddon is a symbolic name for the world’s last stand against God, ended at once by Christ’s coming.

The shortest battle. What isn’t uncertain is who wins, and how little of a battle it is. The kings are assembled here and nothing happens; the fighting is in 19:19–21, lasts one verse, and the weapon is a sword from a mouth. Armageddon is the most famous battle in the world’s imagination and the shortest in the book.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and God’s voice from the throne declares, “It is done!” amid the greatest earthquake in history. God’s wrath reaches its appointed end, and everything that can be shaken is shaken so that only what cannot be shaken remains.

Into the air. The one element the first six left alone, and the one no one can stand outside of. Paul calls the devil “the prince of the power of the air” (Ephesians 2:2). The last judgment falls on the atmosphere the whole world breathes.

“It is done!” From the temple and the throne — God himself. One word in Greek: it has happened, stands accomplished, with permanent result. It echoes two others that frame everything. On the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30) — a different verb, the same force. At 21:6, of the new creation, “It is done!” — the same word. The cross, the end of wrath, the beginning of the new world. What was accomplished at the first makes the second bearable and the third certain.

The wrath finished. Chapter 15 said it in advance: “with them the wrath of God is finished” (15:1). This is that sentence arriving. There is no eighth bowl.

The storm at full strength. John’s signal that God has acted has grown through the book: three elements at 4:5; an earthquake added at 8:5; hail added at 11:19. Here the earthquake gets a clause of its own and a superlative: nothing like it “since man was on the earth.”

The great sorting. God promised through Haggai to shake heaven and earth (Haggai 2:6), and Hebrews explains why: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.” This phrase “indicates the removal of things that are shaken… in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:26–28). That is what the greatest earthquake in history is for. Not demolition for its own sake, but sorting: everything that can be shaken is shaken, so that what stands afterwards is only what was never going to fall.

A test. A believer’s honest question isn’t “Will I survive this?” but “How much of what I am leaning on is in the shakeable category?” Name it — and lean instead on the kingdom that can’t be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great city splits into three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembers Babylon to make her drain the cup of his wrath; islands and mountains vanish, and hundred-pound hailstones fall, yet people curse God. God acts at last on the long record of the godless world-system, and judgment alone still changes no one’s heart — only the gospel of the Lamb does.

The great city. The phrase used at 11:8 of the city “symbolically… called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified” — Babylon, named in the same sentence. Split in three: total collapse; Ezekiel divided his hair in three as a sign of Jerusalem’s ruin (Ezekiel 5:1–2).

“God remembered.” In Scripture God’s remembering never means something had slipped his mind. It is covenant language: he is about to act on what he has long known. “God remembered Noah,” and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant with Abraham, and the exodus began (Exodus 2:24). The thief asked to be remembered and heard, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). So a long-open file has come to the top. Babylon was announced fallen at 14:8; chapters 17–18 will do nothing else. This is the hinge between announcement and account.

Drain the cup. Not sip — drain it to the bottom. The cup of 14:10, poured full strength, and the cup Babylon herself passed round (14:8). She poured; she drinks; she finishes the glass.

No fixed points. Islands and mountains — things that don’t move, what people steer by and shelter behind — are gone. The sixth seal said the same (6:14), more evidence that seals and bowls cover the same ground.

Hail. Egypt’s seventh plague was hail unlike any since the nation began (Exodus 9:24). A hundred pounds is roughly a talent, the largest standard weight. And stones falling on people had one other meaning in the law: stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). The chapter has said three times that these people blasphemed. The sky returns the sentence.

The last word is a curse. Not “they cried out” or “they fell down.” Humanity’s final act in this chapter, with the sky falling, is to curse.

What actually changes people. Revelation offers no picture of a world that finally comes round under pressure; it has now said four times that judgment alone changes nobody. What changes people is what was shown at 11:13, where two witnesses were killed and raised and nine-tenths of a city gave glory to God, and what was announced at 14:6, an eternal gospel flown over every nation. The bowls answer “how long?”, but they save no one. The instrument of salvation is the slain Lamb, at the centre of the throne since chapter 5, and while the sanctuary door is open, it is still working. A test: are you hoping hard times will soften someone you love? Pray, and tell them of the Lamb.

17.title: Babylon the Great: The Seductive City
17.overview:
Chapter 17 introduces one of Revelation’s two great female figures: the great prostitute who sits on many waters, dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations. She is the counterpart to the bride of the Lamb (chapters 19 and 21) — two women, two cities, two ways of organising human life. The bride is pure, faithful, clothed in the righteousness of the Lamb. Babylon is seductive, unfaithful, clothed in the luxury of empire. Every human being in history has been drawn toward one or the other.

The identity of Babylon is both specific and universal. In the first century, every reader knew who she was: Rome. The seven hills (v. 9), the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, the city that rules over the kings of the earth (v. 18) — all of this pointed unmistakably to the imperial city on the Tiber. Preterists and idealists agree on this much. Where they differ is on what Rome represents: preterists see primarily the historical Rome of Nero and Domitian; idealists see Rome as the type of every civilisation that organises itself around wealth, power, and the seduction of the nations away from the living God. The idealist position is followed here: Babylon is Rome, and Babylon is every Rome.

The chapter falls into two movements: the vision of the woman on the beast (vv. 1–6) and the angel’s interpretation (vv. 7–18). The interpretation is deliberately cryptic — ‘this calls for a mind that has wisdom’ (v. 9) — and the details about the seven kings and the eighth king have generated more interpretive proposals than almost any other passage in Revelation. The main options are presented honestly here rather than forcing a specific identification that the text itself refuses to make definitive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman on the Beast
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: one of the bowl angels — tying this chapter to 16:19, where God remembered Babylon — invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters (cf. Jer. 51:13). The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk on her wine. The same invitation will come from the same rank of angel at 21:9: Come, I will show you the Bride.

Verses 3–4: carried in the Spirit into a wilderness (the Bride is shown from a high mountain, 21:10), John sees a woman riding the scarlet beast of chapter 13 — seven heads, ten horns, blasphemous names. She is arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding a golden cup full of abominations (cf. Jer. 51:7; Matt. 23:25).

Verse 5: a name on her forehead, in a book where that is never incidental (7:3; 13:16; 14:1) — Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations, which the ESV prints in capitals. Verse 6: she is drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus — and John, seeing her, marveled greatly, using the verb this book twice uses of the world’s reaction to the beast (13:3; 17:8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Great Prostitute

John is shown Babylon, magnificent in purple and gold, riding the beast, holding a golden cup full of abominations, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is Rome for the first readers, and the mother of every city built to make a name for itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Kings made the arrangements; ordinary people simply drank what was poured.

Now: The cup always looks better than its contents — and even an apostle had to be asked why he marvelled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters.”

The guide is one of the bowl angels, which ties this chapter to the last: 16:19 said that God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup, and gave no further detail. Chapters 17 and 18 are that detail. And the same invitation will be issued once more, four chapters later, in almost identical words: Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9).

Two women, two cities, two invitations from the same rank of angel. That is the architecture of the rest of the book, and it is the frame this chapter must be read in. Every human being is finally a citizen of one of two cities and is married into one of two households, and Revelation is going to describe both so that a reader can tell them apart.

The great prostitute. The image is not chosen for shock. It is the settled prophetic word for covenant unfaithfulness, and it is used most often of the people of God themselves: Israel is the wife who played the whore (Jer. 3:6–10; Ezek. 16; Hos. 1–3), and Isaiah opens a lament with How the faithful city has become a whore! (Isa. 1:21). It was also used of pagan cities — Nineveh and Tyre are both called prostitutes for selling themselves to whoever would trade (Nah. 3:4; Isa. 23:15–17).

The point of the word is transaction. A prostitute offers what belongs inside a covenant, without the covenant, for a price. That is what Babylon does with every good thing there is — beauty, security, belonging, significance — and it is why she is a more dangerous enemy than the beast. The beast demands. She offers.

Seated on many waters. Verse 15 will interpret it: the waters are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. But the image comes first from Jeremiah’s oracle against the original Babylon — O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come (Jer. 51:13) — and historical Babylon literally sat on the Euphrates and its canals. John takes a geographical fact about one city and makes it a statement about influence.

With whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.

Two groups, and the distinction matters. The kings committed immorality with her — the deal made at the top, the arrangement between power and money that every empire runs on. The dwellers on earth merely got drunk — the ordinary population, who never signed anything and simply drank what was poured.

That is a fair description of how a civilisation actually corrupts the people in it. Very few of them are in the room where the arrangements are made. What reaches them is a mood: what everyone assumes, what is obviously worth having, what only a strange person would refuse. And the effect named is drunkenness, which is not primarily wickedness but the loss of judgment — the inability to walk in a straight line while being quite certain that you are.
verseByVerse.note: “Many waters” recalls ancient Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals.

verseByVerse.quote: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness.

The third of John’s four times in the Spirit (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10), and the location is deliberate. To see the Bride he will be carried to a great high mountain (21:10); to see the prostitute he is taken into a desert. And the wilderness is where the woman of chapter 12 fled and was fed for 1,260 days (12:6). The same landscape shelters the true woman and exposes the false one.

And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns.

It is the beast of chapter 13 — seven heads, ten horns, blasphemous names — and she is riding it. That single image says more about the relationship between a culture and its government than a chapter of analysis could. She does not own the beast; she is carried by it. Her whole position depends on a creature she does not control, and verse 16 will show what that arrangement is worth.

The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup.

She is magnificent, and that must be said plainly or the chapter will be misread. Purple dye came from a Mediterranean shellfish and cost more per ounce than gold; a purple garment was the mark of an emperor. Scarlet was the second most expensive colour there was. Gold, precious stones and pearls are exactly the list that will reappear in chapter 18 as the cargo the merchants of the earth weep over. This is not a squalid figure in a doorway. She is the best-dressed woman in the world.

And that is the point of the whole picture. Nobody is seduced by something repulsive. The beast is frightening and can be recognised by a child; Babylon is beautiful, expensive, cultured, and hospitable, and it takes a prophet in the Spirit to see what she is. The church has always found it easier to resist persecution than prosperity, and this chapter knows it.

Compare the other woman while the picture is fresh. The Bride wears fine linen, bright and pure, and John stops to say what the linen is: the righteous deeds of the saints (19:8). One woman is covered in what she bought; the other is dressed in what she did, and even that was given her to wear.

Full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality. The cup is gold on the outside and filth inside, which is precisely the charge Jesus laid against the Pharisees: you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence (Matt. 23:25). Jeremiah said of the first Babylon that she was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken (Jer. 51:7).

Nobody would drink from a cup that looked like what is in it. That is the entire mechanism of temptation, and it has not required updating in nineteen centuries. The vessel is always worth more than the contents, and the contents are always worse than they look.

verseByVerse.quote: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: "BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH'S ABOMINATIONS." And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations.”

The ESV prints that name in capital letters. It is not decoration; it is how a placard reads.

A name on a forehead, in a book where that is never incidental. The servants of God are sealed on the forehead (7:3); the 144,000 carry the Lamb’s name and his Father’s there (14:1); the beast’s worshippers take its mark in the same place (13:16). Everyone is labelled. Roman prostitutes are said to have worn a headband with their name on it, which would have made the detail unpleasantly vivid.

Now: who is she? The question has to be answered, and it can be answered in layers without vagueness.

For John’s first readers she is unmistakably Rome. Verse 9 says the seven heads are seven mountains, and Rome was famous throughout the empire as the city on seven hills; a coin of Vespasian shows the goddess Roma seated on them. Verse 18 calls her the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth, which in AD 95 named exactly one place. Peter, writing from the same city, signs off from she who is at Babylon (1 Pet. 5:13).

A minority reading, held by some preterists, takes her as apostate Jerusalem, pointing to verse 6 — drunk with the blood of the saints — and to Jesus’ own words that Jerusalem is the city that kills the prophets (Matt. 23:37), and to the prophetic use of prostitute for the covenant people. It has real evidence behind it and it does not explain the seven mountains or verse 18 as naturally.

But the name itself is the widest answer, and it is why the chapter uses it. Babylon was a ruin when John wrote — it had been finished for centuries. He is using it the way he used Sodom and Egypt at 11:8: as a type. Babylon in Scripture begins at a tower built by people who said let us make a name for ourselves (Gen. 11:4), and that project has never once closed. She is the mother of prostitutes — not one city but the source of a family of them, reproducing in every generation. Rome was a daughter. So was Babylon itself. There will be others.

And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.

She has been serving a cup all chapter, and now the reader is told what she has been drinking. And the word is drunk, not merely stained: killing Christians has become something she does with appetite, past the point where it serves any purpose.

When I saw her, I marveled greatly.

Stop at that, because the angel does. The verb is thaumazō, and it is the same word used twice in this book of the world’s reaction to the beast: the whole earth marveled (13:3), and the dwellers on earth will marvel to see the beast (17:8). John — an apostle, in the Spirit, on assignment — has just had the reaction that the earth-dwellers have.

What exactly he marvelled at, the text does not say. It may have been horror. It may have been that a figure so magnificent was so foul. It may, uncomfortably, have been fascination. The next verse opens with a rebuke — Why do you marvel? — which suggests he should not have.

Is the great prostitute the Roman Catholic Church, as the Reformers held? Luther, Calvin, Knox and the Westminster divines identified Babylon and the beast with the papacy, pointing to Rome on seven hills (v. 9), its wealth, and its persecution of the saints. They rightly saw that a church can become a harlot. But in John’s day Babylon was imperial Rome, seducing the nations with wealth and idolatry; and the more likely reading is that she stands for every system that seduces the world away from God, including false and apostate religion, of which papal Rome was one example but not the only one.

And there is something in that for any Christian who has noticed himself absorbed by the things this book condemns. It is possible to spend a great deal of time appalled by a culture and still be more interested in it than in God. The line between prophetic concern and simple fascination is thinner than it looks, and an apostle needed to have it pointed out to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: the angel rebukes the marvelling and explains — and vv. 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in the book, saying this is or these are six times. The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction, and those who marvel at it are those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

Verses 9–11: this calls for a mind with wisdom — the seven heads are seven mountains and also seven kings, five fallen, one is, one still to come who must remain only a little while; and the beast is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

Verses 12–14: ten horns are ten kings (cf. Dan. 7:24) who receive authority for one hour and hand their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.

Verses 15–16: the waters are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages; and the ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire (cf. 2 Kings 9:36; Lev. 21:9). Verse 17: they do it because God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose… until the words of God are fulfilled. Verse 18 closes: the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb Will Conquer

The beast was, and is not — a parody of God’s name — and goes to destruction. The seven kings cannot be identified with certainty, but their time is short. The kings make war on the Lamb and lose, and the beast turns on the woman it carried; God put it in their hearts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those with the Lamb are called, chosen and faithful — in that order.

Now: Evil is not loyal: whatever you ride for safety will one day devour its passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to me, "Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.”

The cure for staring at Babylon is being told what she is, and the angel supplies it for the rest of the chapter. Mystery here means what it always means in the New Testament: not a riddle nobody can solve but a secret now disclosed. Verses 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in Revelation — six times the angel says this is or these are.

The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction.

Read that clause slowly against the divine name in this book. God is him who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise. It is a parody of the eternal name, and it is a bad one, because the middle term has collapsed: where God says I am, the beast can only say is not.

That is the most concentrated theological statement about evil in the book, and it should be taken as literally as it is meant. Whatever the beast is, it does not have being in the way God has being. It was; it is not; it will make an appearance; and its itinerary ends at one destination which the sentence names before the journey starts — and go to destruction. Four verbs, and the last one is the only certainty among them.

Historically, the phrase almost certainly plays on the Nero legend: an emperor who died and whom half the eastern empire expected back, a ruler who was, and is not, and is to come. John takes the popular rumour and turns it into a theological joke.

And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast.

The same safeguard as 13:8, and it is the counterweight to everything alarming in the chapter. There is a register. It belongs to the Lamb. The entries were made from the foundation of the world, before anyone had done anything to earn or forfeit a place. And the people who marvel at the beast are the ones not in it.

Which is the answer to the fear this chapter is most likely to produce in a sincere reader, and it should be given plainly: am I in danger of being taken in? The verse does not say the enrolled are cleverer or more discerning. It says they are written, and it says who wrote them, and it says when. John himself marvelled and had to be corrected; the security is not in his reaction but in the register.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

The opening formula is the same as at 13:18, where the number of the beast was set as a puzzle: this calls for wisdom. Both times John invites calculation, and both times readers have been more confident than the evidence allows. Honesty is more useful here than ingenuity.

Seven mountains would have settled the geography for a first-century reader. Rome was the city of seven hills in the ordinary speech of the empire, celebrated in an annual festival and stamped on coins.

They are also seven kings, and this is where certainty has to stop. The obvious approach is to count emperors, and it has never been made to work cleanly. Start at Julius Caesar or at Augustus? Include or omit the three who ruled for months in the chaos of AD 69? Depending on the choices, the sixth — the one who is — can be made to come out as Nero, or Vespasian, or Domitian, and each reconstruction requires decisions the text does not authorise. Several schemes have been produced by careful scholars, and none commands agreement.

Say two things instead of picking one. First, seven in this book is the number of completeness, so seven kings may well mean the full succession of imperial power rather than a list to be checked off — in which case five have fallen, one is, one is to come means what it always means when a prophet says it: most of it is already over. Second, and this is the practical point, the angel says the seventh must remain only a little while. Whatever the count, the message is that the sequence is nearly finished and the last of them is brief.

It is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction. The beast is not a new thing; it is the seven again, one more time, wearing a new number. That is what chapter 13 said by giving one animal the features of Daniel’s four beasts. Empires are not a series of separate problems. They are one problem with a changing letterhead.

And it goes to destruction for the second time in three verses. The angel has now given the beast’s past, its present, its future, and its destination, and he has mentioned the destination twice as often as anything else. A reader who cannot reconstruct the emperor list — and nobody can, with certainty — has still been given the one piece of information the chapter most wants him to have.

Which is the honest and freeing conclusion of these three verses. The identification of the kings is uncertain and has always been uncertain, and centuries of confident schemes have come and gone. The angel’s own emphasis is not on who they are but on how long they last: a little while, and then destruction.
verseByVerse.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.

The ten horns come from Daniel 7, where the fourth beast had ten horns and the interpretation given was ten kings shall arise (Dan. 7:24). Ten in this book is a round number for a full set of a lesser kind — the devil throws some into prison for ten days (2:10) — so this is most likely the complete roster of the beast’s client rulers rather than a list to be filled in with names.

Two details are exact and both cut the same way.

For one hour. One of the shortest measures of time in the book, and it will be used three more times in the next chapter, each time of Babylon’s ruin: in a single hour your judgment has come (18:10, 17, 19). These kings get the same hour they destroy her in. Whatever authority they receive is measured out in the smallest unit John has.

They hand over their power and authority to the beast. Nobody takes anything from them. They are of one mind — the word means a single settled opinion — and they give away the one thing a king exists to hold. That is what every totalitarian arrangement in history has actually looked like from the inside: not a conquest of the powerful, but a queue of them agreeing to hand something over in exchange for a share.

They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.

Here is the sentence the chapter exists for, and it should be read exactly as it stands. Ten kings, the full authority of the empire, a beast with seven heads and the dragon’s throne behind it — against a Lamb. John does not switch to the Lion for the battle. The word he uses is the diminutive one he uses of Christ throughout, the lambkin with its throat cut.

And there is no description of the fighting. The Lamb will conquer them, and the reason given is not a strategy or a weapon or a number of troops. It is a title: for he is Lord of lords and King of kings. The outcome follows from who he is. Nothing has to happen for this to be true, which is why the verse can state it in advance of the event.

The title itself repays a moment. It is an Old Testament name for God — the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords (Deut. 10:17; cf. Ps. 136:2, 3) — and it is applied here to the Lamb without a word of explanation, as this book does everything else concerning his deity. It will be written on his robe and his thigh at 19:16, in reverse order.

And then, almost in passing, three words about the people standing with him: called and chosen and faithful.

Read them in order, because the order is the whole doctrine. Called — God summoned them, and they did not volunteer. Chosen — behind the calling is a choosing, and behind the choosing is nothing but God’s own decision (cf. Eph. 1:4). Faithful — and this is the one they do. But it comes third. Their faithfulness is the visible end of a chain whose first two links were forged before they existed.

That is the answer for a Christian who reads this chapter and feels outnumbered, which is the correct arithmetic and the wrong conclusion. Ten kings, one beast, the whole world drunk, and a handful of congregations meeting in houses. The verse does not encourage them by disputing the numbers. It tells them who is at the front and who put them there.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.”

The angel interprets his own image, and the fourfold phrase is the one used since 5:9 of the whole human race — the same people the Lamb ransomed. Babylon’s seat is popular support. She rules by being wanted.

And water in this book is not solid ground. The sea is chaos; a river was poured out of the dragon’s mouth to sweep the woman away (12:15); the Euphrates dried up in a single bowl (16:12). A throne set on water is a throne set on a mood, and a mood can go out as fast as it came in — which is what the next verse describes.

And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire.

This is the turn of the chapter and it is the last thing a reader expects. Babylon is not destroyed by the armies of heaven. She is destroyed by the beast she was riding and the kings who were her clients.

Four verbs, and they escalate: make her desolate — stripped of everything; naked — the woman in purple and scarlet and gold, with nothing on; devour her flesh, which is the phrase used of the dogs eating Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel (2 Kings 9:36); and burn her up with fire, which under the law was the penalty for a priest’s daughter who became a prostitute (Lev. 21:9).

Every one of them was a clause in her own contract. She sold beauty and is left desolate; she traded on being clothed and is stripped; she drank the blood of the saints and is eaten; she offered a cup of fire and is burned.

And the underlying observation is one of the most useful things this book says about evil, and it should be stated plainly because it is not obvious. Evil is not loyal. It has no capacity for it. The alliance between the corrupt system and the brute power that carries it holds only while both are getting something, and when it stops paying, the beast eats the woman. History is monotonous on this point: the collaborators are purged, the financiers are shot, the useful men are tried by the regime they installed. Nobody who has ever climbed onto the beast has been carried all the way.

Which is a real word to a Christian tempted to make an accommodation for the sake of safety. The arrangement is not what it appears to be. The thing you are riding to keep your position has an appetite, and it is not sentimental about passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.

The verse explains the one before it, and it is the most audacious sentence in the chapter. The reason the kings agreed, the reason they handed everything to the beast, and the reason the beast turned on the woman is that God has put it into their hearts.

Not that God tempted anybody, and not that anybody in this chapter is innocent; every one of them is doing exactly what he wants and will answer for it. But the deepest cause of the collapse of Babylon is a decision taken in heaven, executed through the free and wicked choices of men who thought they were serving themselves.

Scripture says this repeatedly and without embarrassment. God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and Pharaoh hardened his own heart, and both are stated in the same narrative. He turned the hearts of the Egyptians to hate his people (Ps. 105:25). Assyria was the rod of his anger and did not know it: he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy (Isa. 10:5–7). And Peter said of the worst act in human history that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath that lawless men crucified him (Acts 2:23).

The practical weight of that for a persecuted church is considerable, and it is why the verse is here rather than in a theological appendix. A believer watching a hostile power arrange itself has two available accounts. Either history is a contest whose outcome depends on whether the good guys can hold out, or the arrangements being made against the church are themselves the mechanism by which God dismantles what is arrayed against her. The second is harder to look at and is the only one with a floor under it.

Until the words of God are fulfilled. There is a terminus, and it is not the exhaustion of the kings or the collapse of the system. It is the completion of what God said. The permission runs exactly as far as the promise and not one hour further.

And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.

The angel closes the interpretation with a flat identification. In AD 95 that sentence named one place, and every hearer knew it. But the description is functional rather than geographical — the great city that has dominion — and the office has never been vacant for long. Babylon is not primarily a location. It is whatever, in a given century, sits on the peoples, trades with the kings, dresses beautifully, offers everything a person wants without the God who made it, and is prepared to shed blood to keep its position.

So the chapter ends where it began, with an angel showing John a woman. There will be another woman, and another angel, and another invitation in the same words (21:9). Both are cities and both are brides, and a reader is asked to look at them side by side and see which he has been dressing for.

One is arrayed in purple and scarlet and gold and rides a beast she does not control, and is stripped and burned by the thing she was sitting on. The other is clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, and comes down out of heaven from God, and her husband is the Lamb who was slaughtered and is Lord of lords and King of kings. And the Lamb will conquer, because of who he is, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful — in that order, and the first two were settled before the world was made.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters,<sup>2</sup>with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.”<sup>3</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns.<sup>4</sup>The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.<sup>5</sup>And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS.”<sup>6</sup>And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.<sup>9</sup>This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated;<sup>10</sup>they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while.<sup>11</sup>As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.<sup>12</sup>And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.<sup>13</sup>These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.<sup>14</sup>They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”<sup>15</sup>And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.<sup>16</sup>And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Chapter 18 is Revelation’s sustained lament over the fall of the great city. It is one of the longest chapters in the book, and it is deliberately literary in character — structured like the great prophetic dirges of the Old Testament (Isaiah 13–14 over Babylon; Ezekiel 26–28 over Tyre; Ezekiel 27 especially, whose cargo list John adapts in vv. 12–13). The chapter uses the Old Testament’s own poetic forms to announce the end of the Old Testament’s great enemy.

The chapter moves through three distinct movements. First (vv. 1–8): the angelic announcement of Babylon’s fall and the call for God’s people to come out of her. Second (vv. 9–20): the threefold lament of the kings, merchants, and seafarers — three groups whose wealth depended on Babylon, each mourning from a safe distance as the city burns. Third (vv. 21–24): the millstone sign and the sixfold silence — the total, irreversible end of the city that made the nations drunk with her wine.

The economic detail of chapter 18 is one of its most striking features. The cargo list of vv. 12–13 is specific, comprehensive, and damning — ending with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’ Babylon’s economy is built on everything, including people. The city that offered the nations luxury and culture and wealth was also the city that traded in human beings as commodities. This is Revelation’s most direct indictment of the economics of empire, and it is not limited to the Roman slave trade: every economic system that treats human beings as means rather than ends falls under the same indictment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: an angel with great authority comes down and the earth was made bright with his glory (cf. Ezek. 43:2). Verses 2–3: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! — the announcement of 14:8 now given twenty-four verses instead of one. She becomes a haunt of demons and unclean birds, which is exactly what the prophets said of the first Babylon (Isa. 13:21–22; Jer. 50:39). And three groups are named who will structure the chapter: the nations who drank, the kings who traded, and — new here — the merchants, who grew rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Verses 4–5: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Jer. 51:45; Isa. 52:11; cf. 2 Cor. 6:17), for her sins are heaped high as heaven — a tower again (Gen. 11:4) — and God has remembered her iniquities.

Verses 6–8: repay her double in the cup she mixed; and Babylon speaks in her own voice, quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isa. 47:7–8): I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. The three things she says she will never see are the three that arrive: death and mourning and famine, all in a single day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come Out of Her

Babylon is fallen and left a haunt of unclean things. God’s people are called to come out of her — not by emigrating but by refusing to share her sins. She said she would never see mourning; death, mourning and famine come in a single day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the beast enforced by law, Babylon sustained by trade.

Now: Coming out of Babylon happens in small daily refusals; beware the unspoken belief that your comforts will simply go on.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.

The detail is easy to miss and it sets the tone of the chapter. This angel is bright enough that the whole earth lights up as he descends. Ezekiel saw the same thing when the glory of God returned to the temple — the earth shone with his glory (Ezek. 43:2). The city about to be described as the most magnificent in the world is about to be lit by something that makes it look like a candle at noon.

And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” The announcement made in one verse at 14:8 is now made again, and this time the chapter does not move on. Twenty-four verses of it. And the words are still Isaiah’s watchman on the wall (Isa. 21:9).

She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.

This is exactly what the prophets said would happen to the first Babylon, and John is quoting deliberately. Isaiah: wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures… hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces (Isa. 13:21–22). Jeremiah said the same of Babylon (Jer. 50:39) and of Edom.

Consider what that means as a picture. It is a ruin at night. The great houses are still standing; the streets are still laid out; and what moves in them are owls and jackals. Anyone who has walked through an abandoned town knows the effect — the buildings are what make it terrible, because they were built for people and there are no people.

And the word haunt is literally a prison or a place of keeping. The city that offered the whole world its freedom has become a cage for unclean things.

For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Three groups, and this verse is the chapter’s table of contents. The kings will lament in verses 9 and 10, the merchants in 11 to 16, and the seafarers in 17 to 19. But notice the third group, because it is new. In chapter 17 the parties to Babylon’s business were the kings and the drunken populace. Here the merchants arrive, and from verse 11 onward they will dominate the chapter.

That shift is the most striking thing about these two chapters read together. Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a religious and political power — a prostitute demanding worship, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Chapter 18 shows her as an economy. The charge sheet is a cargo manifest. And it turns out the two are the same city, which is the point: what the beast enforces by law, Babylon sustains by trade.

Who is Babylon here, and has her fall already happened? In John’s day Babylon was Rome, and the city did fall, but not in a single hour (v. 10). Some expect a rebuilt city of Babylon. The more likely reading is that Babylon is the world system of wealth, power and false worship that Rome embodied, which has risen and fallen in many forms, and whose final fall comes at Christ’s return.

And the last phrase names the mechanism precisely: the power of her luxurious living. The Greek word means excess, wantonness, the strength that comes from having far more than is needed. Babylon’s hold on the merchants is not that she threatened them. It is that she made them rich.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues.”

The command is quoted from the prophets almost word for word. Jeremiah, of Babylon: Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD (Jer. 51:45; cf. 50:8). Isaiah, of the same city: Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing (Isa. 52:11). And Paul quoted that line to a church living in a Greek port (2 Cor. 6:17).

Two things need saying about what it does and does not mean, because it has been misused in both directions.

It cannot mean physical withdrawal, and the New Testament settles that. Christians stayed in Rome; Paul greeted a congregation there and told them to pay their taxes. Jesus prayed explicitly I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told the Corinthians that avoiding immoral people altogether would require leaving the world entirely (1 Cor. 5:9–10). Whatever coming out of Babylon is, it is not emigration, and it is not a compound in the hills.

And the verse itself says what it is, twice, in two parallel clauses: lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues. It is non-participation. A Christian lives in the city, works in it, pays for it and prays for it — and does not join in what it does, and does not want what it wants.

Which is far harder than moving house, and far more searching. Nobody has to decide whether to leave a country. Everybody has to decide, repeatedly and in small installments, whether to make the arrangement that everyone makes: the invoice adjusted, the thing not mentioned, the standard that quietly relaxes because it is costing too much. Coming out of Babylon happens on Tuesday afternoons, and nobody photographs it.

And the reason given is the second clause, which is a warning rather than a threat: lest you share in her plagues. Sharing the sins means sharing the judgment. When a system falls, the people who were profiting from it fall with it, and they do not get a separate hearing on the grounds that they were only doing what everyone did.

For her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.

The image is a tower — sins stacked up until they reach the sky — and it takes the reader straight back to where Babylon began, at a tower whose builders said let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens (Gen. 11:4). She always did want to reach heaven. She has managed it at last, and it is her record that arrived.

And God has remembered, as at 16:19. In Scripture that never means something had slipped his mind. It is the language of a file coming to the top of the pile, and of a God who is about to act on what he has known all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.

Two things about that sentence. The addressees are not named — the imperatives are plural and unattributed — and the reader should not assume they are the church, because 17:16 has already said who actually destroys Babylon, and it is the beast and the ten kings. Whoever is being commanded, no Christian in this book ever repays anybody.

And double raises a fair question about justice. If the punishment is twice the crime, is it just?
