20.title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
20.overview:
Chapter 20 contains the most debated passage in the most debated book of the Bible: the millennium. The thousand-year reign of Christ with his saints (vv. 1–6) has divided serious, Scripture-loving Christians for two thousand years and continues to do so. The amillennial position is followed here as the Reformed mainstream, with all four major views presented with genuine respect and fairness. The stakes in this debate are high — but the non-negotiables that all four views share are higher: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the wicked will be judged, the righteous will be glorified, and God will be all in all.

The Four Positions — Stated Fairly: Dispensational Premillennialism (MacArthur, Walvoord, Ryrie, Swindoll): After the pre-tribulation Rapture and the seven-year tribulation, Christ returns bodily to earth and establishes a literal thousand-year kingdom centred in Jerusalem, with a rebuilt temple and a restored national Israel fulfilling the Old Testament covenants. Satan is literally bound in the abyss. The martyred saints and tribulation believers are resurrected to reign with Christ. At the end of the millennium, Satan is released, defeated, and cast into the lake of fire. Then the Great White Throne judgment and the eternal state. Historic Premillennialism (Ladd, Grudem): Similar to dispensational, but without the pre-trib Rapture — the church goes through the tribulation. Christ returns, binds Satan, raises the martyrs (the first resurrection), and reigns on earth for a literal thousand years. Postmillennialism (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, Warfield in some respects): The thousand years represents the gospel era of expanding Christian influence, gradually Christianising the world through the preaching of the gospel, before Christ returns to a world largely won for the kingdom. The binding of Satan is the progressive restriction of his power through the gospel. Amillennialism (Augustine, Calvin, Vos, Berkhof, Hoekema, Beale — the position followed here): The thousand years is the entire period between the first and second comings of Christ — the church age. The binding of Satan (vv. 1–3) was accomplished at the cross (John 12:31; Colossians 2:15; Luke 10:18) and restricts his ability to deceive the nations so the gospel can go to all peoples. The first resurrection (vv. 4–6) is the spiritual resurrection of souls reigning with Christ in heaven now, or the new birth through which believers participate in Christ’s resurrection life. The thousand years is a symbolic number (10 x 10 x 10 = complete fullness) for the complete church age. Satan’s release at the end (vv. 7–9) represents the brief intensification of opposition immediately before Christ’s return. The Great White Throne (vv. 11–15) is the final universal judgment of all the dead.

The chapter divides into two sections: the millennium and Satan’s career (vv. 1–10) and the Great White Throne (vv. 11–15). Both sections are eschatologically essential and both are theologically clear on the matters that count: no one escapes the final judgment, no name not written in the book of life survives it, and the last enemies — Death and Hades themselves — are thrown into the lake of fire. Whatever one believes about the millennium, these outcomes are certain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: one angel with a key and a chain seizes, binds, throws, shuts and seals the dragon — named with the four names of 12:9 — for a thousand years, and the binding is given a stated purpose: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer. After that he must be released for a little while, using the word of divine necessity.

Verse 4: thrones, with authority to judge committed to those on them; the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and those who had not worshipped the beast or taken its mark; they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Verses 5–6: the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Then the fifth beatitude: Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him.

Verses 7–8: Satan is released, deceives the nations at the four corners of the earth — Gog and Magog (Ezek. 38–39) — and gathers a host like the sand of the sea. Verses 9–10: they surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, fire comes down and consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Thousand Years

An angel binds the dragon so that he may no longer deceive the nations; those who refused the beast reign with Christ; and after a brief release Satan’s last host is consumed and he is thrown into the lake of fire. Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers differ on the timing, and agree on all that the creeds require.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people the world beheaded and shut out of the market are seen on thrones.

Now: Over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power — on that there is no dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.

Before a word is said about the thousand years, three things in these verses should be noticed, because they are agreed by everybody and they are easy to lose in the argument.

First, the arrest is effortless. One angel, one chain, and five verbs done to the dragon: seized… bound… threw… shut and sealed. This is the creature who had seven heads and ten diadems, who gave the beast its throne, who made war on the woman and on the rest of her offspring, and who deceived the whole world. He is handled by a single unnamed angel with a set of keys. Nobody in this chapter has to fight him.

Second, the four names are the ones from 12:9, in the same order: the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, Satan. John is deliberately reaching back to the fall — the serpent in the garden — and closing the file that was opened in Genesis 3.

Third, and this is the verse that decides the whole chapter, the binding is given a stated purpose. Not so that he could do nothing. The text says: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. Whatever the binding is, John defines it himself, and it is specific.

Now the thousand years, which is the most argued-over paragraph in Scripture. The phrase occurs six times in six verses, and this is the only place in Scripture that speaks of a thousand-year reign. Godly readers have understood it in three main ways, and all three deserve to be set out with what genuinely favours each, rather than one asserted and the others waved at.

The premillennial reading takes the chapter in the order it is written. Christ returns at the end of chapter 19; then Satan is bound; then Christ reigns on the earth for a thousand years; then Satan is released, the last rebellion is crushed, and the final judgment follows. Two forms of it are held. Historic premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) has the church go through the tribulation before Christ returns. Dispensational premillennialism (Walvoord, Ryrie, MacArthur, and the Scofield tradition) adds a rapture of the church before a seven-year tribulation and understands the millennium as the period in which God’s promises to national Israel are fulfilled.

What favours it is considerable and should not be minimised. The narrative flows straight on from chapter 19 with then I saw, which is how John marks sequence everywhere else. The Old Testament promises of a messianic kingdom on the earth — a wolf lying down with a lamb, a child playing over a snake’s hole, a man building a house and living in it (Isa. 11:6–9; 65:20–25) — are given somewhere to land. And the strongest argument is at verse 5, where the same verb used of the martyrs coming to life is used of the rest of the dead, whom everyone agrees are raised bodily. The same word twice in two verses ought to mean the same thing.

The amillennial reading takes the thousand years as the whole period between the first and second comings — the age the church is in now. On this view Satan was bound at the cross, in exactly the sense verse 3 specifies: he can no longer keep the nations in the dark. The reign of the saints is their reign with Christ in heaven, which is why verse 4 says John saw souls. Christ returns once, at the end, and there is one resurrection and one judgment. This is the position of Augustine, the Reformers broadly, Hendriksen, Beale and Vos, and it is the position followed here.

What favours it is also considerable. Numbers in this book are symbolic throughout, and a thousand is ten cubed — completeness raised to its highest power. The chapter never says Christ is on the earth during these years, and never mentions his physical presence at all. And Jesus described his own ministry in exactly this image: how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? (Matt. 12:29). He said on the eve of the cross, now will the ruler of this world be cast out, and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (John 12:31–32) — a binding, and then the nations coming in. Before Christ, God had one nation; since Christ, the gospel has reached every continent, which is precisely what a dragon prevented from deceiving the nations would look like.

The postmillennial reading holds that the gospel will succeed so widely that a long era of Christianised civilisation follows, and that Christ returns at the end of it. It was held by Jonathan Edwards and Charles Hodge, and today by writers such as Kenneth Gentry. What favours it is the trajectory of Jesus’ own parables — a mustard seed becoming the largest of garden plants, leaven working through the whole lump (Matt. 13:31–33) — along with Psalm 2, Psalm 72, Isaiah 2:2–4, the sheer scope of the Great Commission, and Paul’s statement that Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Cor. 15:25). Its difficulty is the New Testament’s equally consistent expectation of apostasy and tribulation before the end (Matt. 24:9–13; 2 Tim. 3:1–5) and the final deception described in this very chapter.

Now the honest part, and it matters more than the schemes. All three hold everything that the creeds require, and they agree on far more than they dispute. Every one of them affirms that Christ has decisively defeated Satan; that he will return bodily, visibly and personally; that the dead will be raised; that there will be a final judgment; that the wicked will be condemned and the redeemed will live in a new creation; and that the church’s duty now is faithfulness under pressure. The disagreement is about the timing and sequence of things all three are certain will happen.

Which means a Christian may hold any of the three and be entirely orthodox, and that the correct response to a brother who reads it differently is not suspicion. Some of the most godly men who have ever lived have been on each side of this, and none of them was able to convince the others.

How can Satan be bound if he still prowls like a roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8) and blinds unbelievers (2 Cor 4:4)? The binding is specific: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer. Before Christ came, the nations were held in darkness; now the gospel goes to every nation, and Satan cannot stop it. Jesus spoke of binding the strong man so that his house could be plundered (Matt 12:29). A dog on a chain is still dangerous to anyone who comes within reach, but it cannot stop the house being plundered.

But does Then I saw mean that this follows chapter 19 in time? Then I saw marks the order of John’s visions, not always the order of events; the seals, trumpets and bowls each reach the end, and chapter 12 goes back to Christ’s birth. And why release Satan for a little while? To show the unchanged hatred of the unrepentant world toward God, and to make the justice of the final judgment plain to all.

And the last clause of verse 3 belongs to all three readings equally: After that he must be released for a little while. Even the release is on a permission and has a term. The word is dei, the divine must that has governed this book since 1:1. Nothing the dragon does, including his final rampage, is outside the timetable.
verseByVerse.note: The thousand years (the millennium) is read in three main ways: Christ’s present reign from heaven through the church age (amillennial); a future reign on earth after his return (premillennial); or a golden age of gospel success before his return (postmillennial).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed.

Thrones, plural, and John does not say who is on them. The promise made to Laodicea was I will grant him to sit with me on my throne (3:21), and Jesus told the Twelve they would sit on thrones judging the tribes of Israel (Matt. 19:28), and Paul asked the Corinthians, apparently expecting them to know, do you not know that the saints will judge the world? (1 Cor. 6:2).

Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands.

Two groups, or one group described twice? The Greek allows either, and it may well be one company seen from two sides: those who died for refusing, and those who lived without yielding. If so, the reign belongs to everyone who did not take the mark, not to a sub-class of martyrs.

Beheaded is a specific word — execution by the axe, the Roman method for a citizen, and the death Paul is said to have died. John does not say killed. He says how.

And there is a phrase here the reader has met before, in the negative: had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. Chapter 13 said nobody could buy or sell without it. These people could not buy or sell, and here they are on thrones.

They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

Everything turns on that verb. The Greek is ezēsan, and it means simply they lived or they came to life.

The premillennial reading takes it as bodily resurrection, and the argument from verse 5 is the strongest single argument in this whole debate: the identical verb is used one sentence later of the rest of the dead, who did not come to life until the thousand years were ended — and nobody disputes that their coming to life is bodily. A word ought to mean the same thing twice in two verses.

The amillennial reading answers that John has told us what he saw, and it was souls — the same word he used of the martyrs under the altar in 6:9, who were conscious, speaking and awaiting the resurrection. On this view the coming to life is what happens to a believer at death: the soul goes to be with Christ, which Paul calls far better (Phil. 1:23), and reigns with him. Some amillennial readers instead take it of the new birth — God made us alive together with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Eph. 2:5–6), and Jesus said the hour is coming and is now here when the dead will hear his voice and live (John 5:25).

Both readings are held by people who take every word of Scripture seriously, and the verb will genuinely bear either. What should not be lost in the argument is what the verse is for, and on that there is no dispute at all.

Look at who is reigning. Not one of them held any office. They were beheaded, boycotted, shut out of the market, unable to buy bread, tried in courts that found against them and buried by people who were afraid to say why. The world’s verdict on them was delivered and recorded and is still on file. And John sees them on thrones, with the authority to judge committed to them, reigning with Christ.

That is what this verse is doing in this book, and it is the same thing the whole book has been doing since chapter 1. It reverses the verdict. Whatever a reader concludes about the thousand years, he is being told that the people the world disposed of are the people who are on the thrones, and that the arrangement is already in force.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection.

One sentence, and it carries the weight of the argument set out at verse 4. On the premillennial reading the parallel is decisive: two groups, two comings-to-life, a thousand years apart, and the same verb for both. On the amillennial reading John distinguishes them by naming only one of them the first resurrection, and by reserving for the other the plainest possible statement that it happens at the end.

And there is a feature of John’s vocabulary in this very passage that bears on it. He speaks of a second death in the next verse and again at verse 14, and the second death is manifestly not a death of the same kind as the first — the first is a body in a grave, the second is a lake of fire. If second death can name something of a different order from the first death, then first resurrection may name something of a different order from the second. That is the amillennial answer, and it is a real one; a premillennial reader will reply that the parallel with verse 5 is closer than the parallel with the deaths. The reader should weigh both.

Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection!

The fifth of the book’s seven beatitudes, and the only one that adds a second adjective. Not merely blessed — blessed and holy, set apart, belonging to God.

Three things are said about this person, and they should be taken one at a time because they are among the great promises of Scripture.

Over such the second death has no power. Not they will probably escape it and not they will be forgiven at the assize. It has no authority over them — the word is exousia, the legal term. The second death has no jurisdiction. It cannot bring a case. Smyrna was promised this in almost the same words: the one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death (2:11).

And that is the answer to the deepest fear underneath everything in this chapter. A Christian may reasonably be uncertain about the timing of the millennium; he may not reasonably be uncertain about this. Whatever is coming at the great white throne, one category of person is outside its reach altogether, and the reason is not their record. It is that their names are in a book that belongs to a Lamb who was slain.

But they will be priests of God and of Christ. The promise of 1:6 and 5:10, arriving. A priest has access, offers, and carries other people’s names into the presence of God. That is what these people will be doing — not standing about being rewarded, but serving in the nearest place there is.

And they will reign with him for a thousand years. The reign is with him, which is the qualifier that keeps it from being a fantasy of vindication. Nobody in this chapter reigns on his own account or over his own patch. Whatever the thousand years turn out to be, the whole substance of them is being where he is and doing what he does.

What is the first resurrection? Premillennial Christians take it as the bodily resurrection of believers before a literal thousand-year reign. But John sees the souls of the martyrs (v. 4), and the rest of the New Testament speaks of one resurrection of the righteous and the wicked at the last day (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15). The more likely reading is that the first resurrection is the life of believers who have died, reigning with Christ now in heaven, matching the new birth by which they first came to life; the second resurrection is the bodily one at the end. Over those who share the first, the second death has no power. And the thousand years is a symbolic number for the whole, complete age between Christ’s comings.

And note the two offices together: priests and reign. That is the combination Israel was promised at Sinai and never managed — a kingdom of priests (Ex. 19:6) — and it is held in one person only, the one who is both King of kings and the Lamb who was slaughtered. His people get both because they are with him.
verseByVerse.note: The fifth of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.

He is released — the passive again, and 20:3 has already said he must be, using the word of divine necessity. Even the last rebellion is on a licence issued from the throne.

And he does exactly what he was bound to prevent him doing: he goes out to deceive the nations. The verb is the one that has defined him since 12:9, where he was named the deceiver of the whole world. Nothing has been learned, nothing has changed, and after a thousand years in a sealed pit the first thing he does is start talking.

That should be said plainly, because it settles a question people ask about the devil’s end. He does not repent, negotiate or reconsider. Evil in this book has no capacity for development; it only ever repeats itself with a larger audience.

Gog and Magog. The names come from Ezekiel 38 and 39, where Gog of the land of Magog gathers a coalition from the far north and comes up against a people living securely in an unwalled land, and is destroyed by fire from heaven (Ezek. 38:22; 39:6). John compresses two entire chapters of Ezekiel into two words and expects them to be recognised.

And he uses them the way he has used every other name in this book — as a type rather than an address. Babylon was not Babylon; Sodom and Egypt were not Sodom and Egypt; here Gog and Magog is not a country but the last coalition of everything opposed to God. The clue is that these nations are at the four corners of the earth, which is not a place either.

Their number is like the sand of the sea. An uncountable multitude — and the phrase is one of the most loaded in the Old Testament, because it is the promise God made to Abraham about his offspring: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen. 22:17).

The enemy assembles a counterfeit of Abraham’s promise. That is the last thing the dragon does in Scripture, and it is what he has done at every stage: a beast who parodies the Lamb’s resurrection, a false prophet with lamb’s horns, a mark answering a seal, a prostitute answering a bride, and now a countless host answering the countless family promised to a childless man standing outside his tent at night.

And a Christian looking at the numbers is being told something he needs at the end of this book as much as at the beginning. The last enemy army is uncountable, and the multitude before the throne in chapter 7 was also one that no one could number. Two uncountable crowds. Only one of them is real, and the other one is about to be described in a single verse.
verseByVerse.note: Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel’s vision of a last great attack on God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them.

Two images for the people of God in one clause, and they should be separated. The camp of the saints is Israel in the wilderness — tents, no walls, a people on the move, defended by nothing but the presence in the middle of them. The beloved city is Jerusalem, Zion, the city God loves (Ps. 78:68; 87:2). Pilgrim camp and settled city, held together, which is what the church always is.

And they are surrounded. Not attacked at a point — encircled, on every side, by a host like the sand of the sea. If John had wanted to describe a hopeless military position he could not have done it more completely.

Then: but fire came down from heaven and consumed them. That is the battle. One clause, no engagement, and the saints do not lift a hand — exactly as in chapter 19, where the armies of heaven rode out in wedding linen and struck no blow.

The image is Ezekiel 39:6 again, and behind it Sodom, and behind that Elijah on Carmel. And it is the one thing James and John once asked permission to call down on a Samaritan village, and were rebuked for it (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is real and it is not the church’s to call.

Which is the whole posture this book has been teaching for twenty chapters. The saints are surrounded and do nothing. They have no weapons, no strategy and no plan of breakout, and they are not rebuked for the lack of one. What they are asked for, from the first letter to the last battle, is endurance and faith — and then the sky opens over the heads of the people who came to finish them.

And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

The unholy trinity is complete and together for the last time. The beast and false prophet went in at 19:20, and here is the third. And John notes, with no comment at all, that they are still there — the lake of fire is not a momentary end. The lake of fire is not an incinerator.

And the dragon is described one last time by what he does rather than what he is: the devil who had deceived them. That is his epitaph. Not the great red dragon with seven diadems, not the accuser of the brothers, not the prince of the power of the air — the one who told lies, thrown into a lake, in the passive voice, by somebody the verse does not bother to name.

Is this the same battle as 19:19–21? The more likely reading is yes: both draw on Ezekiel 38–39, both gather the nations for battle, and both end at once with God’s judgment. Premillennial Christians see two battles a thousand years apart. And it is not a literal siege of Jerusalem but the world’s final assault on the camp of the saints and the beloved city, God’s people wherever they are.

Does this teach that punishment is conscious and unending, and does it apply to lost people as well as the devil? Forever and ever is the strongest phrase for duration in the New Testament, and the lost share the same lake of fire (v. 15; 14:11; Matt 25:41, 46). Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, and that the torment is only for the devil and his agents. But Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life (Matt 25:46). The more likely reading is that the punishment of the lost, like that of the devil, is conscious and without end.

So the serpent that spoke in a garden in Genesis 3 has said his last word here. He was cast out of heaven at the cross, thrown down to the earth, given a short time, bound in a pit, released for a little while, and is now finished. And the head that was promised to be bruised (Gen. 3:15) is under the heel of the child the dragon stood waiting to devour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 11: a great white throne, and one seated on it whom John does not describe — as he refused to describe the one on the throne in chapter 4. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

Verse 12: the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done (cf. Dan. 7:10).

Verse 13: the sea gives up its dead, and Death and Hades give up theirs, and they were judged, each one of them. Verse 14: Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. Verse 15: And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judged by Works, Saved by a Name

Before the great white throne earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and anyone whose name is not found in the book of life follows them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the sea gives up its dead; nobody is missing, and each is judged by name.

Now: The question is not whether you have done enough, but whether your name is in the Lamb’s book — and the water of life is offered without price.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

The book has been full of thrones since chapter 4 — the throne, twenty-four thrones, the throne of the beast, the thrones of verse 4. This is the last one, and it is described with two adjectives. Great, so that its size settles who is in charge. White, which in this book is the colour of purity and of verdicts: white robes, white linen, white horses.

John does not say who is seated on it, exactly as he refused to describe the one on the throne in chapter 4. He says instead what happens in his presence: earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

Stay with that for a moment, because it is the most quietly terrifying sentence in the chapter. Nothing is said to be destroyed. The universe simply cannot remain in the room. The ground under a reader’s feet and the sky over his head — the two things that have always been there, the definition of what is permanent — get up and leave, and there is nowhere for them to go.

Which means the last judgment has no scenery. Every human court sits somewhere: a room, a building, a country whose laws apply. This one has no location, because the location has gone. There is nothing in the frame but a throne, the one seated on it, and the people standing.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne.

Great and small for the last time in this book, and it flattens the last hierarchy there is. Emperors and slaves, the men whose statues filled the forum and the women whose names were never written down anywhere, standing on the same floor. Nobody is represented by counsel and nobody has a better seat.

And books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.

Books, plural, and then a book, singular, and the distinction is the gospel. Daniel saw the same scene: the Ancient of Days took his seat, the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened (Dan. 7:10).

The books contain the record — what they had done. Nothing is missing from them; Jesus said every careless word would be accounted for (Matt. 12:36). And that record is the standard by which the dead are judged, which raises the question a Christian reader must have answered rather than hurried past: if salvation is by grace through faith, how can anyone be judged according to what they had done?

The answer is in the second book, and in the order the two are opened. The New Testament holds both without flinching: nobody is justified by works of the law (Gal. 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done (Rom. 2:6; 2 Cor. 5:10). They are not in tension once it is clear what each is answering. The books of deeds establish the case, and the case is unanswerable; every person standing there is guilty on the record. The book of life is not a second, better record of the same kind. It is a register of names, and verse 15 says it is the only thing that decides anything.

Do believers stand before this throne? All the dead stand there, great and small. For believers, the book of life decides: their names are written, and they are acquitted in Christ, while their works are reviewed for reward (2 Cor 5:10). Premillennial Christians often distinguish a judgment of believers from this one; the more likely reading is that there is one final judgment, where the book of life separates the saved from the lost.

A man is not saved because his file is thin. He is saved because his name is in a book that belongs to the Lamb who was slain (13:8), and the entries were made from the foundation of the world. The deeds are real, and they are read, and they matter — and they are not the thing that gets anyone through.

verseByVerse.quote: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done.

Three custodians, and every one of them hands over what it was holding. The sea is named separately for a reason that any first-century reader would have felt immediately: to be lost at sea was to have no grave, no body, no name on a stone — the most complete disappearance available. The chapter says the sea gives them up.

Nobody is missing. That is the point of listing three, and it reaches every category of the forgotten: the man whose ship went down, the woman in an unmarked grave, the child in a plague pit, the person whose family died out and whose name nobody has said aloud for eight hundred years. Death and Hades kept their records perfectly and hand over the whole file.

Each one of them. John will not let it be a mass. In a scene involving every human being who has ever lived, the judgment is individual — one at a time, on the evidence, by name.

Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire.

The two figures who rode out at the fourth seal (6:8), the reaper and the cart. The risen Christ said in the first chapter of this book, I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18), and this is what he does with them. They are not merely disarmed; they are executed. Paul said it in a sentence: the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26), and the prophet before him, he will swallow up death forever (Isa. 25:8).

Take that as concretely as it deserves. Death is not going to be managed, or explained, or made bearable. It is going to be killed. Everything a reader has lost to it — the funerals attended, the diagnosis that came back, the phone call at four in the morning — was inflicted by something that is itself going to be thrown into a lake and will not be coming back.

This is the second death, the lake of fire. John defines his own term, as he has all through the book. The promise made to Smyrna — the one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death (2:11) — and repeated at 20:6 now has its definition attached, and it is the last thing a reader will want to be uncertain about.

And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.

One sentence, and it is the last word of the chapter. Notice that it is stated negatively — not whoever was found but if anyone’s name was not. And notice the verb again: found. Somebody looked. The same word was used of the blood in Babylon’s foundations (18:24), and it is used here of a search through a register.

This is the sentence that makes Revelation what it is, and it should not be blunted. The book has spent twenty chapters saying that there are two companies and two destinations and that everyone is in one of them, and here the criterion is stated in a single sentence. Not achievement, not sincerity, not how a person compares with his neighbour. A name, in a book, belonging to the Lamb.

And that is either the most frightening sentence in Scripture or the most reassuring one, depending on a single question, which every reader is now in a position to ask and which the book will answer directly in two chapters’ time. It is not have I done enough? Nobody standing at that throne has. It is whether a person has come to the one who says, two chapters later, let the one who desires take the water of life without price (22:17).

The books are opened and the record is read and it is accurate. And there is a second book, and it is not a better record. It is a list of people the Lamb bought with his own blood, written before the world was made, and nothing in the first set of books can get a name off it.
